comments.content: Cell text uses `InnerText` while paragraphs use selective `ParaText`. `InnerText` includes text from SDT content controls, field codes (w:instrText is actually excluded by InnerText but w:fldSimple text is included), nested hyperlinks, etc. that `ParaText` deliberately skips. The fallback `origFile` can therefore disagree with `origModel` lines for any cell containing hyperlinks or content controls, misaligning LCS paragraph matching and producing spurious whole-paragraph replaces. Use `CellText` (already defined in this file) for parity with the in-place flow.

When anchor is a Table element (RowUnit case in `AnchorOf`), `anchorPara` resolves to null because `anchor as Paragraph` is null and `anchor.Ancestors<Paragraph>().FirstOrDefault()` returns null (a Table's ancestors are Body/Document, not Paragraph). Consequently the cloned `pPr` and the source `rPr` are never assigned, so every paragraph inserted after a table inherits default Normal formatting instead of inheriting from the table's row paragraph context. Either special-case the Table anchor to use the last paragraph of the last row, or accept a separate "style donor" parameter.

When `newText.Split(" | ").Length != cells.Count`, the row is only marked-deleted (each cell paragraph gets `w:del`) but the `<w:tr>` stays in the table, and a new free paragraph is then appended after the table. The result is a half-deleted table row with crossed-out cells alongside an unrelated paragraph below the table — the table layout is broken and the new content is outside the table. Either remove the row from the table (after marking its content deleted, insert a `w:trPr` with `<w:del>` author/id), or insert the replacement as a new row inside the same table.

The fresh-document generation path has no exception guard. Unlike the in-place path (which has try/catch and falls back), a mid-construction failure in `WordprocessingDocument.Create` / body / styles / paragraph append leaves `outPath` as a partially-written or corrupt `.docx`, then the program prints "已生成（修订模式...）" and returns 0 — caller cannot tell the document is broken. Wrap the whole fresh-doc block in try/catch; on failure, delete the partial file and surface a non-zero exit / clear error.

The title paragraph uses `ParagraphStyleId { Val = "Heading1" }` but the styles part only defines the `Normal` style. Word silently falls back to Normal for an unknown style id, so title-level pPr properties (spacing, keep-with-next, outline level) don't take effect even though inline `RunProperties` still apply the 黑体/16pt visuals. Either define a `Heading1` style in the styles part, or drop the `ParagraphStyleId` and rely on the inline rPr (matching the rest of the fresh doc).

`.nm-card-hover:hover` adds `transform 0.2s ease` to its `transition` declaration, but the base `.nm-card, .nm-card-hover` block (above) only transitions `background-color` and `box-shadow`. Result: mouse-enter animates the lift smoothly, but mouse-leave reverts `transform` instantly while `box-shadow` still fades — visually jarring asymmetric animation. Add `transform 0.2s ease` to the base transition so the reverse run is also smooth.

`.md-body li br { display: none }` hides **every** `
` inside list items, not only the trailing newline that `remark-breaks` injects between items. Legitimate multi-line content inside a list item (a deliberately wrapped line, an inline image with caption on next line, etc.) is silently dropped. Target only the remark-breaks-injected BR — e.g. scope to BRs that immediately precede another `
  • ` or use a class added by your markdown pipeline — instead of nuking all of them. The in-code comment already acknowledges this is a tradeoff; the risk is real correctness regressions in non-trivial Markdown replies.

Accessibility: this stylesheet defines 0.28s theme color transitions, 0.15–0.2s box-shadow transitions on every `.nm-*` component, and a `transform: translateY/scale` on `.nm-card-hover:hover`, yet provides **no** `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` override. Users with vestibular disorders / motion sensitivity (and anyone on Windows “Show animations” = off) cannot opt out. Add a reduced-motion block that collapses all transitions and disables the hover transform.

Hover transform lacks a compositor hint. `.nm-card-hover:hover` applies `transform: translateY(-3px) scale(1.01)` but does not set `will-change: transform` (either persistently or at least on hover). Without this hint the layer may not be promoted to its own compositor layer, forcing paint on every frame. Given the task board can render many cards simultaneously in the WebView2 host, add `will-change: transform` (or rely on transform-only animation but be aware of layer explosion).

Animating a multi-layer box-shadow on every themed component is a known GPU-unfriendly pattern. The base rule for `.nm-card, .nm-card-hover` (and `.nm-btn`, `.nm-outset`, `.nm-inset`) declares `transition: ..., box-shadow 0.2s ease` while the shadow is composed of 3 layered shadows (one inset + two outset) — interpolating multi-shadow values is expensive and not always GPU-accelerated. On a task board with many cards this can cause noticeable jank, especially in Electron/WebView2 on lower-end hardware. Consider transitioning only an opacity wrapper (e.g. animate `opacity` of an absolutely-positioned pseudo-element that holds the shadow) or shorten/remove the box-shadow transition.

The pre-paint theme script samples `prefers-color-scheme` once at load time but never subscribes to changes. When the user picks "system", an OS dark/light toggle after page load (or a schedule-based switch on macOS/Windows) leaves the React app out of sync until a hard reload — directly undermining the stated "避免闪屏" goal at runtime. Use a `matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').addEventListener('change', ...)` listener (and re-evaluate the persisted `t` value) so the documentElement class follows the OS in real time.

The localStorage key `"wmessage-theme"` and its allowed values (`"dark"`, `"system"`, implicitly `"light"`) are duplicated as magic strings here and presumably elsewhere in the React layer. Any drift between the two copies silently falls back to light mode. Centralize the key and value constants (e.g., a shared module imported by the runtime theme manager and inlined here via a Vite `define` / build-time substitution) so the contract is enforced from one place.

comments.content: The file uses ESM `export default` syntax in a `.js` file. This works with Tailwind v3.3+ only when `package.json` has `"type": "module"` (or the file is renamed `.mjs` / paired with a `.cjs` setup). If `package.json` is missing `"type": "module"`, Node will throw `SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'export'` and Tailwind will fail to load the config silently (often manifesting as no utility classes being generated). Verify the project's module type matches this config's syntax.

comments.content: The `$HOME/**` glob grants the opener permission reach over the entire user home directory, including highly sensitive paths such as `~/.ssh/`, browser profile stores, credential caches, keychain files, and `.gnupg/`. This violates least-privilege and turns any XSS/dependency compromise into a full data-exfiltration vector. Restrict it to the specific subdirectories the application actually needs (e.g. `$HOME/Documents/<app>/**`) or drop it entirely if not required.

`$APPDATA/**` recursively exposes the application-data directory of every program installed on the user's machine, not just this app's own data. Scope it to the app's own bundle identifier directory (e.g. `$APPDATA/com.yourcompany.yourapp/**`) to avoid granting blanket read access to other applications' state.

Both `main` and `widget` windows are bound to the same capability set, so the widget window inherits window-manipulation rights (`set-position`, `set-size`, `always-on-top`, `set-focus`, `start-dragging`, monitor queries) that are almost certainly inappropriate for a small always-visible widget surface and could let widget-side code (or any untrusted content rendered there) reposition, resize, or steal focus from the main window. Split the widget into a separate capability file (e.g. `widget.json`) with a minimal permission set.

comments.content: Fragile regex parsing of Cargo.toml: `^\[package\]` is not anchored on the closing `]` boundary, so it also matches section headers that begin with `[package` such as `[package.metadata.bundle]`, `[package.metadata.foo]`, etc. Because `[^[]*?` is lazy and greedy-walks to the first `^version` it encounters, the regex can capture a nested `version` (e.g. the bundle identifier) instead of the real `[package] version`, silently writing the wrong version into package.json. Suggest tightening the header match (e.g. `^\[package\](?:\r?\n|$)`) or, preferably, using a real TOML parser such as `@iarna/toml`.

comments.content: Missing error handling around file I/O and JSON parsing: `readFileSync` and `JSON.parse` are called without a `try/catch`. A missing `src-tauri/Cargo.toml`, an unreadable `package.json`, or a syntactically broken `package.json` will surface as a raw stack trace rather than a friendly `[sync-version]` message with a non-zero exit code, which is unhelpful for a prebuild hook that developers run frequently. Wrap the file/JSON operations and emit a clear diagnostic before exiting.

Non-atomic write to `package.json`: `writeFileSync` truncates and rewrites the file in place. If the process is interrupted mid-write (Ctrl+C, SIGTERM, power loss, OOM kill) or the disk fills up, `package.json` is left truncated/corrupted and the project's package metadata is destroyed with no backup or recovery path. Use a write-to-temp + rename pattern so the update is atomic on POSIX/NTFS.

comments.content: The three `emit` regexes together miss the Tauri 2.x trait-method call pattern `tauri::Emitter::emit(&handle, "event", payload)` (no leading dot, and the first argument is a borrow/receiver, not the event string). The first regex requires `\.emit\(` (no match without the dot), and the third requires `emit\(\s*"` (no match when `&handle, ` sits between `(` and `"`). Result: backend events emitted via this pattern are absent from `emitted_events()`, so `test_listened_events_have_emitter` will falsely FAIL for events that are perfectly listened to on the frontend. Add a pattern that accepts an arbitrary receiver argument list before the event string, e.g. `r'(?<![\w.])emit\(\s*[^"]*?,\s*"([^"]+)"'`.

The standard NSPasteboard flow is to declare the type set first, then set each type's value, so all writes share a single change count. comments.content: TOCTOU race between read-to-string and write_token_file: if two processes/instances call this concurrently (e.g., user launches the app twice, or a background task fires during startup), both can observe no token, both generate a UUID, and the last writer silently overwrites the other. The check-then-act sequence is also not crash-safe — a process killed between `read_to_string` and `write_token_file` leaves no token but the next caller will (correctly) regenerate; the more dangerous window is two concurrent first-run callers generating different tokens where one is never seen by the server that already started with the other's value. Use an atomic create-new (`OpenOptions::create_new(true)`) and treat `AlreadyExists` as "another writer won, re-read" to make this race-free.

Token write opens via `truncate(true)` which follows symlinks, and `OpenOptionsExt::mode(0o600)` only takes effect when a NEW inode is created — i.e. it does NOT tighten permissions of an existing target file. Between `truncate` (file is now zero-length, still under old perms) and the explicit `tighten_token_permissions` call at the end, the bearer-equivalent secret sits on disk readable by any local user. `flags_dir` is normally under the Tauri-managed data directory so the symlink-attack surface is small, but defense-in-depth here is cheap: combine `create_new(true)` (refuse to follow an existing entry) with the explicit chmod, and use `O_NOFOLLOW` on unix to refuse symlinks at the token path entirely. Also note the empty-file race: if the process dies between `truncate` and `write_all`, the next `load_or_create_token` will see `s.is_empty()` and regenerate a token rather than preserving the previous one — minor consistency issue.

Silent error swallowing in flag persistence will cause runtime vs persisted state to diverge with no observable signal. `write_enabled_flag` silently does nothing when `create_dir_all` fails (e.g., permission denied, read-only volume), so a successful `api_start` can leave no flag and the next launch will not autostart. `clear_enabled_flag` silently swallows `remove_file` errors (e.g., permission denied, file busy), so `should_autostart` can return true after the user/API has been stopped, causing an unintended autostart on next launch. At minimum log a warning, and consider returning `Result<(), String>` so the caller in `commands.rs` can surface the failure (e.g., via `eprintln!` or the existing logging facility) — autostart state silently going wrong is the kind of bug users only discover weeks later.

`verify_bearer` is on the hot path of every authenticated request, yet it allocates a fresh `String` via `format!("Bearer {token}")` on every call even though the token is loaded once at startup and never changes. For a chatty local API (or any API once exposed beyond loopback) this is gratuitous per-request work. Pre-compute the expected prefix once into a `OnceLock<Vec<u8>>` / `OnceLock<String>` after `load_or_create_token`, or — even better — skip the allocation entirely by comparing against the raw header bytes (`starts_with(b"Bearer ")` then constant-time compare on the suffix), which also removes a future foot-gun if someone ever changes the token to variable length (a length-mismatch allocation timing channel). Note: the constant-time property of `ct_eq` itself is fine; this comment is purely about the avoidable per-request allocation.

`should_autostart` only checks that the flag file exists, not that its contents are valid (write_enabled_flag writes `b"1"`). A flag file left behind by a previous install/version with different content, a partially-written flag from a crashed `write_enabled_flag`, or any garbage file at the path will all cause autostart. Combined with the silent-write-failure in `write_enabled_flag`, an empty/zero-byte flag file (truncate completed, write failed) would still trigger autostart on next launch. Either read the file and check the contents equal `b"1"` (or any non-empty value), or have `write_enabled_flag` write atomically via `tempfile::NamedTempFile` + `persist` so partial writes can never appear.

Log sanitization is incomplete: the comment claims 'all control characters' are escaped, but only `\r`, `\n`, `\t`, `\0` are handled. Attacker-controlled request paths / query strings (see callers in handlers.rs:93) can still carry ANSI ESC (`\x1b`), BEL (`\x07`), backspace (`\x08`), DEL (`\x7f`), and C1 controls. That defeats the stated anti-injection defense and enables terminal escape / log forgery. Either iterate bytes once and replace every `c if c.is_control()` / `c < 0x20` / `c == 0x7f`, or use a vetted sanitization helper.

Concurrent `log_line` calls can tear log lines. Each caller independently opens the file with `O_APPEND` and writes via `writeln!`. POSIX only guarantees atomicity for writes `<= PIPE_BUF` (typically 4 KiB on Linux); each line here is well under that, but the `writeln!` macro expands to multiple `write_all` calls on the underlying `Write` adapter — once a `write` exceeds the internal buffer or the runtime decides to flush mid-line, two threads can interleave bytes and produce garbled audit records with mismatched timestamps / split lines. Serialize appends through a process-wide mutex around the open+write, or hold the file open and reuse a single `Mutex<File>` shared across calls.

TOCTOU between `rotate_log_if_large` and `OpenOptions::open`: rotation may rename/recreate the file, but the subsequent `open` re-resolves the original path without re-checking. Under contention, two callers can both observe "size OK, no rotation needed" and both append to the same pre-rotation fd; after rotation one of them may write to a path that was just moved away, silently losing entries or mixing old/new logs. Consider opening the file once (cached) under a process-wide mutex so rotation can re-open in the same critical section, as suggested in the rewrite above.

Silent I/O failure on both the open and the `writeln!` swallows audit events. The open uses `if let Ok(...)` and the write uses `let _ = writeln!(...)`, so disk-full, permission, or quota errors are dropped with no fallback. For an access/change audit log this is exactly the failure mode you cannot afford to swallow — at minimum log the error to stderr (or a dedicated fallback channel) so a monitoring agent can alert.

The doc comment promises the field is skipped to "避免泄露空串" (avoid leaking empty strings), but `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` only suppresses `None`. A caller that constructs `token: Some(String::new())` will still emit `"token": ""` to the UI/IPC boundary, contradicting the stated contract and giving downstream code no way to distinguish "no token configured" from "empty token". Use a custom predicate (e.g. `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none_or_empty"` via `String::is_empty`, or a small helper fn) so `Some("")` is also dropped, or normalize the value to `None` at the construction site.

`ApiStatus` permits inconsistent combinations that the struct itself does not enforce: `{ enabled: false, token: Some("...") }` will silently serialize the secret (violating "disabled 时为 None"), and `{ enabled: true, token: None }` is ambiguous between "no token configured" and "token hidden by policy". Either encode the rule in the type (e.g. a dedicated `enum ApiStatusState { Disabled, Enabled { token: Option<String> } }`, or make `token` a non-public field with a `new(enabled, port, token)` constructor that clamps `token` to `None` whenever `!enabled`), or drop the prose contract and document that callers are responsible for keeping the pair coherent.

comments.content: TOCTOU race between `service_present` recheck and `write_enabled_flag`. The recheck acquires `state.0` only briefly to sample `g.is_some()`, but the flag write happens later outside any lock. A concurrent `api_stop` that lands in the gap (between the recheck returning `Some(true)` and the `write_enabled_flag` syscall) can take the lock, run `api_stop_locked`, drop `g` to `None`, drop the guard, and call `clear_enabled_flag`; this thread then writes `api-enabled.flag`, leaving the on-disk flag "enabled" while the in-memory service is gone. Next launch will auto-restore a service the user explicitly stopped. The current comment ("写前重新抢锁复核") describes the intent but the recheck doesn't actually cover this window. Consider treating the enabled flag as state that must be written while holding the lock (e.g. update it inside `api_start_locked`), or use a generation/version counter so the flag write can be skipped if state changed.

Symmetric TOCTOU race in `api_status` between `service_present` and `clear_enabled_flag`. `service_present != Some(true)` only samples whether a concurrent `api_start` has *finished* populating `g`. A concurrent `api_start` that has taken the lock, run `api_start_locked`, dropped the guard, but not yet reached `write_enabled_flag` will still show `g.is_some() == true` — but the longer race is the inverse: if `service_present` returns `Some(false)` (no service yet) and then `api_start` fully runs (load token → lock → start_api_locked → drop → service_present→Some(true) → write flag), this thread's `clear_enabled_flag` runs *last* and wipes a freshly written flag for a freshly started service. The cleanup path and the start path are now racing on the flag file with no serialization. Same fix idea as the `api_start` flag write: hold the lock while touching the flag, or use a guarded compare-and-set on a state version.

`service_present` poison semantics are "conservative" only in the comment, not in the call sites. Returning `None` means "I cannot confirm"; the doc claims callers should be conservative, but both call sites treat `None` as the *write/clear* branch: `api_start` uses `!= Some(false)` so `None → write_enabled_flag`, and `api_status` uses `!= Some(true)` so `None → clear_enabled_flag`. Net effect: a single poisoning panic in any holder permanently drives the flag in opposite directions from these two paths, and the recovery heuristic is exactly backwards — when we *can't* see state, neither writing nor clearing the flag is justified. Either add a poisoned-recovery path (e.g. `.lock().unwrap_or_else(|p| p.into_inner())` after auditing the holder) or make both call sites treat `None` as "no-op" so the flag is only mutated when we positively observed the relevant state.

`start_api` is invoked while `state.0` is held by `api_start_locked`. The doc-comment "accept 线程不等 worker,持锁清理安全" is documenting an invariant that belongs to the `start_api` implementation in another module — this file cannot enforce it. If `start_api` ever does a blocking syscall that retries (port bind in TIME_WAIT, DNS, file sync of the persisted event-id file via `EventHub::persisted`), every concurrent `api_stop` / `api_status` / `api_rotate_token` serializes behind it, and worse, a panic inside `start_api` poisons `state.0` permanently (see previous finding). Please add an explicit contract check or move the `start_api` call out of the critical section — capture the new `RunningApi` outside the lock and assign `*g = Some(running)` under the lock in a separate brief critical section.

Speculative token file write creates a durable inconsistency window in `api_rotate_token`. `write_token_file(&path, &token)` runs *before* `rotate_apply`; if the process crashes (or `rotate_apply` panics, or even is cancelled by Tauri's command-cancel path) between the write and the in-memory restart, `api-token.txt` holds the new token while the live `RunningApi` is still bound to the old one — every subsequent restart will read the new token and fail authentication until the user manually rotates again. Phase 3 only rolls back on the explicit `Err` branch. Either (a) write the new token with `tempfile::NamedTempFile::persist` (atomic rename) and make the in-memory swap conditional on the rename succeeding, or (b) defer the on-disk write until after the in-memory swap, accepting that the token file lags by one restart on the happy path. The CAS guard `disk_is_ours` only protects against *concurrent* rotate, not crashes.

`api_rotate_token` Phase 3 comment "尽力用旧 token 恢复服务" contradicts the actual code: the recovery reads `authoritative` from disk *after* Phase 1's speculative write, so `tok` is the *new* token, not `old`. The longer comment block correctly explains "重读磁盘 token 作为权威值,不再用捕获的 old_token", but the short header comment is misleading. A reader skimming the file will think Phase 3 restores `old` and could decide to drop the on-disk read entirely — please reconcile the comments so they describe the same behavior.

`after_change` calls `store.notify_change` and writes the log line **before** invoking the user-supplied `emit_fn`. If the closure panics, observers (other SSE clients / dashboards) have already received a change notification that may then be left out of sync with the originating request, which fails before sending its response. Because `emit_fn` is `Fn` (no `Result`) there is also no way to propagate callback failures back to the caller. Consider wrapping `f(task)` in `AssertUnwindSafe` + `catch_unwind`, or changing the contract so the callback returns a `Result` and the broadcast happens after both the DB write and the callback succeed (or document the panic-safety contract explicitly).

Field-length caps are re-exported as `pub(crate) const API_MAX_* = crate::bot::MAX_*`. This creates a hidden, two-way coupling: any rename or removal in `crate::bot` breaks this file's compilation (since these are not `pub use` aliases but full `const` items), and any value change in `crate::bot::MAX_*` silently changes API validation limits used by handlers and tests — the comment "值对齐由定义处保证" asserts an invariant that the code itself does not enforce. Either mirror the values explicitly (and lose the "single source" benefit, but gain decoupling), or use `pub(crate) use crate::bot::{MAX_TITLE as API_MAX_TITLE, ...};` so the dependency is explicit at the alias site.

`now_ms()` silently collapses `duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)` failures to `0`. A pre-epoch or otherwise-broken system clock (NTP misconfig, VM clock skew, suspend issues) would produce zero-valued task timestamps with no diagnostic surfaced to the caller or the log. Either log a warning when the conversion fails (via `crate::api_handlers::util::internal_err`-style logging or `eprintln!`), or return a `Result<i64, SystemTimeError>` so callers can decide. Note that `as_millis() as i64` is also a `u128 -> i64` truncating cast — fine in practice for ~292k years, but worth a comment given the silent fallback path right above it.

Both `internal_err` and `upsert_err` discard the result of `req.respond(...)` with `let _ = ...`. When the response write itself fails (client disconnect mid-request, broken pipe, server shutdown), the failure is not logged anywhere — only the original DB error is captured in `api.log`. In production, this hides transport-layer problems (slow consumers, DoS, broken proxies) that would otherwise be visible in the same log stream. Either log the `tiny_http::Error` (and the request method/URL) when the respond fails, or thread a `Result<(), Error>` back to the caller so the handler can decide.

`CreateReq` / `UpdateReq` deserialize `file_path` as a raw `Option<String>` and `tags` as a raw `Option<Vec<String>>`, with **no validation at the type level** — only the `over_limit` length cap is available as a util. Path canonicalization, traversal protection (e.g. rejecting `..` segments or absolute paths outside an allowed root), per-tag length checks, and a tag-count cap (note `API_MAX_TAGS` exists but is never applied here) are pushed entirely to individual handlers. Any handler that forgets one of these checks admits attacker-controlled strings straight into filesystem / DB operations. Either add a typed `FilePath` / `Tags` newtype with validation in `try_from`/`deserialize_with`, or centralize the path/tags validation helpers next to `over_limit` so handlers cannot skip them.

comments.content: Writer thread has no write timeout: `stream.write_all(&data)` and `stream.flush()` are synchronous, and a slow/unresponsive peer (or a half-open TCP) can park the thread inside the syscall indefinitely. `stop_w` is only polled between writes, so `api_stop` (and `stop_sse_writers`) cannot actually halt a writer that's stuck on write — the 5 s `SSE_STOP_JOIN_TIMEOUT` will always trip, audit `sse_writer_leaked` will fire, and the handle is dropped (detached), but the OS thread keeps running and holding the old `rx`/`tx`. That defeats the "writer 必须纳入追踪" goal stated at the top of the file — the leak persists, only the JoinHandle goes away. Consider a write deadline (e.g. push the `stream` into a dedicated write thread fed by an `mpsc` whose recv has a timeout, or use `socket2`/`set_write_timeout` on the upgraded fd), or at minimum audit the `is_finished()==false` case with the elapsed time so the leak signal isn't lying about the cause.

Replay dedup assumes strictly-monotonic, never-reused event IDs from `event_hub`, but this contract is not enforced or even documented in this file. The race is acknowledged (clients.push happens before the replay snapshot, so events can appear in both history and the live channel), but if `hub.hub_id()` ever wraps, if a single id can be reassigned across hub generations, or if a producer emits two events with the same id in the same "burst" (e.g. broadcast fanout races), the `id <= last_sent` filter will silently drop the second one. Worse, the live branch uses `if id > last_sent { last_sent = id; }`, so an out-of-order live id that is *less than* `last_sent` is dropped without any audit — a real correctness bug. Suggest asserting monotonicity inside the hub (and/or having the writer emit `id:` lines in the SSE payload so the server side filter becomes self-checking) and adding an audit/log when an out-of-order live id is dropped.

The connected handshake carries `lastEventId` *inside the JSON payload* but does not emit an SSE `id:` field. Browser `EventSource` (and most SSE clients) track the reconnection cursor via the protocol-level `id:` line, not via JSON contents. As written, an `EventSource` reconnect will resume from id 0 (or whatever the default is), and the documented `?since=`断线重放 path will only work for hand-rolled clients that parse the JSON. Suggest emitting `id: {hub.last_id()}\n` (and using `hub.last_id()` as the next-event id on the *first* real event) so browser-native reconnect actually resumes correctly.

Per-client `sync_channel(256)` silently drops events under backpressure (the producer side will either block the broadcaster with `send` or fail silently with `try_send`), and there is no dropped-event counter, log line, or audit hook. The doc comment justifies this as "广播不阻塞", but in a hub-and-spoke topology a single slow SSE client shouldn't be able to make event loss invisible — at minimum a `let dropped = 0;` counter incremented in a `try_send` fallback (or a periodic "[sse_drop] client=N events=M" line) would let ops detect a wedged client without code changes elsewhere.

Sync trait methods implement `block_on` over async db fns — this relies entirely on the undocumented invariant that callers run on a plain std::thread (not a tokio runtime). If a future caller (or a callback inside `db::db_load`/`db::db_upsert`) ever invokes these from an async context, `block_on` will panic on a multi-threaded runtime or deadlock on a single-threaded one. The trait signature gives no compile-time safeguard. Consider making `load`/`upsert` `async` on the trait, or wrapping the sync entry-point with an explicit runtime check and a panic message that points to the call-site invariant.

`expected_updated_at` is typed as a timestamp but `BASELINE_NULL_ROW` overloads it to mean "row must not exist yet". This conflates optimistic-concurrency state with a domain timestamp value, is fragile (relies on the sentinel never colliding with a real timestamp), and the type system can't help — a typed `enum ExpectedRowState { NotExists, Matches(DateTime<Utc>) }` (or `Option<Option<DateTime>>`) would make the contract explicit and prevent accidental collisions.

`e.to_string()` flattens SQLite/diesel/sqlx errors to a `String` at the trait boundary, discarding structured information (error kind, source chain, location) that handlers and logs need to distinguish unique-constraint violations from I/O failures from lock timeouts. Define a typed `StoreError` (thiserror) on the trait, or propagate the original error via `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>` so callers can downcast.

The `Mutex` guard `g` is held across the entire `for t in tasks` loop, and each iteration performs `g.iter().find(...)` plus `g.iter().position(...)` — O(n) lookups per task while every other reader is blocked, giving O(n·m) wall-time per call. Build a `HashMap<&str, usize>` of id→index under the lock (or sort by id and bisect), or split into check-then-apply phases so the lock window is shorter.

`Mutex::lock().unwrap()` panics on poisoning, so any earlier panic while holding the lock permanently bricks the store — every subsequent `load`/`upsert` panics with "poisoned lock". Either propagate the `PoisonError` (recover the inner guard), or document that poisoning is treated as a fatal invariant violation and add an explicit error path.

Exposing `tasks: Mutex<Vec<db::Task>>` as `pub` lets any holder mutate state without going through `TaskStore::upsert`, bypassing conflict checks and `notify_change`. Even with `#[allow(dead_code)]`, this leaves the invariant "all writes go through the trait" unenforced — gate it with `#[cfg(test)]` or provide a narrow `with_tasks_for_test` accessor.

`SSE_WRITERS: Mutex<Vec<SseWriterReg>>` is a process-wide lock taken on every connect AND every stop. Both `register_sse_writer` and `stop_sse_writers` also do an O(n) `retain`/`remove` pass under the same lock, so connect/stop churn scales as O(n²) in the number of historical writers and serializes all SSE bookkeeping across threads. Two additional concerns: (1) the `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` poisoned-mutex recovery silently masks inconsistent state after a panicking holder — the doc says "审计" but it just prints and proceeds; (2) the keepalive idle-ticks vs. `register_sse_writer`'s `retain(is_finished)` means finished-but-not-yet-reaped writers keep consuming a slot in the global vec. Consider `Mutex<HashMap<u64, SseWriterReg>>` (or `dashmap`) keyed by `(hub_key, handle_id)`, and either drop `into_inner` (propagate the poison) or at least increment an audit counter when recovery fires.

comments.content: `Header::from_bytes(...).expect("静态 header 字节不可能失败")` panics on a worker thread if the byte sequences are ever changed to anything containing non-token / control bytes. The literal byte slices today happen to be valid, but the *runtime* contract of `from_bytes` (it rejects `\r`, `\n`, NUL, and non-ASCII in both name and value) means a future copy-paste edit can take down the whole SSE pipeline for every connected client. Either build the headers once via `OnceLock`/`Lazy` so a panic fails the process at startup instead of in a hot path, or replace `.expect` with `match` + `json_err(500)`.

Inconsistent flush-error handling inside the same writer loop: the live-event branch treats `flush().is_err()` as a connection break, but the heartbeat branch does `let _ = stream.flush();` and keeps looping even if the flush keeps failing forever. A wedged socket (write succeeded into a TCP buffer that the kernel can no longer drain, e.g. dead peer behind a NAT) will then spam keepalives every 15 s into a connection that is effectively gone, and the writer never exits — the only way out is the recv-timeout-driven `stop_w` check, which is unreachable until api_stop. Treat keepalive flush failures symmetrically with the live path:

`stop_sse_writers` calls `let _ = h.join();` and silently discards both a normal return and a `JoinError` (panic / cancel). Combined with the `is_finished()` short-circuit, the function only audits `sse_writer_leaked` on a timeout, so a writer thread that panics inside the loop is silently dropped — the connection is gone, the hub is fine, but no operator signal is emitted. Given the file's stated goal of "泄漏审计", at minimum log the panic payload via `audit` when `join` returns `Err`:

`internal_err(req, log, &e)` is called while `_rmw` is still alive. Because `req.respond` writes to the client TCP socket, slow/blocked clients will hold `API_RMW_LOCK` for the duration of the response, serializing every concurrent API write behind that I/O. The same pattern recurs at the `store.upsert(...)` `Err` branch immediately below. Restructure so the error is captured, the block ends (releasing the lock), and only then is `req.respond` invoked — e.g. by computing `Result<_, E>` inside the block and matching outside.

Same lock-held-across-I/O pattern in `update_task`: the 404 `req.respond` (and the `store.load()` failure path above it) executes with `API_RMW_LOCK` still held. A slow client aborting the connection here stalls every other API write. Pull the response out of the locked block.

`delete_task` has three `req.respond`/`internal_err` call sites that fire while `_rmw` is alive: store.load failure, 404, and the idempotent re-delete 200. Each holds `API_RMW_LOCK` across HTTP I/O. Additionally, the idempotent re-delete branch returns 200 without calling `after_change`, so SSE clients never see this no-op event — fine in isolation, but combined with the under-lock response it means a slow consumer can stall all writes while a redundant delete is being reported.

`serde_json::to_vec(v).unwrap_or_else(|_| b"{}".to_vec())` silently converts every serialization error into a 2xx with the literal body `{}`. A caller that successfully POSTs/PUTs may see a success status while the body is the empty JSON object — a data-integrity hazard at the HTTP boundary. Either propagate the error (return 500 with a clear message) or at minimum log it before falling back. Returning `{}` is misleading because clients cannot distinguish "field legitimately absent" from "whole object failed to serialize".

Lock poisoning is silently swallowed with `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`. If any code inside the critical section panics (e.g. an unexpected `unwrap` in a future change, or a panic from a malformed invariant), subsequent writes will proceed against a potentially-mutated `store` state where the prior thread's `prepare_for_upsert`/`upsert` side effects were partial. At minimum, log the poisoning so a panic mid-RMW is observable; preferably poison the mutex and reject writes until the store is reconciled.

While the lock prevents the *concurrent* race, the long-term invariant "order is unique and increasing" still breaks as the store ages. Either use `i64`/`u64` for `order` or switch to a millisecond/timestamp-based sequence.

comments.content: Default `--out` path is silently derived from `cfg.eval_set_path` and only announced via `[eval-run] 写入：...` *after* the file is written. If the user's `eval_set_path` points somewhere unexpected (e.g. a directory inside the repo, a synced folder, or a read-only location), the append can silently create/overwrite a file there before any error or warning appears. Either require `--out` explicitly, or print the resolved default path in the pre-run log block (next to `eval_set` / `feedback` / `period`) so the user can see and abort before writing.

TOCTOU race on the worker cap. `active.load(...) >= MAX_WORKERS` and `active.fetch_add(1, ...)` are not atomic; under a burst, multiple concurrent iterations of the accept loop can both observe `active < MAX_WORKERS` and then both increment, so the worker count can transiently exceed `MAX_WORKERS` (and `active.fetch_add(1)` returns the previous value, which is exactly what's needed for an atomic compare-and-cap). Use `fetch_add`'s return value to check the cap atomically, e.g. `let n = active.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1; if n > MAX_WORKERS { active.fetch_sub(1, ...); respond 503; continue; }`, so the cap is enforced exactly.

Silent failure of the A6 id persistence. `let _ = db::atomic_write(p, &id.to_string())` discards the `Result`; if the write fails (disk full, permission denied, FS error, rename race, etc.) the on-disk id falls behind the in-memory `next_id`, so on restart the hub resumes from a stale id and any client reconnecting with `Last-Event-ID >= persisted_id` will silently drop the events that were already broadcast but never persisted — exactly the failure mode the persistence was added to prevent. At minimum log via `on_error` / `audit_event!`; preferably either retry on transient errors or refuse to advance `next_id` (i.e. write first, then commit the id) so broadcast and disk state stay in lockstep.

Test mutates process-wide state without isolation. `tiny_http::HTTP_READ_TIMEOUT_MS` is a global mutable; the only protection is the `RestoreReadTimeout` Drop guard, but cargo's parallel test runner will execute other tests (or even a second instance of this test) concurrently, racing on the same global and producing flakes. Guard the test with a `static TEST_LOCK: Mutex<()>` (or a `serial_test` crate) so the mutate/restore window is exclusive; otherwise the test can pass or fail depending on interleaving with unrelated tests in the same binary.

Per-broadcast allocations scale with client count. `format!` allocates one `String`, `msg.clone()` duplicates it into history, and `msg.as_bytes().to_vec()` re-allocates once per connected writer — with 256 clients that's ~258 allocations per human-driven event, and history stores `String` while the channel carries `Vec<u8>` so the same payload exists in two different types. Switching history to `Arc<str>` and channel payload to `Arc<[u8]>` (or storing the byte payload once and cloning the `Arc`) eliminates the per-event and per-client clones and removes the String↔Vec<u8> type mismatch.

Test-only re-exports from private modules permanently widen the crate's public API. `AuditLevel` is referenced ONLY by `tests/llm_integration.rs:529` and `tests/task_chat_exec.rs:21`; `PersistedSkillOutcome`/`upsert_skill_outcome`/`load_all_skill_outcomes` are referenced ONLY by `tests/skill_e2e.rs` (internal callers all go through `crate::db::*` directly, not via this re-export). Recommend gating with `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "test-support"))]` or moving into a `#[doc(hidden)] pub mod test_support` so the public surface only contains production items. Also note `StopGuard` re-export on line 35: the comment claims it is for `tests/llm_integration.rs` stop-guard construction, but the type is already reachable as `crate::bot_slash::StopGuard` from internal callers — making it `pub` here only adds another public path; consider `#[doc(hidden)] pub use` or removing if no production consumer is using `crate::bot::StopGuard`.

Model-loop internals are publicly re-exported at the crate root, but the surrounding comment explicitly directs new code to import them from `bot_chat` / `bot_model_loop` directly. Items like `ModelLoopDeps`, `LlmHttp`, `run_model_loop_core`, `accumulate_tool_call_delta`, `drain_sse_lines`, `noop_replan` are implementation details of the loop; exposing them at the crate root invites downstream consumers (or future contributors) to take dependencies on them. Recommend either `#[doc(hidden)] pub use` to suppress docs while keeping the path, or — better — splitting into a `pub(crate) use` for internal callers plus a `#[doc(hidden)] pub use` shim for the listed external call sites that genuinely need the crate-root path.

`add_allowed_dir` is the function that mutates the tool-execution directory allowlist (`allowedDirs` in bot-config.json) — see `bot_fs.rs:215` invoking it from the "always allow this directory" confirmation dialog. The function is `pub(crate)` (good — not externally callable), but `pub(crate) use` here makes it reachable from any module in the crate. Review every `crate::bot::add_allowed_dir(...)` call site in the codebase and confirm the `dir` argument is always sourced from the post-dialog handler (i.e., never directly from a user-supplied Tauri command body without the same trim/dedup/persist-to-disk round-trip that `bot_fs.rs` performs). If a future command bypasses the dialog and forwards raw user input, the allowlist will silently expand.

comments.content: Duplicate argv parsing loop silently breaks the `--synthetic` isolation contract. The first loop (lines ~37-94) consumes all flags and sets `proposals_path`/`changes_path`/`applied_path`/`output_path` from CLI. Then the `if use_synthetic` block (lines ~96-103) replaces those paths with `../evolution.synthetic/...` and `./observe-report.synthetic.json`. But a *second* identical `while i < args.len() { match ... }` loop (starting at the re-declared `let mut i = 1;` below) re-runs the full parser, so any user-supplied `--proposals/--changes/--applied/--output` flags will overwrite the synthetic defaults. Trace example: `cargo run -- --synthetic --proposals /tmp/foo.jsonl` ends up reading from `/tmp/foo.jsonl` instead of the synthetic directory, silently defeating the "synthetic 隔离" guarantee documented in the comment and (in `--synthetic` mode) even writing generated synthetic data to a user-specified path. The second loop should be deleted entirely — the synthetic override belongs after a *single* parse, or it should be applied with the user-supplied values taking precedence and `--synthetic` only toggling data generation (not output paths).

Stop-condition thresholds `30`, `14.0`, and `5` are duplicated as bare literals inside the binary instead of being sourced from the same constants the library's `check_stop_condition` uses. This guarantees the printed status line will drift the moment the library thresholds change (e.g., the operator decides `>= 30` becomes `>= 25`). Either re-export the thresholds from `wmessage_lib::evolution::observe` as `pub const` (e.g., `MIN_COMPLETED_CHANGES`, `MIN_DAYS_ELAPSED`, `MAX_ROLLED_BACK`) and reference them here, or have the binary print fields directly from `StopStatus` (which presumably already encodes the limit it compared against). Note the asymmetry: `MIN_DAYS_ELAPSED` (14.0) is a floating-point threshold but `completed` and `rolled_back` are integer counts — confirm `StopStatus` exposes the limits it actually applied.

`print_help` and the module-level doc comment advertise defaults (`默认：../evolution/evolution-proposals.jsonl`, `--check-stop 必填`) but never mention that `--synthetic` *overrides* the four path flags with `../evolution.synthetic/...` and `./observe-report.synthetic.json`. Given the duplicate-loop bug above, the actual runtime behavior is "the later loop wins, so the override is silently undone by any user path flag" — which contradicts the explicit inline comment `老板 21:38 拍板：synthetic 隔离`. At minimum document the override ordering in `print_help` (e.g., "`--synthetic` 默认写到 `../evolution.synthetic/`，与 `--proposals/--changes/--applied/--output` 同用时以用户指定路径为准"), and ideally fix the underlying parse-once issue so the documented contract matches behavior.

Markdown-header false positive: after `strip_markdown_prefix` strips `#`/`-`/`*`/`+`/`N.`, a header body like `# 失败：原因` or `# 错误：错误信息` is reduced to `失败：原因` / `错误：错误信息`. The subsequent `has_keyword_after` then matches because the next char (`：`/`:`) is in `SEPARATORS`. The docstring claims headers like `# 失败案例分析` are filtered, but the filter only protects bodies whose keyword is followed by a non-separator (e.g. `案`/`原`). Headers whose body starts with keyword+separator will still be misclassified as failed — for example, an LLM/tool reply that begins with `# 失败：xxx` will trip this and may mark a skill step as failed when it is just a documentation header.

Inconsistent failure-detection scope: every other branch of `tool_call_failed` is constrained to the first 120 chars (via `failure_keyword_after_separator`) or uses `starts_with`, but `text.contains("已强制终止")` scans the whole body. A long document whose body merely mentions this phrase (e.g. a SPEC.md read by `read_text_file`, or a long prompt containing the literal substring) will be misclassified as a tool failure even though the first line is benign — silently flipping `tool_call_failed` to true and marking downstream skill steps as failed. Either restrict this match to the first line / 120-char prefix, or drop it (it is already covered by `failure_keyword_after_separator` once the message is structured).

comments.content: `BOT_LOG_LOCK` is exposed as `pub static` rather than `pub(crate)`. A global `Mutex<()>` at crate-public visibility lets any downstream crate lock the same mutex; if such code locks it and then calls `write_event` / `write_at` (which also lock), it will deadlock. The comment states use is "in-crate" (`bot::audit_log`), so `pub(crate)` is sufficient and avoids an externally-lockable invariant. Consider tightening visibility.

`append_kv_escaped` allocates a fresh `String` per kv pair via `format!(" | {k}={}", escape_for_log(v, KV_VALUE_MAX))`, then pushes it into the line. For events with many kv (post-execute hooks routinely carry tool name, duration, refs, preview, err fields, ...) this is N short-lived allocations per write. Writing each fragment directly with `write!` into the existing `line` buffer, or building the kv tail via `escape_for_log`'s caller-controlled `String` parameter, would avoid the intermediate heap traffic in a logging path that runs on every step.

Non-atomic update: keyring writes (api_key/tavily_key/brave_key) are committed before write_bot_config_file, with no rollback. If the file write fails (disk full, permission denied, IO error), the OS keyring already holds the new keys while bot-config.json on disk is stale — the user's frontend would read a config view that disagrees with what the agent now sees, and there is no compensating action. Reorder so the file is written first and keys second, or wrap the sequence in a compensating handler that deletes any keys that were written if write_bot_config_file returns Err.

`let _ = io::migrate_legacy_key(&app);` and `let _ = io::migrate_search_keys(&app);` discard the Result of migration steps that exist precisely to scrub secrets from disk. If migration fails (permission denied on the config file, locked keyring, partial migration), plaintext Tavily/Brave/LLM keys may remain on disk while the frontend happily reports `has_*_key = true` based on the (migrated) keyring. Either log the error via `tracing` at warn/error level, or return `Err` so the caller knows the view may still reference secrets that are not yet fully protected.

Production tauri command writes diagnostics to stderr via `eprintln!`, bypassing the crate's structured logging. `shadow_enabled` is a config/feature flag that should be captured by `tracing`/`log` with proper levels, rotation, and span context so it can be filtered or correlated with user reports. Direct stderr writes also leak into the host process's pipe (and may surface in crash reports) without a consistent log format.

Silent trim-and-drop semantics: when the caller passes `Some(" \n")` (a common artifact of pasting from a terminal or a clipboard manager), the trimmed key is empty, the write is skipped, and the function returns `Ok(())`. The frontend has no way to distinguish "user intentionally left the field blank to keep the existing key" from "user pasted a key and we silently rejected it". Either accept the trimmed key unconditionally (current code already trims, so empty-after-trim is rare), or surface an error / return value indicating the write was skipped so the UI can warn the user.

Asymmetric API: LLM key has a dedicated `bot_clear_api_key` command, but Tavily and Brave keys have no equivalent way to be removed through the public tauri surface — `bot_set_config` deliberately treats `None`/empty as "no change" so it cannot clear them either. Users who need to rotate a leaked Tavily/Brave key from the settings page have no supported path. Consider adding `bot_clear_search_key(slot)` mirroring `bot_clear_api_key`, or extending `bot_set_config` to accept an explicit `clear_*` flag distinct from "not provided".

Transfer-Encoding: chunked bypasses the Content-Length pre-check. The fast-path rejection only fires when a single parseable Content-Length is present; a chunked request with no Content-Length skips `if declared > MAX_BODY_BYTES` entirely and is bounded only by the read-loop's `take(MAX+1)` plus the 35s deadline. That contradicts the module-level doc comment ("声明 >1MB 的 body 不必读") which is only true for Content-Length-bearing requests. Either (a) extend the pre-check to reject `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` outright when combined with Content-Length (RFC 7230 §3.3.3), or (b) document that chunked bodies are bounded only by the read loop.

On every non-`Ok` return path (`TooLarge`, `IoFailed`, `Malformed`) the function drops `req.as_reader()` while bytes may remain unread. Whether tiny_http keeps the underlying connection alive on a partially-consumed body is the textbook precondition for HTTP request-smuggling on keep-alive sockets; a subsequent pipelined request could be interpreted as the tail of the rejected body. Either explicitly drain the body (still bounded by the existing size/deadline checks) before returning rejection, or document and verify that tiny_http drops the connection on these paths.

The module doc comment ("分块读循环在每次 read 返回后检查总时长，滴注最迟 35s 被拒（408）") promises a hard 35s upper bound on body-read time, but the deadline is only inspected *after* `read()` returns. Because the per-read timeout is 30s, a read that succeeds just under the timeout (e.g. 29s) contributes 29s to cumulative elapsed time before the check runs, so total rejection time can reach ~60s in the corner case where several reads cluster near the timeout. Either tighten the contract (e.g. compute a per-iteration deadline and check it before reading, so the worst case is "35s + one slow read"), or correct the doc comment to match actual behaviour.

Test name (`change_log_line_escapes_title_newline`) advertises only newline escaping, but the third assertion `!line.contains("| x")` silently binds the implementation to also escape the pipe character (`|`). Since the input is `标题\n[2026-01-01] forged | x`, a `change_log_line` that only replaces `\n`→`\\n` would leave `| x` intact and the third assertion would fail. The test name should reflect the dual-escape contract (e.g. `change_log_line_escapes_newline_and_pipe`) or split into two scoped tests, otherwise future contributors will unknowingly narrow the escaping and break this test without warning.

`bare_task` enumerates every field of `db::Task` with explicit `None`s. Any new field added to `db::Task` will break this helper at compile time. Prefer `..Default::default()` (or whatever defaulting the rest of the codebase uses for `db::Task`) to make the test resilient to additive schema changes; only the fields the test cares about (`id`, `title`, `column`) need to be set explicitly.

`SabotageStore::upsert` releases `g` at the end of the `for` loop and then calls `self.inner.upsert(tasks)`, which re-acquires the same `Mutex`. The gap between release and reacquire is not needed for the test to simulate a concurrent writer (the handler has already returned from `load` before this point), and it widens the race window where another upsert could land and either mask the sabotage or compound it. Holding the lock across both the sabotage and `inner.upsert` (or moving the sabotage into a separate, dedicated mutex) would make the simulated race deterministic.

`SabotageStore::upsert` drops the inner `Mutex` guard `g` at the end of the `for` loop and then re-acquires the same mutex inside `self.inner.upsert(tasks)`. The released window between the sabotage (`x.updated_at = x.updated_at.unwrap_or(0) + 1`) and the actual write is not needed for the test to demonstrate the 409 path: the handler's `load` has already returned before `upsert` is called, so the simulation only needs the in-memory state to be advanced before the row is committed. Keeping a single critical section over both steps (or wrapping the whole impl with a dedicated `parking_lot::Mutex` for the sabotage state) removes an unnecessary release/reacquire that would mask real interleavings under any future concurrent test driver.

The hand-rolled `http()` test client parses the response with two naive strategies: status is extracted from `resp.lines().next().and_then(...)` and silently defaults to `0` on parse failure, while the body is sliced with `resp.split("

Although the production server under test is simple, the helper is reused across many assertions; consider at minimum adding a `dbg!`/panic on parse failure or a small helper that locates the `

` boundary after the status line so failures surface as actionable test errors instead of silent `0`-status diffs.

audit_log holds BOT_LOG_LOCK across db::data_dir (path resolution, often a filesystem syscall on first call / cache miss), db::rotate_log_if_large (stat + rename, potentially copying several MB) AND the open/write/close inside append_bot_log_line. Every concurrent audit writer in the process is serialized behind whatever the slowest of those calls does — a slow rename or any I/O stall will starve unrelated writers. Resolve the data dir and run rotation OUTSIDE the lock, then take BOT_LOG_LOCK only for the actual open + append + drop, so rotation latency cannot stall other writers (rotation just renames bot.log → bot.log.1, which is safe to perform before any concurrent open-for-append on the now-empty path).

`let _ = append_bot_log_line(&p, line);` discards the boolean failure flag returned by append_bot_log_line, so audit_log / audit_log_hook have no way to surface persistence errors to their callers — only the side-effect eprintln inside the helper remains. Combined with the () return type, the audit_log contract is opaque: a failed disk write is indistinguishable from a successful one, and there is no path to retry, back off, route the failure into audit_event!, or alert monitoring. Either propagate a Result up the call chain, or at minimum route the failure through the same audit_event! mechanism used by bot_log_read so an outage is visible in the log.
comments.existing_code: let _ = append_bot_log_line(&p, line);

comments.content: read_log_tail uses std::fs::read_to_string to load the entire bot.log into a String, then allocates Vec<&str> for every line, slices the tail, reverses in place, and joins — memory and CPU are O(file size) even though the requested `limit` (default 200, max 2000) only needs the last few hundred lines. Rotation currently caps the file at 5 MiB, but if rotation ever fails or the cap is raised this becomes a memory spike on every read, executed on a Tauri command worker thread. Stream the file with BufReader::lines(), keep a bounded ring (VecDeque) of the last `limit` lines, and emit them in reverse order without ever materializing the full buffer.

Check-then-act race on SCHEMA_MIGRATION_CHECKED. The first process-wide caller passes the `load(...) == false` check, then enters `migrate_config_file` (read → mutate → write) and only afterwards calls `store(true, …)`. Any other thread that enters `migrate_bot_config_schema` during that window also observes `false` and performs the same read/mutate/write. The static is intended to gate a once-per-process migration, but it only protects after the write succeeds, so the flag does not actually deduplicate concurrent first-callers. Claim the slot up front with `compare_exchange(false, true, …)`, or guard the migration body with a `Mutex<()>`/`OnceLock`, so only one thread runs the file rewrite even under contention.

Non-atomic write of the live config file. `std::fs::write` truncates and rewrites bot-config.json in place; a crash, power loss, or FS error in the middle leaves the file empty/truncated, and per the file-level doc it can still hold the plaintext `apiKey` not yet moved into keyring — so this single call can simultaneously destroy the user's base_url/model and the un-migrated secret. Write to a sibling temp path, `fsync` the file, then `rename` over the original (and ideally fsync the parent dir) so the migration is at least crash-consistent.

Cross-writer race with bot_set_config. `migrate_config_file` does a free-standing read → mutate → write of the same path that `bot_set_config` writes to, with no file lock, advisory lock, or shared mutex. While the TOCTOU window on `SCHEMA_MIGRATION_CHECKED` is open, a user-triggered save can interleave (migration reads stale JSON → save writes fresh JSON → migration overwrites it with the stale snapshot), silently dropping the user's edits or the schemaVersion bump. Coordinate writers via a process-wide `Mutex` around the read/write pair, or move schema bumping into the same critical section as `bot_set_config` so the two writes cannot interleave.

Stale/incorrect provider needle for MiniMax. The function's doc comment advertises recognition of "MiniMax" (and the returned label is `MiniMax`), but the host substring checked is `u.contains("minimaxi")` (eight chars). That substring does not appear in any reasonable MiniMax base URL (it would only match a literal `minimaxi` token), so every MiniMax URL falls through to the generic `"默认"` label and is indistinguishable from an unrecognised provider. The needle should almost certainly be `"minimax"` so that hosts like `api.minimax.chat` actually trigger the intended branch.

Silent fallback to `list.first()` can mask configuration drift and persist surprising data. When `active_id` is set but absent from the current provider's bucket (e.g. provider switched from OpenAI to Anthropic while the OpenAI `active_model_id` still points at an OpenAI-only entry), `or_else(|| list.first())` quietly overwrites `cfg.base_url`/`cfg.model` with some unrelated Anthropic entry on the next save. Either skip the sync in that case (and surface a clear error / audit event that the active id is missing), or always derive from the active id and leave `base_url`/`model` untouched when it isn't found, instead of silently picking a different model.

The default `model: "deepseek-v4-flash"` may not be a valid DeepSeek API model identifier. The comment notes that `deepseek-chat` was deprecated and replaced with "V4 Flash", but as of this codebase state there is no widely-known DeepSeek API model by that name. Fresh installs that have not edited the config will fail on the first chat call with a 404/model-not-found error from DeepSeek before the user ever reaches the settings page. Verify this is a real model exposed by DeepSeek's `/v1/models` endpoint; if not, switch the default to a model ID that actually exists today (e.g., `deepseek-chat` / `deepseek-reasoner`) or document the deployment this targets.

The `api_key`, `tavily_key`, and `brave_key` fields are `pub` and serializable (only gated by `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"`). The "set to None before write-back" invariant that protects plaintext keys from being re-serialized to disk lives entirely in migration code elsewhere — the type offers no defense in depth. Any future write path (a new save command, a config-clone helper, a panic-recovery path, an in-place edit that forgets to clear the key) can silently re-exfiltrate the key to `bot-config.json`. Consider (a) splitting migration input into a separate `BotConfigLegacy` struct that only implements `Deserialize`, (b) wrapping the legacy-only fields in `#[serde(skip)]` gated on `schema_version >= N`, or (c) moving them behind a private `#[serde(skip)]` field plus a documented getter so non-migration code can't accidentally round-trip them.

`KEYRING_SERVICE = "wmessage.bot.v1"` and `BOT_CONFIG_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` are two independent version counters that must move together whenever the keyring entry shape changes (e.g., adding a new key slot, renaming `api-key`). Nothing in this module enforces or even cross-references them — bumping `schema_version` without bumping `KEYRING_SERVICE` silently strands existing users' stored credentials, while bumping the service without the schema leaves the migration code reading from a service nobody wrote to. Either (a) derive the keyring service name from `BOT_CONFIG_SCHEMA_VERSION` (`format!("wmessage.bot.v{BOT_CONFIG_SCHEMA_VERSION}")`) so they cannot drift, or (b) add a `const _: () = assert!(KEYRING_SERVICE.ends_with(...)...)` style compile-time invariant tying the two together, and document the co-bump step in a single comment block.

`ApiProvider::from_cfg` and `PermMode::from_cfg` only `trim()` the raw string — they do not normalize case. JSON values like `"Anthropic"`, `"ANTHROPIC"`, `"Yolo"`, or `"YOLO"` (and any user-edited config with accidental capitalization) silently fall through to the `Openai` / `Ask` fallback, misconfiguring the active protocol and perm mode with no error to the user. The trim-only behavior is also inconsistent with the doc comment's "防御回退" intent, which implies tolerance. Add `to_ascii_lowercase()` (or `eq_ignore_ascii_case` matching) before the pattern arms so `"YOLO"` and `"anthropic"` are both recognized.

delete_api_key_at — v0 cleanup short-circuited by `key_entry(slot)?` and its result silently discarded: if v1 `delete_credential` fails (locked keychain etc.), the function returns via `?` before touching v0; if v0 cleanup itself fails silently (`let _ = ...`), the legacy v0 entry survives and the next `prepare_system_backend → migrate_legacy_keyring_entry` will re-migrate it into v1, resurrecting a key the user thought they deleted — exactly the failure mode the inline comment warns about, but the fix is incomplete. Either (a) best-effort-try the v0 cleanup before short-circuiting on v1 errors (compute v0 result first, then return v1 result), and (b) on v0 cleanup error write a WARN audit so the inconsistency is at least visible.

write_key_file_to — Windows plaintext fallback files have no restrictive ACL: both `OpenOptionsExt::mode(0o600)` and the post-write `set_permissions` chmod are gated by `#[cfg(unix)]`. On Windows the file inherits the parent directory's default ACL, so other local Windows users (or services running under other accounts) can read the API key, contradicting the 'Unix 0600' invariant the inline comment relies on for the PlaintextFile backend. Add a Windows ACL equivalent (e.g., narrow DACL via `windows` crate or a helper) or document the platform gap explicitly so callers know the Windows path is not equivalently protected.

migrate_legacy_keyring_entry — persistent `set_password` failure leaves KEYRING_SERVICE_MIGRATED unset, so every subsequent read across all three slots repeats the full new-entry get + old-entry get + set-attempt triple indefinitely, with no backoff and no detection of permanent (e.g., backend ACL denial, platform restriction) vs transient (e.g., keychain locked) failure. Under a sustained lock this produces measurable per-read keyring churn and potentially platform keyring prompts on every read. Either bound the retries (e.g., mark a separate `KEYRING_MIGRATION_FAILED[idx]` once a hard error is observed, or count attempts and give up after N), or treat repeated identical errors as permanent.

read_search_key — TOCTOU between `has_key_of_slot` and `read_key_of_slot` can break the documented "未配置 → 空串" contract, and the NoEntry handling is asymmetric across the two paths. `classify_has_key` maps `keyring::Error::NoEntry` to `Ok(false)`, but `classify_get_password` maps the same `NoEntry` (and every other error) to `Err(KeyringError(...))`. So if the entry is removed between the has-check and the read (or the platform simply returned different variants for two calls), `read_search_key` surfaces a KeyringError instead of `Ok("")`, even though the key is logically unconfigured — and the same underlying condition is reported under two different error codes to the frontend. Consider a single source-of-truth read that returns `Option<String>` (None = unconfigured / real-error wrapped separately), then `read_search_key` maps both None and an explicit empty value to `Ok("")`. Also note this path triggers `prepare_system_backend` twice (once in has, once in read), doubling keyring I/O on each search-key read.

warn_fallback_once — the single process-wide `WARNED` AtomicBool is shared across LLM/Tavily/Brave, so whichever slot triggers the plaintext fallback first wins the audit entry; the inline comment promises "审计文案带触发 slot 的文件名" but in practice only one slot's filename ever appears in `bot.log`. If LLM is configured normally (System backend) and Tavily is the first to fall back, a later fall-back of Brave is silently swallowed and shows up in no audit trail at all. Promote the flag to `AtomicBool` per slot (e.g., `[AtomicBool; 3]` mirroring `KEYRING_SERVICE_MIGRATED`), or replace the global with the `KeySlot -> &mut bool` flag pattern, so each slot's first fallback use is independently audited.

Dispatch uses an O(1) HashMap lookup (`tools_index().get(name).copied()`) right above this block — the T7 comment celebrates moving from O(n) to O(1) — but the post-execute audit then walks `TOOLS_TABLE` linearly with `iter().find(|t| t.name == name)` purely to read `max_output_chars`. Two separate name lookups per call. Fix by making `tools_index()` map to `&'static ToolEntry` (or a parallel `HashMap<&'static str, usize>` keyed by name) so the dispatch and the over-budget check share one lookup.

`commit_and_report` returns `ToolResult::ok` on DB failure with only a textual `{fail_prefix}：{e}` body. The doc-comment justifies this so the LLM severity classifier doesn't mark it fatal, but any downstream automation, retry logic, or assertions checking `result.status` will see `Ok` and proceed as if the task was persisted — silent data loss when the model continues reasoning on the assumption the mutation succeeded. Either return `ToolResult::warn(...)` (which surfaces a non-Ok status without escalating to error) or have the failure path also emit an audit event with level=Error so the status mismatch is observable.
comments.suggestion_code:
Err(e) => crate::bot::registry::ToolResult::warn(
            format!("{fail_prefix}：{e}"),
            Vec::new(),
        ),
comments.existing_code:
Err(e) => crate::bot::registry::ToolResult::ok(
            format!("{fail_prefix}：{e}"),
            Vec::new(),
        ),

comments.content: `serde_json::from_str(args).unwrap_or(serde_json::Value::Null)` silently converts any malformed JSON (truncated stream, garbled quote, model hallucination) into a `Value::Null` that downstream tools will deserialize as `None`/missing. The caller gets no signal that parsing failed and there is no audit/log record, so this kind of bug can persist undetected for a long time. Consider returning `Result<Value, serde_json::Error>` from this `pub(crate)` helper, or at least emitting a `tool.args.parse_failed` audit event with a short preview when the parse fails.

Every `tool.call` audit event writes the first 80 chars of the raw `args` string as `args_preview`. Tools like `fetch_url` (URL with embedded tokens), `write_file` (paths that can leak directory layout), or any future tool whose args carry credentials/PII will have those surfaced verbatim into `bot.log` and any downstream sink (telemetry, log shippers, front-end debugging). The audit preview is useful but should run through a redaction helper (strip `Authorization`, `token=`, `password=`, file:// URLs to path-only, etc.) before being persisted, or be opt-in per tool rather than the default.

NEXT_STOP_ID is a process-global AtomicU64 that is never reset. Combined with the FALLBACK singleton above, this means all integration tests in a single tests/*.rs file (and all lib unit tests in the same process under cargo test --lib) share a single monotonic counter; any test asserting on a specific stop id will see non-deterministic values, and id collisions across tests (StopGuard registering the same id into the shared fallback's stop_registry) become possible. Consider a test-only reset hook, or move id generation into AppState so each managed instance gets its own counter.

Every write path over bot-config.json uses std::fs::write directly, which is non-atomic. A crash/power loss mid-write truncates the file; on next load_config, serde_json::from_str fails and BotConfig::default() is returned, silently wiping the user's allowedDirs, bypass_llm, search keys settings, etc. For settings that include secrets cleanup (migrate_legacy_key / migrate_search_keys), a partial write could leave the disk holding neither the migrated plaintext nor the cleared slot in a usable state. Use a write-temp + fs::rename pattern (with fsync of dir on Unix) so the live file is always either the old or the new version.

add_allowed_dir performs read-modify-write of bot-config.json with no file lock; a concurrent update_config_file / migrate_* call (or even a second add_allowed_dir invocation) will race and the last writer wins, silently dropping the other's changes. The same hazard exists between migrate_legacy_key and migrate_search_keys when both run at startup. Consider an exclusive per-file lock (fs2 / fdlock / rust-flock) wrapping load_config + the corresponding write, or use an atomic CAS pattern.
comments.suggestion_code:
cfg.allowed_dirs.push(d);
    write_bot_config_file(&db::data_dir(app), cfg).map_err(|e| e.to_string())

comments.content: base_url_is_safe is a prefix match on a hand-lowercased URL and is trivially bypassable: 'http://localhost.evil.com' / 'http://127.0.0.1.evil.com' / 'http://[::1].evil.com' all pass, and embedded userinfo ('http://attacker.com@127.0.0.1') or URL-encoded variants are never parsed. Since this gate decides whether the user sees a plaintext-API-key warning, false negatives defeat the SSRF / cleartext defense the comment promises. Parse with the `url` crate (or at minimum split on '@' and validate host with authority-bearing checks) before classifying.

load_config swallows the schema-migration error with `let _ = ...`. If migrate_bot_config_schema fails (transient FS error, permission issue, partial-write recovery), the function silently falls through to the parse-or-default branch; a parse failure on the unmigrated file then returns BotConfig::default(), discarding the user's entire config. Surface the migration error (log it, or return early after retrying) so this failure mode is observable.

migrate_legacy_key / migrate_search_keys perform a check-then-act against the keyring (`has_api_key` / `has_search_key` followed by `write_api_key` / `write_search_key`) with no compare-and-set semantics. Two concurrent invocations — for example the startup hook racing the settings-page fallback — can both observe `has == false`, both attempt to write, and the second writer's plaintext overwrites the first. The same pattern recurs for `KeySlot::Tavily` / `KeySlot::Brave` inside the search-key migration loop. Use an atomic create-or-noop primitive in keyring (set_entry with compare_exchange-style semantics, or treat existing-entry errors as success) rather than this optimistic two-call dance.

The trailing `use std::io::Write;` plus a `#[allow(dead_code)] fn _write_marker(_w: &mut dyn Write) {}` is a hack to keep an unused trait import alive. It signals an abandoned write path or an import that should have been dropped, and it permanently silences real `dead_code` lint hits elsewhere in the module. Either drop the import + marker, or actually wire it into the write paths (preferred, since they should use `Write::write_all` for atomic-temp writes as noted above).
comments.suggestion_code: // (removed; use std::io::Write was only kept alive by the marker above)

comments.content: These accessors hand out &std::sync::Mutex by reference. The accessor itself is fine, but the type does not prevent an async caller from holding the std MutexGuard across an .await point (e.g. inside park_pending / take_pending_for, oneshot::Receiver::await, tokio::join), which will block the tokio runtime worker thread for the entire await duration. The file documents the design but the asymmetry with artifact_registry (which is tokio::sync::Mutex) makes it easy to miss at the call site. Consider either (a) returning Arc<Mutex<...>> like the RAII-guarded tables so callers can take the guard synchronously and drop it before any await, or (b) switching pending_map and confirm_requests to tokio::sync::Mutex so the type encodes the await-safety contract.

The leading `#[allow(dead_code)]` and the comment about suppressing unused warnings for `escape_for_log` / `truncate_for_log` are no longer accurate: both names are already re-exported at module scope via `pub(crate) use audit::{escape_for_log, truncate_for_log}` (line 62), which counts as a use for dead-code-elimination purposes. The function itself is `#[allow(dead_code)]`, so the call to `audit::escape_for_log("", 0)` never actually runs and provides no warning suppression. This is leftover scaffolding from before the facade re-export landed — delete the marker (and its misleading comment) entirely. If the goal was to keep a deliberate "no-op" for compile-time symbol touch, prefer a `const _: fn() = || { let _ = audit::escape_for_log; };` so the intent is explicit.
