// (delete this whole block — escape_for_log / truncate_for_log are already
// kept alive by the `pub(crate) use audit::{...}` re-export at the top of the file.)

comments.content: Mutex-poisoning recovery is silently swallowing a real signal here. If a previous test panicked while holding `BOT_LOG_TEST_LOCK` (e.g., a failing assertion inside `append_bot_log_line_*` that left the lock poisoned), this `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` will simply continue and re-run assertions against whatever half-written state was left in `target/debug/deps/bot.log`, turning a hard failure into a flaky one. The canonical pattern used in `src-tauri/src/audit.rs:669` at least logs `eprintln!("[mutex_poisoned] ...")` before recovering — mirror that here so a poisoned lock surfaces in test stderr instead of being silently masked. Better still, propagate the poison with `.lock().expect("BOT_LOG_TEST_LOCK poisoned by prior test")` so the failure stays loud.

Test depends on a shared on-disk file at `current_exe().parent().join("bot.log")` (typically `target/debug/deps/bot.log`) with only best-effort cleanup via `let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&log)`. If any assertion before line 592 panics, the file persists into the next test run and bleeds state. Combined with the silent mutex-poison recovery above, a single failing audit test can produce a cascading-flaky run rather than a hard CI failure. Defensive fix: read the file before the write at line 583 and assert it does not pre-exist (or truncate it first with a logged removal), so stale content from a previous aborted run cannot masquerade as a fresh audit line. Also consider a panic-safe cleanup helper (Drop guard) so the file is removed even on early return.

The tests use `crate::bot::config::io::read_bypass_llm_switch_at` and friends, while the public facade at the top of this file only re-exports the no-suffix `read_bypass_llm_switch`. The `_at`-suffixed helpers (taking an explicit `&Path`) are leaked as `pub` for white-box testing. Since the module-level comment (lines 1-30) explicitly states that "所有外部调用走 `crate::bot::<item>`，不直接访问 `crate::bot::config::<item>`", the test-only API leak should be tightened: either demote these helpers to `pub(crate)` (the modules are declared `pub mod`, which is broader than necessary — `pub(crate) mod io` / `pub(crate) mod keyring` / etc. would close the leak while preserving test access) or accept a `Path` parameter on the public function so callers do not need a separate test-only variant.

Same std::sync::Mutex-by-reference concern as confirms above: an async caller that holds the guard across .await (e.g. waiting for user reply in the PendingExec flow) will block a tokio worker thread. The doc says '锁只在 park/take 期间持有' but the accessor does not enforce that — the returned &Mutex is just as easy to hold across await as confirms's is. See the confirms comment for the same trade-off; if those two are migrated to tokio::sync::Mutex, this one should follow.

artifact_registry uses tokio::sync::Mutex while every other field in AppState uses std::sync::Mutex. The accessor returns &tokio::sync::Mutex, so callers must use .lock().await — but nothing in the type prevents confusion: a future refactor that extends a critical section across .await on one of the std fields by analogy with the tokio one will silently block the runtime. Either move artifact_registry to std::sync::Mutex (the doc says the critical section is brief and there's no Drop cleanup), or migrate the other small-lock tables to tokio::sync::Mutex for consistency. The current mixed state hides the actual rule.

The StopGuard split-brain hazard is documented in the accessor comment ("守卫会注册进兜底实例、而 /stop 查注入实例，停止功能就真的坏了"), but the accessor itself is the only way stop_registry is reached, so the entire correctness of /stop depends on every StopGuard::new / new_task_exec call site passing exactly the same AppHandle the /stop dispatcher uses. There is no compile-time enforcement of this — any helper, test, or refactor that constructs a guard without an app (or with a different app) silently degrades to a non-functional stop. Consider adding a debug assertion that stop_registry(app).as_ptr() == the registry the /stop handler reads from, or wiring StopGuard construction through a single new() that takes &AppHandle as a non-optional parameter with a clear name (e.g. StopGuard::acquire(app, ...)) so the misuse is visible at the call site.

TOCTOU race between `should_emit`/`peek` and `confirm_artifact_batch`/`take_all` causes silent data loss. `should_emit` clones the registry contents for the dialog, then the user later confirms via `confirm_artifact_batch`, which calls `take_all` and removes everything for that task_id. Any `register()` call (e.g., a late `tool_link_file_to_task`) issued for the same task_id in that window will be silently discarded. The flow must either be atomic (e.g., a `drain_and_return` that hands the snapshot to the caller together with the removal) or use a versioned snapshot so that subsequent registers aren't dropped.

comments.content: Incomplete optimistic concurrency in `confirm_artifact_batch`: `next.expected_updated_at = next.updated_at` is set from the snapshot returned by `db_load_for`, but neither `db_load_for` (full-table scan, no row-level `updated_at`) nor `db_upsert` (verified — see `db/tasks.rs`, `upsert_tasks` does not compare `expected_updated_at`) actually verifies that the row hasn't changed between load and write. Concurrent edits to the same task in the window between `db_load_for` and `db_upsert` will be silently overwritten. Either remove the dead assignment or add a guarded upsert path that checks `expected_updated_at` and returns a conflict error.

O(n) full-table scan to resolve a single task: `db_load_for(&app)` loads every task card from the DB into memory and then `.find()` linear-scans for `task_id`. For any non-trivial task count this is wasteful, and it widens the TOCTOU window with the subsequent `db_upsert` and `broadcast_after_mutation`. Add (and use) a `db_load_one(app, &task_id)` (or a `db_get` that takes a typed `TaskId`) and replace this call site.

Stringly-typed domain state for `task_column: Option<&str>` invites typos at every call site (only `\"done\"` is meaningful here). Per the type/API-design checklist, model this as an enum (e.g. `TaskColumn::{Todo, Doing, Done}` or a `Column` newtype) so the compiler enforces the Manual/Scheduled/Batch contract instead of relying on comment discipline, and `should_emit` becomes an exhaustive match.

Error context is dropped by `format!()` in `map_err`: both closures stringify the underlying error into a localized message without preserving the source. The original `CommandError`/`DbError` is discarded, so frontend diagnostics and server-side logs lose the underlying cause and any source chain. Prefer `#[source]` / `anyhow::Error` wrapping (e.g. `map_err(|e| format!("读取任务卡失败：{e}")).map_err(CommandError::from)` plus a contextual message) so the root cause is still attributable from logs.
comments.existing_code:
.map_err(|e| format!("读取任务卡失败：{e}"))?
        .into_iter()
        .find(|t| t.id == task_id)
        .ok_or_else(|| format!("任务卡不存在：{task_id}"))?;

comments.content: Excessive cloning of `task`/`next` in `confirm_artifact_batch`: `task.clone()` creates `next`, then `next.clone()` is passed twice (once to `db_upsert`, once to `broadcast_after_mutation`), plus `app.clone()` for the upsert. Since `db_upsert` takes ownership of the `Vec<Task>` anyway, move `next` into the upsert call and then keep one clone only for the broadcast — or restructure as `let next = ...; let snapshot = next.clone(); db_upsert(app, vec![next]).await?; broadcast_after_mutation(&app, vec![snapshot], vec![]);`.

openai_msgs_to_anthropic discards the `skipped_images` count returned by convert_all (skipped count becomes `_skipped_images`). Callers therefore cannot tell when a multimodal image was silently dropped because Anthropic does not accept HTTP(S) image URLs, only base64 inline images. For a multi-image request, data integrity loss is silent — the round-trip sees fewer images than the user provided. Either propagate the count in the public Result or log/warn on `> 0` so callers (and the audit trail) can react.

`crate::audit::tool_call_failed("", &text)` passes an empty string as the `name` argument. Today `tool_call_failed`'s implementation has `let _ = name;` so the value is ignored and behavior matches other call sites, but other call paths in `bot_model_loop`/`bot_skills/runtime` pass the real tool name. If a future change makes `name` load-bearing (e.g. per-tool failure semantics), this Anthropic-side classification will silently drift from every other call site. Either thread the tool name from the preceding assistant tool_calls message (require keeping tool name in step state) or add a sentinel constant and a doc note that this site intentionally passes empty because the tool name is unavailable here.

Empty-string fallbacks for `tool_use_id`/`id` (`unwrap_or("")`): a missing or blank id on either side of a tool round-trip causes Anthropic to return 400 ("tool_use_id not found" or "tool result id mismatch"). The defensive filter above ("tool_call_id/empty fallback") rejects only missing name, not blank names; a blank string flows through and only fails server-side at request time. Consider treating blank/empty after trim the same as missing — drop the block or convert it to a 400-shaped upstream error before serializing. Same applies to `tc["id"]` on the assistant side.

ToolSlotMapper mutates a HashMap<usize, usize> and is documented as strictly per-stream state ("每轮响应流开始时新建一个"). The type itself enforces nothing — there is no `&mut self`-only lifetime guard or constructor that consumes a stream handle. If a future refactor shares the mapper across turns (or across two parallel Anthropic streams on the same task), dense slot indices collide and the very 400 error this mapper exists to prevent reappears silently. At minimum, add a `consume_on_done: bool` flag gated on `message_stop` so accidental cross-turn reuse is observable in logs; or split the type into `Owned` vs `Reusable` shapes so reuse requires an explicit reset() call.

parse_anthropic_response filters the non-stream `content` array to text blocks only and concatenates them — `stop_reason` (`refusal`, `max_tokens`, etc.) is discarded and a refusal-only payload (e.g. `{"content":[{"type":"refusal","refusal":"..."}],"stop_reason":"refusal"}`) silently returns `""`. The non-stream callers in `bot_chat::summarize_messages` and `bot_plan::call_planner` treat `""` as a generic "empty model response" error, conflating refusal/empty-model-output two distinct user-visible conditions. Surface `stop_reason` (or a structured result) so callers can return "model refused: …" rather than "模型返回了空摘要" / "Planner 输出无法解析为计划: …".

convert_tools silently drops entries whose `function.name` is missing or non-string via `filter_map(... f["name"].as_str()?)`. With multiple callers (Planner / chat), a malformed tool declaration disappears with no signal; the next request to Anthropic simply has fewer `tools`, and the model is free to invent tool names or refuse. At least log `warn!("anthropic: dropping tool entry without name: …")` (or count it like `skipped_images`) so the upstream tool loader can be fixed.

**Symlink-escape bypass when persisting "Always allow".** `canonical` is the symlink-resolved path from `std::fs::canonicalize` (line above). When the user passes a path like `/allowed/sub/link.txt` and `link.txt -> /etc/passwd`, `canonical` becomes `/etc/passwd` and `canonical.parent()` becomes `/etc/`, which is then persisted into `allowedDirs` and accepted by the next `allowed_dirs()` snapshot. A user clicking "始终允许" thinking they're allowing `/allowed/sub` permanently widens the allowlist to `/etc/`. The same shape applies when the resolved target is a directory symlinked outside the allowlist. Compute the to-be-added directory from the user's input tree (e.g. `expand_tilde(p)`'s parent, or walk upward from the canonical path and add the first ancestor that lies outside any current allowlist entry) — never from a symlink-resolved target.

**Blocking filesystem syscalls on the Tauri async runtime.** `std::fs::canonicalize`, `std::fs::read_dir`, `std::fs::read_to_string`, `std::fs::File::open`, and `metadata()` are all synchronous and are called directly from `async` functions here (`resolve_with_perm`, `allowed_dirs`, `tool_read_text_file`, `tool_grep_files`, `tool_list_files`, and the `walk` helper they share). On slow disks, network mounts, contended antivirus, or simply a large workspace, these calls block the runtime thread that drives every other Tauri command / event — the whole UI stalls. The recursive `walk` + grep path is the worst: it `read_to_string`s every matched file up to 2 MiB before yielding. Wrap the sync I/O in `tauri::async_runtime::spawn_blocking` (or `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`) and `await` the handle, so the executor keeps making progress.

**TOCTOU between canonicalizing the target and recomputing the allowlist.** `resolve_with_perm` calls `canonicalize(&expanded)`, then separately calls `allowed_dirs(app).await` (which reads config + DB + canonicalizes every directory on disk), then checks `is_within_allowlist`. Between those three filesystem reads and the subsequent read of the file, the symlink target could be swapped, the file could be replaced with a hardlink, or another invocation (e.g. a sibling "always allow" decision in flight) could have mutated `bot-config.json`'s `allowedDirs`. The deny/allow verdict is computed against a stale snapshot. Hold a single snapshot (or a guard) for the duration of the read, and re-check that the final file descriptor points at a path still within the recorded allowlist before returning bytes to the model.

**Exponential-time glob matcher.** The `b'*'` branch retries the remainder of the pattern at every position in the name (`(0..=n.len()).any(|i| inner(&p[1..], &n[i..]))`), giving the classic catastrophic-backtracking behaviour. A model-supplied pattern like `*a*a*a*x` evaluated against a long file name during `walk()` can spike CPU and stall the runtime; `walk` is called from both `grep_files` and `list_files`, so any tool call can trigger it. Replace the naive recursion with a linear two-pointer (or iterative DP) matcher that advances the `*` cursor without re-scanning, and/or cap the recursion depth / input length.

**Binary detection only inspects the first 8 KiB.** A file with a text header (e.g. ELF magic, PNG, Office OOXML, gzip stream) followed by binary payload past the 8 KiB window will be classified as text and fed to the model verbatim. Combined with `GREP_MAX_FILE_BYTES = 2 MiB`, this can leak arbitrary binary content (which the LLM may then regurgitate or hallucinate context for) as if it were text. Either reject such files up front (scan the whole file up to a hard cap, e.g. 256 KiB, with the same NUL heuristic), or in `read_capped_file` additionally verify the entire buffered region is UTF-8 and abort otherwise — don't trust the first 8 KiB alone.

**Unused import.** `TaskRef` is imported but never referenced in this file (the tool signatures here take `AppHandle`, `&str`, `bool`, `Option<&str>` only — no `(String, Vec<TaskRef>)` argument). This will produce a dead-code / unused-import warning under `-D warnings`. Either remove the import or document why it's intentionally re-exported / reserved for a future dispatcher signature.

`std::fs::canonicalize` is called inside `sanitize_task_files_in`, but this function itself runs inside `sanitize_task_files_arg` which is invoked from an async tool path (`tool_create_task` / `tool_edit_task`). Blocking filesystem syscalls on the async runtime worker; under directory iteration with many entries this can stall the worker. Also, the canonicalize-then-compare pattern is a classic TOCTOU window — a symlink inside `gen_canon` could be swapped to point outside between this check and the eventual file registration/use. Recommend resolving via `spawn_blocking` and (where the file is later opened) preferring `openat`-style APIs or re-canonicalizing at the point of use.

The task-file whitelist check iterates every task × every file and calls blocking `std::fs::canonicalize` per file, all inside async `extract_path_check`. With M tasks and N files each, this is O(M·N) sync FS calls (potentially slow on spinning disks / network FS / antivirus). Recommendation: pre-compute and maintain a canonical-path HashSet as tasks are bound/unbound (in `apply_files_to_task` / broadcast hooks), or at minimum hoist to `spawn_blocking`; also bail out early once a match is found (current code does, but across tasks it still scans the rest).

Silently swallows all DB load failures as an empty task list. Callers like `tool_list_tasks` will then report "no tasks", `tool_complete_task`/`tool_delete_task` will report "未找到 id=..." and refuse to mutate. A transient DB failure masquerades as "task doesn't exist", which can mislead the user into recreating tasks or aborting flows. Notably inconsistent with `tool_query_single_task`, which surfaces an explicit "数据库读取错误". Recommend propagating the error or at minimum logging via `audit_log` so silent DB outages are observable.

`order = min(all_orders) - 1.0` is computed locally after a single read snapshot, then written without an `expected_updated_at` RMW check (this path uses no RMW because new rows have no prior row). Two concurrent `tool_create_task` calls (e.g. parallel bot sessions or a scheduled task firing while the user creates another) can both compute the same `min` and both pick `min - 1.0`, colliding. Recommendation: derive order from a strictly monotonic source (`uuid_v7` time prefix, or fractional `next_in_sequence` maintained under a DB-side constraint / `INSERT ... MAX(order) - 1` in a single statement) so collisions are detectable. If sticking with the read-then-write, at minimum take a single atomic SQL statement.

`tool_complete_task` and `tool_delete_task` explicitly set `next.expected_updated_at = next.updated_at` BEFORE mutating fields / `updated_at`, capturing the snapshot's `updated_at` as the optimistic-concurrency baseline. `tool_edit_task` (and the subtask tools) instead rely on `prepare_for_upsert(&mut next)` to do this. Verify `prepare_for_upsert` indeed copies the in-memory `updated_at` (i.e. the snapshot value) into `expected_updated_at` *before* mutations later in the same pipeline; if it instead sets it from a fresh `db_load` it would have a self-inflicted race. Adding an explicit assignment here, like the sibling tools do, removes the hidden coupling.

`tool_link_file_to_task` is async but performs `std::fs::canonicalize` (twice — once on the path, once on the gen dir) directly on the runtime worker, and `crate::db::gen_dir` may itself trigger FS access. Combine both into a single `spawn_blocking` call. Also note the whitelist check uses an unguarded `unwrap_or_else(|_| PathBuf::from(&path))` fallback — if canonicalize fails, subsequent `canon.starts_with(&gen)` compares against an uncanonicalized path; on Windows / macOS `/var` vs `/private/var` resolution this can either over-permissively admit or over-restrictively reject. Log the fallback via `audit_log` so it's observable.

The function is in the per-reply hot path that runs on every LLM response text to detect hallucination claims — paying the Vec growth + filter+flat_map cost every time is wasteful and easy to eliminate.

comments.content: StopGuard cancellation is effectively broken outside run_python. Only `call_run_python` captures `ctx.stop`; every other mutating adapter (`call_delete_task`, `call_complete_task`, `call_edit_task`, `call_add_subtask`, `call_toggle_subtask`, `call_remove_subtask`, `call_create_word`, `call_create_word_revisions`, `call_create_excel`, `call_create_ppt`, `call_create_pdf`, `call_link_file_to_task`, `call_remember_fact`, `call_record_lesson`) silently drops it. Given that StopGuard is a first-class ToolCtx field, and these tools can hit user-confirmation dialogs or be queued behind a long-running Python call, user-initiated cancellation won't propagate. Wire `ctx.stop` through the mutating adapters whose underlying fns accept it.

`call_use_skill` wraps `tool_use_skill(...)` in `Box::pin(async move { ... })` with no `.await` inside, because `tool_use_skill` is a synchronous fn. The dispatch path therefore pays for an unnecessary state-machine wrapping just to fit the uniform `Pin<Box<dyn Future<...>>>` adapter type. Either give `call` a separate variant for sync fns, or replace the `async move {}` wrapper with `std::future::ready(...)` to avoid the state machine.

Hallucination-guard pattern overlap across mutating tools. claims_mutation() unions ALL mutating tools' `claims_patterns` into a single set, and the phrase "已记住你的偏好" is duplicated in both `remember_fact` and `record_lesson`. A reply that legitimately claims a `remember_fact` will be attributed as a `record_lesson` claim (or vice versa), and any overlap also makes it impossible for downstream audit to know which tool the model claimed. Either dedupe overlapping patterns at registration, or change claims_mutation to return the matched tool name(s) so the guard can attribute correctly instead of losing specificity.

Any cosmetic change to the fixture (delimiter count, comment, trailing newline, leading line) makes the test panic with the cryptic `expect("fixture 缺 r#\"")` instead of a meaningful JSON diff. Extract the body more robustly, e.g. by stripping the `pub const TOOLS: &str = r#"` prefix and `\"#;` suffix explicitly via stable string markers.

TOCTOU race between the canonicalize-based whitelist check and the subsequent read. `canonicalize(p)` is used only to derive `c` for the whitelist comparison (`c.starts_with(&rc)`), but the read re-opens the original path `p` (`std::fs::read(p)`). An attacker who can swap `p` between these two syscalls — symlink replacement, bind mount, or path contents that get rewritten after the prompt is constructed — bypasses the whitelist entirely and exfiltrates arbitrary files (size-bounded only by MAX_IMAGE_BYTES) as base64 to the LLM API. The whitelist mitigation explicitly documented a few lines above is rendered ineffective. Read from the canonical path that was actually checked, or use openat/O_NOFOLLOW, to close the window.

`_body: String` and `_session_id: Option<&str>` are declared but never read inside the function body — `stop.session_id()` is used in their place. This forces every caller (e.g. `bot_chat` in `apply_skill_route(&app, meta.clone(), body.clone(), &stop, session_id.as_deref())`) to clone `meta` and `body` — potentially a large DSL body — purely to satisfy a parameter the function discards, even though both values are still needed afterwards (the caller moves the body into `pre_routed_active_skill` and reads `meta.max_rounds`). While the inline comment documents "绝不弄挂主对话" as a deliberate design constraint, this means persistent memory subsystem failures (vector store down, embedding API outage, schema drift) are completely invisible — the chat continues as if semantic recall was never injected, and the operator has no signal that recall quality has degraded. A poisoned `chat_running` or `exec_running` mutex indicates a panic that crossed the lock boundary — exactly the kind of bug that needs durable observability — but stderr is not aggregated with the structured audit pipeline that the rest of this file relies on (`pre_step.route_failed`, `memory.summary_save_failed`, …). The same pattern is repeated in `ChatGuard::Drop`, `ExecGuard::acquire`, and `ExecGuard::Drop`. Replace the eprintln with a Warn/Error `crate::audit_event!` so the diagnosis survives alongside the rest of the operational trail.

comments.content: `register_exec_session(&sid, origin)` is called immediately after `create_exec_session`, but its symmetric `unregister_exec_session(&sid)` lives at the bottom of the function and is only reached when `run(...)` returns normally. If `ChatGuard::acquire` fails (the "会话锁串号" branch), the early `return Err(...)` skips the unregister, leaking the sid→origin mapping in `tool_guard`'s registry for the lifetime of the process. The DB row from `create_exec_session` is also leaked in that path. Move `register_exec_session` to immediately after `ChatGuard::acquire` succeeds, or wrap it in an RAII guard mirroring the existing `ChatGuard`/`ExecGuard` pattern, so registration and unregistration bracket the same scope.

`set_bot_assigned(app, &task.id, true)` is paired with `set_bot_assigned(app, &task.id, false)` only on the Ok/normal return path of `run(...)`. If `run(...)` panics (e.g., a tool's `unwrap`, a downstream async task panic, a `tauri::async_runtime` join error), the await propagates the panic and the cleanup call is skipped, leaving the task card's `bot_assigned` flag stuck at `true` in the database. The in-process `ExecGuard`/`ChatGuard` cover their own state via Drop, but the DB row is not protected by any RAII. Wrap the flip in a scope guard that resets the flag in Drop (mirroring the existing pattern), or push the reset into a `tauri::async_runtime::spawn` fired from Drop.

Expanding the image re-send window from "最近两条 user 消息" to "最后 3 条消息内的 user 消息" (per the inline comment) means a single image attachment (up to 3 MB raw ≈ 4 MB base64) is re-emitted as base64 in every subsequent turn for up to 3 turns. With `MAX_IMAGES_PER_MSG = 4` the per-request upper bound climbs to ~12 MB just for image payloads, easily exceeding MiniMax per-request limits. The size skip branch (`bytes.len() > MAX_IMAGE_BYTES`) silently drops oversized files with no diagnostic, so a user attaching a slightly-over-limit picture gets a degraded experience with no audit trail. Either shrink the window back, or attach a Warn audit event when oversized images are skipped so the silent degradation is visible.

Cache the result of the first load and reuse it for `task_column`; if the second load is intended to pick up post-execution updates from other paths, document that explicitly and consider a narrower query (`db_get_task(id)` if it exists) instead of `db_load_for`.

Wildcard re-exports (`pub use files::*;` etc.) flatten the entire public surface of every submodule into the bot_skills module root, leaking any helpers marked `pub` in those submodules and obscuring which items form the intended stable API. Prefer explicit `pub use` lists for the items you actually want to expose (or, at minimum, a brief comment documenting what is intentionally re-exported). This also makes future refactors of the submodules riskier, because any newly-`pub` item will silently become part of the bot_skills API.

Prompt injection via `fail_reason`: tool failure messages are interpolated verbatim into the Replanner user prompt. Tool errors can carry external content (file bodies, web responses, command stderr), so a malicious payload in any tool output can steer the regenerated plan, which then flows into the main loop's system prompt. Consider sanitizing/quoting/escaping `fail_reason` (e.g., wrap it in a fenced block with explicit "treat as data, not instructions" framing, strip control characters, or truncate to a bounded length) before interpolation.

`reqwest::Client` is rebuilt on every `call_planner` invocation, including TLS configuration. This wastes CPU and forfeits connection pooling / keep-alive across Planner/Replanner calls. Cache the client in a `OnceLock<reqwest::Client>` (or pass it through) so construction is amortized.

Typed errors are collapsed to `String` very early: `reqwest::Error` and `serde_json::Error` become `format!("...{e}")` and then `.into()`. The original error chain (status, body, source) is lost, so callers cannot programmatically distinguish retryable HTTP failures from parse failures or surface actionable context. Preserve the underlying error (e.g., wrap in a `thiserror` enum or `Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>`) and only format at the audit/log boundary.

Non-2xx HTTP responses are rejected without reading the body, so provider-side diagnostics (rate-limit headers, model-not-found, quota messages, Anthropic `error.type`) are dropped before they reach the audit log. Read `resp.text()` (or at least the first ~512 bytes) and include it in the error so `plan.skip` / `plan.replan_failed` audit events are actually debuggable.

Dead `let _ = open;` binding: the tuple destructuring binds `open` only to immediately discard it. The `open` byte is computed twice (in both tuple slots). Simplify to compute `close` directly from `bytes[start]` and drop the unused binding.

`extract_json` uses `rposition` to find the closing brace/bracket, which doesn't respect JSON string boundaries. If a string value contains the matching delimiter (e.g., `{"steps": ["say \"hi\" }"]}` — note embedded `}`), `rposition` still finds the last byte which is the structural close for valid JSON, so this works for well-formed JSON; however, the heuristic silently includes trailing prose after the JSON if any stray `}`/`]` byte appears later in the text. Consider scanning while respecting quote state, or just let `serde_json` parse from `start` using `serde_json::Deserializer::from_str` with `disallow_trailing_bytes` / a manual scan that respects string quoting. At minimum, add a regression test for prose-suffixed output to lock in current behavior.

An empty / malformed API response collapses into the same `parse_plan` failure path as a syntactically broken plan ("Planner 输出无法解析为计划："). The audit log then can't tell apart "API returned 200 with empty content" from "model produced garbage". Distinguish the two: check for empty `text` after `strip_think_blocks` and emit a dedicated `plan.empty_response` audit event / error variant so operators can diagnose provider-side problems quickly.

Cancellation-safety bug: the 1.5 s retry sleep does not consult `stop.stopped()`. If the user clicks `/stop` (or the StopGuard trips) during the sleep, the loop still `continue`s and re-sends the full request body — wasting a second LLM call and the re-serialization cost on top of ignoring user intent. Insert a check before `tokio::time::sleep` (and use `tokio::select!` with a stop signal so the cancellation is immediate, not after the full 1.5 s).

Synthesized `call_synth_{i}` IDs are placed into the assistant `tool_calls` block AND into the corresponding tool result `tool_call_id` for the next round. Strict APIs (Anthropic; some OpenAI-compatible gateways) require server-issued IDs and will 400 the next request with `tool_use ids were provided without a corresponding tool_result block` / `tool result's tool id not found`. The code's own comment documents this, but the impact is real: a single permissive gateway that omits IDs will silently break the entire conversation on a strict provider. Safer approach: detect synthesized IDs pre-execution and skip the tool call (with audit), or drop the response and emit a clarifying `tool_call_id = "skipped_synth_*"` so the next request is not malformed.

Recovering from a poisoned `py_run_gate()` via `e.into_inner()` silently re-enters the critical section. The eprintln explicitly references `py::runtime::py_run_gate`, indicating this mirrors production behavior. If a task holding the gate panics, subsequent callers will silently bypass the gate's "MAX == 1" invariant — the very invariant this test asserts. The recovery should fail loudly (propagate the error or panic) rather than hiding the corruption, otherwise concurrency regressions in production code will not be caught by this gate.

Source-grep regression locks in `exiting_tests` and `platform_tests` are brittle: `exiting_check_is_after_gate_lock` and `unix_scripts_get_parent_watchdog` match on substring positions in the source file. A cosmetic reordering of imports, a refactor that moves `pub fn run_python` before `py_run_gate` declaration, or any unrelated whitespace change inside the first 1500 chars of `dotnet_revisions_entry` / `run_python_ungated` will fail these tests with misleading "必须过并发闸门" / "必须有看门狗前导常量" messages. Consider either (a) compiling these invariants as compile-time checked items (e.g. a `const _: () = assert!(...)` referencing a marker `pub const` placed in the source), or (b) narrowing the search to a tighter scope with explicit anchors. Brittle string matching on source files for correctness invariants is a known anti-pattern that gets disabled the first time a developer is annoyed by it.

Severity: medium

`let dll_s = dll;` then `Some(&dll_s)` is an unnecessary rename — `dll` is already in scope and `Some(&dll)` would work identically. The shadowing suggests the author was worried about moving `dll`, but `dll` is used by-reference here, never moved. Drop the indirection; it just adds a line and a name to track.

Severity: low

The same `let dll_s = dll;` shadowing is duplicated in `dotnet_revisions_in_place_preserves_formatting`. If the rename is kept (e.g. to satisfy a false-positive clippy lint), it should at minimum be a `let &dll_s = &dll;` borrow to make the intent explicit and avoid the redundant move.

Severity: low

Multiple subprocess-lifecycle invariants silently early-return when Python or the dotnet tooling is missing: `run_python_at_grandchild_pipe_readers_joined`, `run_python_at_timeout_writes_audit_line`, `run_python_at_stop_token_interrupts_promptly`, `python_revisions_tool_generates_valid_track_changes`, etc. In a dev environment without python3 / python-docx / dotnet, the most fragile code paths in this file (drain timeout, reader lifecycle, stop-token propagation, revision equivalence lock) get zero coverage. Confirm CI always runs these, otherwise the `kind=drain_timeout` / `kind=timeout` / `kind=stopped` audit assertions and the docx format-preservation lock can regress undetected. Consider gating the test target on a `#[cfg(...)]` feature or emitting a `cargo:warning` (not just `eprintln`) so dev environments surface the skip loudly.

Severity: medium

`escape_for_log_truncates_after_escape` asserts `out.chars().count() == 301` for input of 400 plain 'x' chars at `max_len=300`. Since 'x' has no escape expansion (no newline, no pipe), the truncated output is exactly 300 chars + '…' = 301 — this passes but does NOT exercise the "truncate-after-escape" semantic the test name claims. A meaningful test should include characters that expand (e.g. `"\n"` → 2 chars, `"|"` → 3 chars) so the post-escape truncation actually truncates escaped output. As written, the test would still pass if the implementation truncated before escaping (the trivial "truncate the input, then escape" path).

Severity: medium

The `use std::io::Read as _;` inside `read_docx_document_xml` is brought into the function body, but the `use` is only effective after its declaration. The function calls `read_to_string` below the `use`, which is fine. However, the same `Read` trait is implicit-required throughout the test module — consider hoisting this `use` to the top of `mod tests` to avoid the per-function import and the visual surprise of seeing a bare `read_to_string` call without an obvious trait source.

Severity: low

The module-level docstring says glob `pub use crate::py::*` "只展开 py 的顶层项即子模块声明本身，不递归 re-export 子模块内部 pub 项". This is the explicit rationale for the 7-line per-submodule re-export block. But the comment only documents *what* is being done, not *why* each re-export is needed by external callers (`crate::bot_py::X` paths used by lib.rs / tools.rs). If a future maintainer adds a new public item in a `py/` submodule, they must remember to add the `pub use` here. Consider listing the external callers in the doc comment, or replacing the 7-line re-export with a single `pub use crate::py::{audit, commands, document, env, harvest, io, runtime}::*;` once Rust stabilizes nested glob re-exports — this would be a one-line change instead of a 7-line audit burden.

Severity: low

`mode_explicit = true` is set unconditionally, before validating the value. Combined with the post-loop coercion `risk_level == "low" && !mode_explicit → auto`, this means a skill that writes an invalid mode value (e.g. `mode: bg`) silently fails to get the documented `low → auto` promotion that an undeclared mode would receive: `risk_level: low` with no `mode:` field promotes to `auto`, but `risk_level: low` with `mode: bg` stays at the default `interactive`. Only set `mode_explicit = true` when the value matched the allowed set, so a malformed declaration is treated like an absent one for the risk-mode promotion. No existing test covers this branch (`meta_defaults_and_clamps` only checks `risk_level: dangerous` + `mode: auto`).

The duplicate-detection loop only catches repeated `index` values via `HashSet::insert`, but the error message itself tells the user "请修正编号为连续不重复" (please fix to consecutive non-repeating numbers). A skill with `## Step 1` then `## Step 3` (gap) passes silently and `${step3.*}` substitution may end up with no `CompletedStep` for `step2` if downstream code expects contiguous indices, or the `Vec<SkillStep>` execution order diverges from the declared numbering. Either drop "连续" from the message or extend the check to assert a contiguous 1..=N range.

The top-level value preprocessor only strips double quotes (`v.trim().trim_matches('"')` at the top of the match block), so single-quoted YAML scalars keep their quotes and silently misroute through the rest of the parser. Concrete failures: `name: 'foo-bar'` → `m.name = "'foo-bar'"` → fails `SKILL_NAME_CHARS_OK` and falls back to `dir_name`; `resumable: 'true'` / `enabled: 'false'` → literal string `"'true'"` / `"'false'"` doesn't match the `"true"|"1"|"yes"` set, so the field silently takes its `Default`. Only `intents` (line ~137–141) additionally calls `trim_matches('\'')`. Apply the same single-quote strip to the shared top-level `v`, or use a small YAML scalar unquote helper for every field.

`find("
---")` matches the `
` inside a `
---` closing fence, but `trim_start_matches('
')` only strips `
`. For Windows-authored SKILL.md files the returned body starts with `
`, leaving a stray `` as the very first character. This is currently masked downstream by `.trim()` and `.lines()` in `parse_skill_steps`, but the contract of `strip_frontmatter` should be "clean body" — apply `trim_start_matches(['
', ''])` (or `trim_start()`) so CRLF handling matches `parse_meta`'s `.lines()` behaviour and avoids surprising callers if a future caller inspects the first byte.

`risk_level`, `mode`, and `rollback` are stored as plain `String` despite each having a small, fixed set of legal values enforced by `matches!` in `parse_meta`. Every downstream consumer (scheduler, risk engine, UI, persistence) has to re-validate the same set and can drift silently if the parser ever accepts a new value (e.g. a future `"review"` mode). Modeling them as `#[derive(...)]` enums with `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]` (or hand-written `FromStr`) would (a) make invalid states unrepresentable, (b) centralize the legal-set validation in one place, and (c) let the risk→mode coercion live on a typed `match` instead of `String == "low"` string comparisons that have to be kept in sync with the parser's allowed-set literal.

comments.content: Poisoned mutex is silently recovered as if it were healthy: every guard acquisition uses `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` (with or without an `eprintln`). Mutex poisoning means a holder panicked mid-update, so registry invariants (state ⊕ session_id ⊕ actions) are no longer trustworthy. Subsequent writers happily overwrite a half-updated run; readers clone a corrupt snapshot. Replace with explicit `Result`-propagation or, at minimum, reset-and-flag via an audit/event so callers know the registry was inconsistent. Note: `is_skill_active_for` already diverges — it returns `false` on poison — so the policy is also inconsistent within this single file.

`is_skill_active_for` is the only function in this module that returns `false` on a poisoned mutex (`let Ok(guard) = registry.lock() else { return false; };`) — every sibling helper (`reopen_*`, `restore_*`, `active_skill_run_for`, `clear_terminal_*`, `test_hook_*`) silently recovers via `e.into_inner()`. This inconsistency means tool_guard can refuse to gate atomic tools while the rollback path / test hooks happily mutate the same registry in a corrupted state. Pick one policy and apply it uniformly.

`clear_terminal_skill_runs` evicts terminal runs globally — no `session_id` argument — while every other public helper in this module (`is_skill_active_for`, `reopen_failed_run_for_rollback`, `restore_failed_run_after_rollback`, `active_skill_run_for`) is strictly per-session. When session A's main loop clears at round entry, session B's terminal run from the previous round (still visible to B's `active_skill_run_for` until B itself clears) is silently destroyed. Either (a) accept the global semantics explicitly and document them as «race on round entry is OK because every entry clears before observing», or (b) take `session_id: Option<&str>` and only evict the caller's own terminal runs.

`load_skill_meta` discards the underlying `std::io::Error` via `map_err(|_| format!("..."))?`. `error::CommandError` already has `impl From<std::io::Error>` (→ `IoError`) and a dedicated `SkillLoadFailed { name, reason }` variant — both give frontend code-routing for IO_ERROR / SKILL_LOAD_FAILED (different hints) and a recoverable signal. `format!("…")?` falls through `From<String>` → `Internal` (code INTERNAL, recoverable=false), so a transient permission/lock error looks like a programmer error to the user. Use the typed variant + preserve the original io::Error in `reason`.

`active_skill_run_for` holds the registry mutex across `.values().find(...).cloned()` — and `SkillRun` clones `name`, `rollback`, `actions: Vec<String>`, `end_reason`, `session_id`. Under contention (round entry storms, rollback windows) this extends the critical section for an arbitrary number of bytes and blocks `reopen_*` / `restore_*` / `clear_terminal_*`. Snapshot only the keys/state you need (e.g. a small `SkillRunSnapshot { name, state, step, max_steps, ... }`) inside the lock and let the caller pull fields lazily, or release the lock first and copy via `try_clone` semantics.

`SkillRun::new` defaults `session_id: None`, and every filter in this module uses `r.session_id.as_deref() == session_id`. Any caller that forgets to assign `session_id` will (a) collide with every other background/cron-style task that also forgot, and (b) match a `None` query from non-session-aware code paths. Either make `session_id` a required `String` (e.g. `""` for background tasks, with the background case using a dedicated stable id generator), or split background-task runs into a separate registry key so they don't compete with foreground `None`.

`test_hook_insert_skill_run` / `test_hook_remove_skill_run` / `test_hook_skill_run_state` are declared `pub fn` (only `#[doc(hidden)]`). `#[doc(hidden)]` hides them from rustdoc but does **not** restrict visibility — every downstream crate (and any future consumer) can call them and mutate live skill state in production builds. They are gated to integration-test use only; tighten to `pub(crate)` (or `pub(crate)` inside a `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "test-hooks"))]` module) and keep the existing cfg-gated `test_*` siblings as the model.

`reopen_failed_run_for_rollback` collapses two distinct conditions into a single `false` return: (1) the run does not exist, and (2) the run exists but is in the wrong state / wrong session. The doc-comment promises the contract — but the caller (`rollback` driver) needs (1) to log "skill evicted while rolling back" vs (2) "wrong state, abort". Returning an enum or `Result<bool, RollbackOpenError>` lets callers distinguish and react appropriately.

Classic TOCTOU in `load_skill_meta`: `path.exists()` then `std::fs::read_to_string(&path)`. Between the two calls the file can be deleted / replaced (Skill edited by user during a hot reload, or symlink swap). Drop the `exists()` probe and rely on `read_to_string`'s `io::ErrorKind::NotFound` to drive the `continue` branch — single syscall per dir, no race window.

`MAX_SKILL_BODY` silently truncates with `text.chars().take(MAX_SKILL_BODY).collect()` — there is no signal in the returned `(SkillMeta, body)` that the body was cut off. Downstream code that joins `body` into a prompt will embed a malformed Skill doc on any skill >50KB. Either (a) reject oversize skills at load time with `CommandError::SkillLoadFailed`, or (b) return both `body` and `truncated: bool` / `total_chars: usize` so the prompt path can decide.

`in_quotes` detection is a naive byte-level heuristic that misfires on common JSON shapes: (1) escaped quotes inside the placeholder's enclosing string — e.g. `{"a":"say \"${step1.x}\" now"}` — the trailing `\"` is a single byte, but the next char is `n` not `"`, so this specific case is OK; however if the placeholder is followed by `\"` the byte after the match is `\` not `"` and we correctly skip escaping, BUT (2) the byte immediately after the match being `"` does NOT mean the placeholder is inside a string — e.g. `{"k":"${step1.x}"}` next to `{"k":"${step1.x}": "v"}` (key follows), or `"${step1.x}":` (placeholder is the value but followed by `":` from the next kv pair in unquoted context). The real defect: `bytes.get(m.end()) == Some(&b'"')` is true for any text where the next byte happens to be `"`, even if the placeholder is in a key position or unquoted template text — causing escape injection that wasn't needed. Conversely `m.end() == text.len()` correctly skips escaping (no byte after), so end-of-input is fine, but the asymmetric guard at the start (`m.start() > 0`) plus the requirement that the *next* byte be `"` is too strict for placeholders preceded by an opening quote that is the JSON structural opening of a value where the closing quote is many bytes later (still triggers correctly), yet too loose for cases where adjacent quotes are coincidental. A real parser walk (or `serde_json` aware scan) is needed for soundness; at minimum this should be flagged and documented as best-effort, with tests for adversarial inputs.

Silent mutex poison recovery. A poisoned `Mutex` means a panic occurred while the lock was held, so the `SkillRun` HashMap behind the guard may be in an inconsistent state (e.g., state set to Failed without `end_reason`, or `step` already incremented past `max_steps`). This pattern silently discards the poison via `e.into_inner()` and continues, propagating the corruption to subsequent readers. The same pattern is duplicated in 6 call sites (start_skill, skill_on_step, skill_on_step_post, skill_mark_paused, skill_confirm_result, skill_finish), making it hard to fix consistently. Recommended: propagate the poison (return the error), or at minimum log to the audit subsystem and abort the operation rather than continue with potentially corrupt skill state. Consider extracting a helper that returns `Result<MutexGuard, CommandError>` to enforce this policy at one place.

comments.content: `audit_log_hook` is invoked while still holding the `skill_runs` mutex. Audit hooks commonly write to disk, push to a queue, or take other locks; calling them inside this critical section violates the "don't hold guards across calls into user code" discipline and risks deadlock if the audit path ever re-enters the registry (e.g., a hook that itself touches `skill_runs`). Additionally, `runs.get(n)` is called on the same lock from within the loop, which is fine re: aliasing but further extends the critical section. Recommended: collect the (name, steps) pairs under the lock, drop the guard, then iterate the collected list and call `audit_log_hook`. The `runs.insert(meta.name.clone(), run)` on the next line is also part of this oversized critical section — splitting it into "check + record completed names" / "insert + audit" phases would shrink the window materially.

`load_skill_meta(app, name)` performs blocking file I/O (it reads `SKILL.md` from disk per `name`) and is invoked inside the `runs.iter_mut()` loop *while still holding the `skill_runs` mutex*. Every rollback='auto' skill with non-empty actions triggers one full file read per skill, all serialized behind the global lock and blocking any concurrent `start_skill` / `skill_on_step` / `skill_confirm_result` calls on the same registry. Recommended: snapshot `runs.iter().filter(...).map(|(n, r)| (n.clone(), r.actions.clone(), r.rollback.clone())).collect::<Vec<_>>()` under the lock, drop the guard, then perform `load_skill_meta` and rollback-section construction outside the critical section. Even better: cache the rollback section alongside the SkillRun at parse time so this function never touches disk.

`step_check` only short-circuits on `Paused`; it happily increments `run.step`, evaluates max-steps/timeout fuses, and appends to `run.actions` for any other state, including terminal states (`Failed`, `Terminated`, `Completed`). Because the state machine is updated from multiple call sites (`advance_skill` reports `Fail`/`Terminate` without mutating, but `skill_confirm_result`/`start_skill`/`skill_finish` mutate), there is a real window where `skill_on_step` arrives after the run is already terminal — and currently it will still count, possibly re-firing the max-steps fuse (writing a fresh `end_reason`, overwriting the prior one) and recording an action for a tool call that ran on a dead skill. Recommended: at function entry, treat `Failed` / `Terminated` / `Completed` as no-op (mirroring `skill_on_step_post`'s pre-filter) and only proceed when `state` is `Running` or `Paused`.

Pre-flight blacklist check is wasteful and fragile: (a) `format!("{} {}", meta.description.to_lowercase(), meta.intents.join(" "))` allocates a fresh lowercased description string and a freshly-joined intent string on every call, even when `meta.intents` is empty; (b) `BLACKLIST.iter().find(|b| hay.contains(&b.to_lowercase()))` recomputes `b.to_lowercase()` per keyword per call, but every literal in `BLACKLIST` is already lowercase, so the per-keyword allocation is dead work; (c) joining intents with a space means a keyword like "清空所有" can match across the boundary of two adjacent intents (e.g., intent "...清空" + "...所有..."), producing false positives that silently block legitimate skills. Recommended: lowercase the blacklist once at compile time (or use a `&[&str]` of ASCII-folding-safe literals and case-fold both sides with a stable helper), lowercase the description once and reuse it, and search each field independently (description OR each intent) instead of gluing them into one haystack — that also prevents cross-intent boundary matches.

`escape_json_str_inner` swallows serialization errors as an empty string via `unwrap_or_default()`. If `serde_json::to_string(v)` ever fails (e.g. NaN/Infinity via unusual input, or a future type change), the placeholder silently expands to nothing, producing malformed JSON downstream with no diagnostic — defeating the very intent of the function ("avoid silent Null fallback"). Additionally, the `.unwrap_or(&s)` fallback on the strip chain returns the still-quoted JSON literal (`"..."`) if prefix/suffix stripping ever fails, which would corrupt the output by injecting raw `"` characters. Since `serde_json::to_string(&str)` is total, document the invariant explicitly and prefer `serde_json::to_string(v).expect("&str is always valid JSON")` (or match on the Result and propagate), and replace the strip fallback with a clearer single-string slice (`&s[1..s.len()-1]` after a length check) so a bug surfaces as a panic rather than silent corruption.

`re.captures(m.as_str()).expect("已匹配的文本必然能再捕获")` is a panic in production library code. The invariant "a `find_iter` match implies `captures` will succeed on the same span" is plausible but not part of `regex`'s public contract, and the closure shape (`FnMut(&Captures) -> Option<String>`) already requires a `Captures` value — yet `find_iter` only yields `Match`. The clean fix is to use `re.captures_iter(text)` instead of `find_iter`, which yields `Captures` directly without any re-matching and removes the `expect` entirely. That also avoids re-scanning the matched text and is more idiomatic.

comments.content: `bot_sessions_load` issues a SELECT against SQLite without taking DB_WRITE_LOCK (or any read-side guard), while every write path does. With rusqlite's default journal mode and busy_timeout, concurrent writes can still surface SQLITE_BUSY on the read side, or produce torn reads if the connection is not opened in WAL mode. Either enable WAL + busy_timeout in `open_db`, or serialize all DB access through DB_WRITE_LOCK (or a separate read lock) so the read path is consistent with the writers.

DB_WRITE_LOCK is acquired before `super::open_db(&app)`, so connection setup (filesystem I/O, schema initialization, WAL open) happens under the global write mutex. This widens the critical section unnecessarily and can serialize all writers behind an unrelated I/O stall. Open the connection first, then take the lock around the actual write, mirroring what `bot_session_delete` already does inside `spawn_blocking`.

Same lock-hold-across-open pattern as `bot_session_create`: DB_WRITE_LOCK is taken before `open_db`. Opening the connection inside the lock serializes unrelated writers behind connection-setup work; move `open_db` above the lock acquisition.

`title.trim()` is written straight into the database with no empty check, unlike `bot_session_create_inner` which filters empty titles and falls back to "新对话". A rename with whitespace-only input (or an empty string) will silently persist an empty title and corrupt the session list. Reject empty results with `CommandError::InvalidInput` (or any typed error), or apply the same `filter(|t| !t.is_empty()).unwrap_or_else(...)` fallback used on create.

The `execute` result (number of affected rows) is discarded, so a rename against a non-existent `id` returns `Ok(())` and silently updates nothing — the caller cannot distinguish "renamed" from "no such session". Check the returned `usize` and return a `CommandError` (e.g. `NotFound`) when it is `0`.

`unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` silently recovers from a poisoned `DB_WRITE_LOCK`. If a previous holder panicked mid-write (e.g. partway through `bot_session_delete_inner`'s transaction) the database state can be inconsistent, and silently continuing lets later commands act on that corrupted state. At minimum, log the poisoning; ideally propagate it as a `CommandError` so callers see the failure instead of potentially observing torn state.

`bot_history_save_inner` stamps every inserted row with the same `now` captured once before the loop, so after a full overwrite the entire history collapses to one timestamp. The schema explicitly models per-row `created_at INTEGER NOT NULL`, so any downstream consumer sorting/grouping/deduping on `created_at` (timeline UI, sync, retention) will break — ordering only survives via the auto-increment `id`, not the documented temporal column. Either preserve `m.created_at` (add it to `BotMsgRow`) or stamp each row incrementally (e.g., `now + index as i64`).

`bot_history_clear` deletes rows but never refreshes `bot_sessions.updated_at`, contradicting `bot_history_save_inner` (which does) and `bot_session_rename` (which also bumps `updated_at`). After a clear, the session still looks "recently active" in `bot_sessions_load`, which orders by `updated_at DESC`. Add `UPDATE bot_sessions SET updated_at = ?1 WHERE id = ?2` (with the same `now`) before returning, ideally inside a small transaction so the delete and bump are atomic.

`bot_history_clear` issues a bare `DELETE` and returns `Ok(())` without wrapping in a transaction, while the sibling `bot_session_delete_inner` in `bot_sessions.rs` deletes the matching rows and the session row atomically inside a `tx`. Even for a single statement this is fine on its own, but combined with the missing `updated_at` bump (see other comment) the natural fix is to wrap both statements in `conn.transaction()` so the session timestamp cannot diverge from the message delete on crash.

`bot_history_save_inner` returns `Result<(), String>` and the body chains `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())` on every `prepare`/`execute`. The caller then re-wraps as `CommandError::DbError(...)`. The structured `rusqlite::Error` (code, offset, SQL) is discarded at the boundary, so logs and any future error-mapping lose actionable detail. Prefer a small enum like `DbOpError(rusqlite::Error)` or propagate `rusqlite::Error` directly until the `CommandError` conversion, mirroring `bot_session_delete_inner` which keeps `CommandError::DbError` typed end-to-end.

`bot_history_load` reads `bot_messages` without any synchronization. WAL mode lets readers and writers proceed concurrently, so a `bot_history_save` DELETE+INSERT run can overlap with a load and the caller may observe (a) the transient empty state mid-overwrite or (b) only the tail of the new batch. Even if the UI treats this as a fresh load, the inconsistency is silent — consider either holding a `DB_WRITE_LOCK.shared`-style guard (e.g., `parking_lot::RwLock`) or wrapping the load+save contract in a "load returns last committed snapshot" invariant via a monotonic read epoch. At minimum, document that callers must retry on empty/unexpectedly short results.

`bot_set_enabled(false)` discards the `remove_file` error: if removal fails (Windows file lock, AV holding the file, permission denied, read-only volume), the flag persists and `bot_get_enabled` keeps returning `true`, so the user has turned the bot off in the UI but it's still enabled on disk. Either propagate the error (`?`) or `match` the result and convert a failure into a typed error so the command caller can react. The write branch (`std::fs::write(...)?`) already propagates, so symmetry is also broken.

Byte-level slicing `&request_id[..8.min(request_id.len())]` on a string the frontend controls will panic if the 8th byte lands mid-codepoint (e.g. CJK char straddling byte 8). The `.min(len)` only protects against out-of-bounds, not against non-UTF-8 boundaries. The caller in `bot_confirm_response` already takes `request_id: String` from a Tauri command, so this is reachable by any UI client. Use a char-aware slice (e.g. `request_id.chars().take(8).collect::<String>()`) or guard with `is_char_boundary`; same fix needed for `take_confirm`'s `&request_id[..8.min(request_id.len())]` below.

comments.content: `impl Drop for StopGuard` swallows lock poison (`if let Ok(...)` with no else branch) while every other call site here does `unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!(...); e.into_inner() })`. Asymmetry matters: if the registry mutex is poisoned (e.g. a previous panic mid-insertion), every subsequent `Drop` silently skips deregistration, so `active_execution_count` never returns to zero and the process-exit drain loop documented at `active_execution_count` waits forever. Use the same `into_inner()` recovery path used elsewhere so a poisoned registry still unregisters (and so the leak is observable in logs).

Log injection risk: the comment claims session_id is escaped ("转义防日志伪造/多行撕裂"), but the helper used is `crate::bot::truncate_for_log` whose name suggests truncation only — there is no evidence here that it strips `\n`, `\r`, or ANSI/control bytes. Since `bot_stop` accepts `session_id` directly from the frontend Tauri command, a client (or compromised renderer) can inject arbitrary log lines by submitting `"sess\nERROR | fake | …"`. Either ensure `truncate_for_log` also strips/escapes newlines and control chars, or sanitize here before formatting. The same shape recurs in the `confirm | ... | {detail}` audit line below (`detail` is also user-supplied).

`force_stop` is `pub` on `StopGuard` even though the doc comment says it's for unit tests and bypasses the registry. This widens the API surface to the whole crate (and any downstream binaries using `bot_slash` as a lib): any caller can now flip a guard's flag out of band, with no audit log and no Skill-scheduler coordination, defeating the whole point of the registry/confirm pairing. Restrict to `pub(crate)` or gate with `#[cfg(test)]`.

`tauri::async_runtime::spawn` is used for the `clear_for` cleanup task with no `JoinHandle` retained. If the future panics (e.g. an `unwrap` inside `exec_steps::clear_for`) the panic propagates to the runtime's task and the failure is invisible to `bot_stop`'s caller, who already returned `Ok(())` to the frontend. Either keep the handle and log on join error, or move the cleanup into `bot_stop` directly (it's quick — a map clear — and doesn't need to be detached). Also: detach-on-drop forfeits cancellation propagation if the runtime is shutting down.

`emit("bot-confirm", ...)` failure is swallowed by `let _ =`. The oneshot timeout will eventually resolve to deny, so this is not a safety bug — but the loss of telemetry means a regression where the main window is closed mid-ask (or any IPC failure) is indistinguishable from a user ignoring the prompt for 60 s. Log the emit failure so the difference shows up in `audit_log`.

`bot_stop` only forwards `flag_session_stopped`'s `Result` to the frontend (`stopped.map(|_| ())`) but discards the actual count of stopped guards. Worse, the `usize` count is the only signal callers have for "did /stop do anything this time" (empty stops vs. multiple active executions). Either return it (change command signature) or at least log it via `audit_log` so the audit trail distinguishes "user pressed /stop while idle" from "user stopped 3 in-flight runs".
