    // 本会话在途确认弹窗立即按拒绝收尾——sender 随条目 drop，

comments.content: Log injection: model-controlled `name`, `args`, and `result` are formatted into a single audit-log line without newline/control-character sanitization. `truncate_for_log` only bounds length. A prompt-injected (or simply verbose) model can craft a tool name like `x\nERROR: forged` to inject arbitrary log lines and mislead downstream audit analysis. The author's own comment acknowledges the risk ("工具名是模型给的字符串，直插可伪造日志行") but no fix is applied. Recommend sanitizing control chars (escape `\n`/`\r`/`\t` to literal sequences or replace with ` `) before formatting, e.g. via a small `sanitize_for_log` helper in `crate::bot`.

Log injection (companion of the tool-line finding): `final_text` is model-controlled and is formatted into the hallucination-guard audit-log line without newline/control-character sanitization. `truncate_for_log` only truncates length. A prompt-injected model can use this to forge arbitrary log lines here as well. Apply the same `sanitize_for_log` treatment before formatting.

Cancellation ignored during retry sleep: this branch sleeps `LLM_RETRY_DELAY` (1.5s) before re-issuing the HTTP request, without consulting `StopGuard::stopped()`. If the user clicks /stop during the sleep, the second request still goes out — wasting bandwidth, re-serializing a potentially large body, and continuing to consume API quota after the user already cancelled. The symmetric `Ok(r)` retryable-status branch above has the same gap (`drop(r)`; `tokio::time::sleep(...).await; continue;`). Fix: either check `stop.stopped()` immediately after the sleep (and break out with an error), or use `tokio::select!` with a `stop.cancelled()` future so the sleep is itself cancellable.

Synthesized tool_call IDs (`call_synth_{i}`) are sent back to the API on the next round via the assistant `tool_calls` array AND paired tool-result messages. Strict providers (Anthropic, OpenAI strict mode) require server-issued IDs and reject the next request with 400 invalid params ("No tool with id X found" / similar). The code's own comment documents the known limitation but the workaround only succeeds against lenient gateways and silently degrades against strict ones — the loop will simply fail on the next request with no tool calls executed, even though `mutation_done` may have been set incorrectly along the way. Consider one of: (a) pre-scan and abort this round with a user-facing explanation before sending; (b) per-provider config flag controlling whether synth-IDs are sent; (c) report the omission as a hard error so the user sees the real cause.

When `advance_dsl` returns `Finish` mid-loop (e.g. external completion signal, step-check circuit breaker), the code `break`s and falls through to the post-loop block, which (a) builds a summary header `✅ 自动执行完成（{} 步）` using `steps.len()` instead of `results.len()`, falsely claiming full completion; (b) calls `skill_finish(app, true, "done", session_id)` which may overwrite the legitimate finish reason set by `advance_dsl`; and (c) persists outcome kind=`done` and returns `DslOutcome::Done`. The Finish branch should early-return with an outcome that reflects the actual run state, not silently coerce to a Done summary.

The Done path discards the result of `skill_finish` with `let _ = ...`, but the preceding comment explicitly states that failing to transition Running→Completed leaks a "zombie Running" run that keeps the atomic-tool gate open and contaminates subsequent tool calls until the step-count fuse fires. If `skill_finish` returns `Err`, that exact failure mode materializes silently. At minimum log the error via `audit_log_hook` so an operator can correlate; ideally propagate or retry so the state transition is observable.
comments.existing_code: let _ = super::runtime::skill_finish(app, true, "done", session_id);

comments.content: `let _ = crate::db::upsert_skill_outcome(&conn, &outcome)` silently drops the Result. The function's name advertises "quiet failure", but the inline comment already acknowledges that without `DB_WRITE_LOCK` writes would silently fail under load — now that the lock is taken, dropped write errors hide schema mismatches, disk-full, or genuine SQL errors that should be visible in audit. Either propagate the error to the caller (and let the scheduler log a `skill_dsl_persist_failed` audit hook) or emit an `audit_log_hook` warning here so the failure is observable rather than silent.
comments.existing_code: let _ = crate::db::upsert_skill_outcome(&conn, &outcome);

comments.content: The `runs` registry lock is held for the entire iteration, including while `crate::bot::audit_log_hook` is invoked for each terminated run. If `audit_log_hook` ever performs I/O that re-enters the skill_runs registry (or any other lock ordered before this one), this is a classic lock-while-doing-I/O deadlock risk; even when it does not, it serializes I/O across every termination. Collect `(name, reason)` pairs under the lock, release the lock, then iterate and emit audit logs. The poisoned-mutex recovery via `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` also masks a poisoning incident that other call sites presumably want to know about.
comments.existing_code: crate::bot::audit_log_hook(app, &format!("skill_terminated | name: {name} | {reason}"));

comments.content: `reopen_failed_run_for_rollback` flips the SkillRun from Failed→Running so atomic tools pass the gate; the matching `restore_failed_run_after_rollback` is called conditionally only if `reopened` is true. If any rollback `execute_tool(...).await` panics, or `restore_failed_run_after_rollback` itself errors/panics, the run is left in Running state with the AtomicGuard reopened — the very contract the rollback window is supposed to enforce is then permanently broken. Wrap the restore in a Drop guard or RAII scope-guard (`scopeguard::defer!`) so it runs on unwind as well as on the success path.

SchedGuard::Drop silently absorbs mutex poisoning (no log), unlike `acquire` which eprintln's. A panic-or-poison event between acquire and Drop becomes invisible, defeating the mutex's bug-detection role and potentially allowing a stale task id to leak if the cleanup itself panics mid-iteration.

find_due_tasks silently swallows optimistic-lock upsert failures and performs up to 3 sequential `db_load` calls per tick. A concurrent user edit during the scan window can make `expected_updated_at = fresh.updated_at` stale, causing `db_upsert` to fail; the code branches only on `is_ok()` with no `audit_log`/retry. The stale at: cleanup and missed-recurring `sched_last` update can be permanently lost with zero visibility. The 1-3 load pattern also widens the race window between detection and write.

start_scheduler has no shutdown signal and no panic recovery. The spawned `loop { ticker.tick().await; ... }` runs forever; if any awaited operation inside the loop panics (db_load, audit_log, broadcast, or `find_due_tasks` itself), the entire scheduler task dies silently and no scheduled tasks ever run again until app restart. There's also no bound on the number of concurrent `run_scheduled` spawns, so a burst of newly-due tasks could overwhelm the async runtime.

`Duration::days(1)` shifts wall-clock across DST boundaries for recurring schedules. After `resolve_local` returns today's `DateTime<Local>`, adding exactly 24 real hours advances by absolute time, not wall-clock; a `daily:09:00` becomes effectively `daily:10:00` after spring-forward and `daily:08:00` after fall-back. The same issue applies to weekly's `+= Duration::days(7)` and monthly's day-roll loop, though monthly is partially mitigated because it rebuilds `from_ymd_opt` each iteration.

run_scheduled silently abandons execution if the initial sched_last upsert fails. The optimistic-lock update of `sched_last` is gated only by `is_ok()`; if a concurrent user edit conflicts, the task is not run and only an audit log entry is produced. Next tick re-detects the task as due and retries — but if the conflicting edit pattern persists (e.g., a sync client continuously rewriting the task), the task can indefinitely skip while still appearing scheduled to the user. Same silent-`is_ok` pattern recurs in the post-execution note write below.

`resolve_local` returning None for a DST gap (no valid time within +3h) propagates through `occurrence_after` via `?`, causing the entire schedule to return None for that day. `classify_due` then reports `NotDue` with no audit log, so the task silently pauses for one day and the user has no indication. This is rare in practice (3+ hour DST gaps are unusual) but the silent-skip is the wrong default — should at minimum emit an audit entry on resolve failure.

first_open_tag("...<abbr>...</abbr>...", "<a") incorrectly matches "<abbr>" because `find("<a")` is a prefix-prefix match. The same is true for first_between. In parse_bing and parse_baidu, the search for `<a` should use `<a ` (trailing space) or `<a>` to skip `<abbr>`, `<acronym>`, `<address>`, `<area>`, etc. Otherwise h3/h2 blocks that contain a leading <abbr> will produce wrong titles or missing links.

first_between("...", "") will match the first `` etc., and then find the first `` which corresponds to that same tag. Result: titles get extra text or wrong boundaries. This compounds with the first_open_tag bug — the title and the link can come from different DOM nodes in the same h2/h3.

The `unwrap_or_else(|_| reqwest::Client::new())` fallback silently produces a client with no timeouts and no `redirect::Policy::none()`. If builder() ever fails (some TLS backend init failure, runtime misconfig, etc.), every subsequent request — including all SSRF-protected fetches — has no overall deadline. An attacker-controlled slow target can hold open a fetch_text task indefinitely, pinning an executor worker and starving the bot. Either panic loudly, log+abort, or at minimum keep a hard upper-bound request timeout via reqwest's middleware.

check_public_url accepts both http and https, so a redirect from `https://attacker.com/` → `http://victim.internal/` will pass validation even though it crosses an insecure boundary. With auto-redirects disabled and TLS exposed only on the first hop, an attacker who controls the initial https target can downgrade the user-visible request to cleartext for any subsequent hop — mid-flight tampering of the returned HTML. Either reject `http` from `https` chain origins, or downgrade `https→http` only to a same-eTLD+1 host and log a warning.

When the static extractor returns <100 chars, the raw user-supplied URL is sent verbatim to `https://r.jina.ai/`. This is a third-party data-exfiltration boundary that is NOT audit-logged by bot.rs (audit_log is only called on Tavily/Brave failure, not on Jina use). The user is also not notified. At minimum, call `crate::bot::audit_log(app, &format!("web_fetch.jina_fallback | {host}"))` and consider gating behind a setting.

Semantic-div matching uses `attrs.contains(k)` for ["article","content","post","entry","main"]. This is a substring match on the lowercase-ified attr string, so "post" matches "postponed", "postscript", "comment-posting-form", etc. Combine with the "comment" exclusion that also uses `contains`, and a page with `<div class="comment-post">` gets *excluded* (correct) but a page with `<div class="reposted-article">` and a small real `<article>` gets selected by "article" anyway. Tighten to a token-boundary match (split by whitespace/'"'/'\'' and check whole tokens) or use a regex.

parse_alt_ipv4 only kicks in for strings that are *pure* digits/hex (the `chars().all(is_ascii_digit)` guard fails the moment a `.` appears). The defense then falls back to `host.parse::<IpAddr>()`. This relies on Rust's `Ipv4Addr::from_str` accepting octal/hex per-component ("0177.0.0.1", "0x7f.0.0.0.1"). It does, BUT the `url` crate's host parser may surface the raw string form to `host_str()` (e.g. `http://0177.0.0.1/`), and if a future std/url change rejects one of those notations, this would silently route the request to a hostname that DNS resolves back to 127.0.0.1 — bypassing the IP-literal path entirely. Consider explicitly normalizing via `s.parse::<IpAddr>()` (which accepts the full inet_aton grammar) *and* `Ipv4Addr::from_str` as a second pass before treating as a hostname.

The output-cap truncation iterates the string twice (`chars().count()` then `chars().take(...).collect()`). With max 6000 or 30000 chars this is negligible, but consider a single-pass `char_indices` accumulator + early break to avoid allocating a temporary String from `chars().take(SEARCH_OUTPUT_CAP)` for the common non-truncated case.

Reading `seen.contains(&key)` for every result is O(n²) within web_search (max 8 results so it's 64 comparisons in the worst case). Likewise the `domain_count` vec is searched linearly twice per result. With n capped at 8 it's not a real perf issue, but a HashSet<&str> + HashMap<&str, usize> would make the intent ("dedup by title; cap per domain") clearer and protect against future caps being raised.

When extracting Baidu snippets, the snippet is taken from the first 200 chars of any qualifying <span> after the h3. This snippet is later shown to the LLM. There is no length normalization, language detection, or de-HTML-entity pass — `strip_tags` removes tags but the text might still contain residual entities or be truncated mid-word. This is a benign correctness note, but combined with the fact that the search snippet isn't cryptographically authenticated, a search-engine MitM (via a compromised frontend or hostile Bing/Baidu response in an HTTP-only corporate env) could pre-stage prompt-injection content. Worth flagging at the bot.rs audit layer rather than re-validating here.

Both `crate::db::open_db` and `crate::db::load_all_skill_outcomes` failures are silently swallowed via `if let Ok(...)`. If the settings DB is locked, schema-mismatched, or migration failed, the user sees a perfectly normal-looking skill list with empty `last_outcome` badges — no log, no telemetry, no surfaced error. This hides data-integrity and migration problems from operators and makes "why are the badges gone?" reports very hard to triage.

Two correctness issues in the same critical section:

1. **TOCTOU race**: `dest.exists()` then `copy_dir_all` are not atomic. Two concurrent `skills_import` calls for the same skill (rapid double-click from the settings page, or parallel IPC) can both pass the existence check and then race to write — producing an interleaved directory and a confusing `IoError` instead of the intended `SkillLoadFailed` "already exists" error.

2. **No rollback on partial copy failure**: `copy_dir_all` can fail mid-recursion (disk full mid-write, permission revoked, etc.), leaving a half-installed `dest/` directory. The function returns `Err`, but `dest` stays on disk — the next `scan_skills` will surface this broken skill, and the user has no signal that the install was partial.

Every filesystem error in `copy_dir_all` is collapsed to `e.to_string()`, dropping the failing path, the syscall (`read_dir`/`copy`/`create_dir_all`), and the OS error code. From the user-facing side a permission denial on `scripts/foo.sh` and a missing directory entry produce indistinguishable strings, and the file path that actually failed cannot be reconstructed from logs. The same pattern appears in `skills_import` (`create_dir_all(&dir).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?`) and `skills_delete` (`CommandError::IoError(e.to_string())` for `remove_dir_all` failures).

`parse_frontmatter` returns a `(name, error)` pair but only the `name` is used here — the `error` is discarded. A malformed SKILL.md frontmatter (unclosed `---\n---\n` block, invalid YAML, etc.) silently degrades to the directory-name fallback with no user-visible warning. The user has no signal that the resulting `name` does not match what they wrote in `name:`, and if the fallback happens to also fail `validate_skill_name` they get a generic "无效" message that doesn't point at the real cause (broken frontmatter, not a bad name choice).
comments.existing_code: let (name, _) = parse_frontmatter(&text, &dir_name);

comments.content: `rebuild_intent_routes` returns `()`, so any internal failure (invalid regex in the newly imported skill's `intents`, regex-compile error, etc.) is invisible. After a successful `skills_import` / `skills_delete`, the command reports success while the in-memory intent router can be inconsistent with the on-disk skill set — the next chat may silently route to a skill that no longer exists or fail to route to one that does. There's no log or surfaced error to indicate the divergence, and the user only discovers it as a routing anomaly later.

Missing transaction in legacy binding migration: the UPDATE loop runs one row at a time without wrapping them in `conn.transaction()`. A crash, panic, or concurrent writer between iterations leaves the table partially migrated — some rows already on `files` JSON, others still on `file_path`/`file_is_dir` — breaking the idempotency contract and the SELECT filter (`files IS NULL OR files = '' OR files = '[]'`) used by the next run. Wrap the loop in a single transaction and commit at the end (or use a single `UPDATE ... CASE id WHEN ...` statement).

Silent error swallowing in column check: `.unwrap_or(false)` collapses any prepare/query error into `false`, making "DB is broken / table missing / driver error" indistinguishable from "column already present". If the check silently fails, later SELECTs/UPDATEs against `files` will surface the corruption much later as confusing runtime errors. Return the prepare error instead so the migration caller can react.

Silent row-error drop during data.json import: `filter_map(|r| r.ok())` discards every row whose `id` fails to decode, producing an under-counted `existing` set. Tasks present in the DB but unreadable (type mismatch, NULL, corrupted page) are then treated as missing and re-inserted, which can violate UNIQUE/PRIMARY KEY constraints and either fail the migration or — if no UNIQUE on id — silently duplicate rows. Surface the error (or at minimum log it) instead of dropping it.

TOCTOU race on the one-shot atomic: `done.load(Ordering::SeqCst)` followed by `exec()` is a classic check-then-act. Two concurrent callers can both observe `false` and both invoke `exec()`, so the "run once" contract is not actually enforced. Replace with a `compare_exchange` loop (or wrap `exec` in a `Mutex`) and downgrade the ordering — `Acquire`/`Release` (or `Relaxed` on the load side) is sufficient for a "did we run?" flag, not `SeqCst`.

PRAGMA journal_mode result not verified: `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` returns a row with the *actual* mode that took effect. On a read-only mount, network FS, or locked DB SQLite silently falls back to `delete`, but `execute_batch` discards the result. The caller then operates under WAL durability assumptions while still being in rollback-journal mode, which can break `synchronous=NORMAL` crash-safety expectations and surprise readers expecting the single-writer WAL semantics. Query the pragma and return an error (or log) if the returned mode is not `wal`.

Error context dropped at every boundary: `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())` is applied uniformly, so the original `rusqlite::Error` (with code, SQL, position info) and `serde_json::Error` (with line/column) are flattened to a bare string before they leave the function. Wrap them with `anyhow::Error`/`thiserror` and `map_err(|e| format!("migrate_legacy_file_bindings: {e}"))` (or equivalent context-bearing wrappers) so log output and tests can attribute failures to the migration step that produced them.
comments.existing_code: .map_err(|e| e.to_string())

comments.content: Every `rusqlite::Error` in this file is collapsed to `String` via `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())` at the public API boundary — not only in `upsert_skill_outcome`, but also in `conn.prepare(...).map_err(...)`, the `query_map(...)` builder, and the per-row `row.map_err(...)` inside `load_all_skill_outcomes`. This discards the typed error and any actionable context. Prefer a dedicated error type (`enum SkillOutError` with `#[from] rusqlite::Error`, or `anyhow::Result`/`thiserror`) so callers can match on the cause, attach context (e.g. the failing SQL), and avoid leaking raw driver strings into UI layers.

comments.content: `kind: String` represents a closed domain value (likely something like `completed` / `failed` / `rolled_back`, given the surrounding `reason`, `completed_summary`, and `rollback_attempted` fields). Modeling it as `String` lets any typo or out-of-set value pass silently through both serialization and SQL. Per the domain-modelling checklist item, replace it with a `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` enum so invalid states are unrepresentable and unknown values fail loudly at the boundary instead of being miscategorized downstream.

comments.existing_code: pub kind: String,

comments.content: `load_all_skill_outcomes` streams every row of `skill_outcomes` into a `HashMap`, but allocates the map with `HashMap::new()`, causing repeated reallocation as rows arrive. The expected size is known at this point — either issue a cheap `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM skill_outcomes` first, use a documented estimate, or, if the schema stores `skill_name` as `PRIMARY KEY`, count rows with the same `query_map` iterator. Passing that count to `HashMap::with_capacity(...)` removes avoidable growth cost on the load path.

let estimated = /* COUNT(*) or known cardinality */;
    let mut map = std::collections::HashMap::with_capacity(estimated);

comments.content: Information leakage via serialized error payloads: `LlmApiError.body_preview`, `DbError`, `IoError`, `KeyringError`, and the catch‑all `Internal` carry raw inner strings that are returned verbatim to the renderer. Provider error bodies (Anthropic / OpenAI / etc.) routinely echo request IDs, account info, or even API‑key fragments; SQL error strings can leak table/column names; `io::Error` messages embed absolute file paths. Once these reach the renderer they’re also at the mercy of client logging. Recommend a redaction/sanitisation step before `message()` is built (drop secrets, hash paths, truncate bodies, or send a generic message plus a server‑side correlation id), and restrict `body_preview` to a tight length/character set.

`From<String>` / `From<&str>` blanket `→ CommandError::Internal` defeats the file’s own design goal: every `Err("…".into())` collapses to `INTERNAL` with `recoverable=false`, silently degrading real domain failures (missing arg, blocked tool, etc.) into non‑retryable internal errors that the frontend will hide the retry button for. Even with the “migration aid” rationale, this is a footgun that gets exercised from call sites via `?` without any reviewer noticing. Consider (a) deleting the impls and forcing explicit `CommandError::Internal(...).into()`, or (b) gating them behind a `#[cfg(feature = "legacy_string_errors")]` so the production path is the typed variants.

`From<CommandError> for String` is a public, project‑wide trait impl whose doc says “仅 tool→model 边界用”, but nothing in the type system enforces that. Combined with `From<String> for CommandError::Internal` it enables a silent round‑trip loss: `Result<_, CommandError>` → `?` into `Result<_, String>` → `?` into `Result<_, CommandError>` returns a fresh `Internal` with the human message, losing the original code/recoverable entirely. Either narrow the visibility (e.g. a free `fn cmd_error_to_string(e: &CommandError) -> String` that borrows `&self`, or a tuple struct newtype `ToolBoundaryError(CommandError)` with its own `Display`), or at minimum remove the `From<CommandError> for String` impl so `?` cannot accidentally cross the boundary.

Wire‑protocol string is triplicated per code: `#[serde(rename = "…")]`, the `as_str()` match arm, and the position in `CommandErrorCode::ALL`. Tests cover `as_str` ↔ serde rename and the `ALL`‑membership invariant, but they do not pin `ALL` order against the enum declaration order, and any “add a code” change still requires three coordinated edits (variant, `as_str`, `ALL`) with no compile‑time check that the `ALL` slice is in sync. Consider replacing the slice with an exhaustive match returning `()` (so a missing variant fails to compile) and/or a const‑generated table via a build script, and add a test that asserts `ALL.iter().zip(declared_variants)` align.

comments.content: `Serialize` uses `serialize_struct("CommandError", 3)` and passes a fixed arity. JSON ignores the name and arity, so this is fine for the current IPC, but if the same error type is ever sent through a binary serializer (bincode / postcard / msgpack with schema) the name will be emitted as a discriminator and the 3‑field arity will be checked, causing either an opaque error or a mis‑serialised payload. Use `serialize_tuple(3, …)` for an order‑sensitive anonymous 3‑tuple, or define an internal `#[derive(Serialize)]` struct `{ code, message, recoverable }` and serialise that, so the wire shape is owned by the type system instead of the hand‑written impl.

When the stored `links` JSON is malformed, the row is returned to the caller with an empty `Vec` and only an `eprintln!` log. The UI then silently sees a missing link list for an item whose data is still in the DB, and the bad JSON is never reported back to the front-end (no error, no warning surfaced). Prefer returning `Err` with the parse error (or a tagged variant like `Result<WorkspaceItem, DbError>`) so the caller can decide whether to surface it, quarantine the bad blob, or back it up before overwriting. Silently substituting `Vec::new()` is a data-integrity hazard.

`serde_json::to_string(&it.links).unwrap_or_else(|_| "[]".into())` silently replaces the user's links with `[]` if serialization fails. The surrounding `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` then writes that `[]` to disk, so a transient serialization glitch (non-finite floats, broken Serialize impl, etc.) wipes the user's links from the database. Surface the serde error via the surrounding `Result` and refuse to upsert that row instead of substituting a placeholder that destroys data.

comments.content: `workspace_load` (and the read inside `workspace_export`) skip `super::DB_WRITE_LOCK`, while every mutating command (`workspace_upsert`, `workspace_delete`, `workspace_import`) takes it. If `super::open_db` returns a shared long-lived `Connection`, the read can race with an in-flight write transaction and observe either intermediate state or `SQLITE_BUSY`. If `open_db` returns a fresh per-call connection, the global mutex is only serializing writers against each other and the read is unprotected by the lock the rest of the file relies on. Make the policy consistent: either swap `DB_WRITE_LOCK` for an `RwLock` (read guard here, write guard in mutators) or document that connections are per-call and that cross-call serialization is delegated to SQLite's own file-level locking.

`delete_workspace` runs one parameterized `DELETE` per id inside the transaction. For a large id list this is N round-trips through the SQLite VDBE. Replace the loop with a single `DELETE FROM workspace_items WHERE id IN (?1,?2,...)` using generated placeholders (chunked to stay under SQLite's SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER, default 999) so the whole batch executes in one statement.

`workspace_import_merge` issues one `SELECT updated_at FROM workspace_items WHERE id = ?` per imported row, on top of the later `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`. For a large export this is N+1 statement executions inside the transaction. Batch the existence check (e.g. a single `SELECT id, updated_at FROM workspace_items WHERE id IN (...chunk...)`), build a `HashMap<String, i64>` of existing timestamps in Rust, and then drive the upsert. The current pattern also re-parses and re-prepares nothing per row, but it still pays one round trip per row.

Partial-copy data integrity: after `fs::rename` puts the main DB in place, any failure in the subsequent WAL/SHM sidecar copies leaves the destination with a DB whose `-wal`/`-shm` no longer match the source. If the checkpoint reported BUSY (uncommitted frames still in source WAL), those frames are silently lost on the destination side; SQLite recovery on next open may also refuse to start. Either copy the main + sidecars into a fresh temp directory first and rename them all atomically, or roll back the main DB rename (delete `db_path`) if any sidecar fails so the caller can retry.

Corrupted/unreadable source is silently propagated: when `rusqlite::Connection::open` fails (corrupt file, encryption, wrong format, transient IO error), only a warning string is appended and execution still falls through to `std::fs::copy`. A caller that only checks `warns.is_empty()` will treat a corrupted destination as success and start using it. Either propagate an error (return `Result<_, MigrateError>`) or at minimum distinguish the open-failure case from successful-copy-of-valid-DB.

Rotation failures are invisible: the `metadata` read failure is silently bypassed by `if let Ok`, and the `rename` failure is discarded via `let _ = ...`. If rotation cannot run (target `.log.old` locked, read-only volume, permissions, AV scanner holding the handle), the log will keep growing past `size_limit` indefinitely with no telemetry. Surface at least the rename error through the existing logging facility so operators can detect rotation regressions.

Two concerns: (1) errors are stringified at the I/O boundary via `format!` (Result<(), String>), losing the underlying `std::io::Error` and its `Error::source` chain — prefer `Result<(), std::io::Error>` with `?` so callers can localize and chain context. (2) When `fs::rename` fails after `fs::write` succeeded, the `.tmp` file is leaked on disk (paired with the same crash-recovery concern in `copy_legacy_db`'s `.db.copying`). Use a small guard that removes `&tmp` on the rename error path.

`data_dir` returns the exact same path as `db_dir` (both delegate to `probe_log_dir`), so the tokens and credential files used by the local HTTP API sit alongside the SQLite database. In portable mode on a removable drive, losing the media exposes credentials with no additional protection beyond the file system. Consider whether portable-mode credentials should live in their own (optionally encrypted) subdirectory, or use a platform keychain even when the DB is co-located with the executable.

`with_extension("db.copying")` only works for `wmessage.db` → `wmessage.db.copying` because `with_extension` treats its argument as a single replacement extension token; this is non-obvious and brittle. If the DB naming convention ever changes (e.g. `wmessage.sqlite`, or a path with no extension at all), this will silently produce wrong temp names. Prefer the explicit form already used in `atomic_write`: build the tmp with `path.with_file_name(format!("{}.copying", path.file_name().unwrap_or_default()))`. Note also that a stale `.db.copying` left over from a prior crashed run is silently overwritten with no cleanup or warning.

comments.content: The doc comment (and inline comment) promises a path resolved two levels above the exe (`src-tauri/` -> project root), but the body just returns the relative literal `PathBuf::from("bot-config.json")`, which is resolved against the process's current working directory. Any caller that relies on this default outside the project root will fail to find the config; the implementation does not match its stated contract.

`std::fs::read_to_string` is blocking I/O. In a Tauri project, `load()` is likely to be invoked from a `#[tauri::command]` handler or other async task; running synchronous filesystem I/O on the runtime thread will stall the async executor and any other in-flight IPC. Prefer `tokio::fs::read_to_string` (or move the call off the runtime) when this is reachable from async code.

Using `String` as the public error type collapses `io::Error` and `serde_json::Error` into an unstructured blob, and the tests have to rely on substring matching (`e.contains("缺少 evolution")`) to distinguish failure modes. A typed error (e.g. a `thiserror` enum with `Io`, `Parse`, `MissingEvolution`, `MissingEval` variants) preserves the cause, lets callers branch on kind, and makes the contract testable without brittle string matching.

`RunFrequency::as_str()` hand-codes the same `'daily'/'hourly'/'manual'` strings that the `#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]` derive already produces. This is two sources of truth for the wire format: adding a new variant (e.g. `Weekly`) must be remembered in both places, and a typo here would silently disagree with what serde serializes. Either delete `as_str` and let consumers call `serde_json::to_value` / pattern-match, or generate `as_str` via a single helper such as `serde_json::to_value(self).ok().and_then(|v| v.as_str().map(|s| s.to_owned()))` or a `strum`-style macro.

`eval_set_path` and `feedback_path` are deserialized as raw `PathBuf` values with no canonicalization, existence check, or containment check against an expected root. If the JSON config is ever sourced from an untrusted channel (e.g. a network sync, a user-uploaded profile, or a tampered file) these become arbitrary-file-read / arbitrary-file-write vectors for the downstream JSONL reader and feedback writer. At minimum, validate that the paths exist and resolve to absolute paths inside an expected directory before handing them off.

The three file-loading tests allocate a temp dir, write a fixture, run `load()`, then `let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&dir);` ignores any error. If any `unwrap()` between the create and the cleanup panics (including the `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_nanos_opt().unwrap_or(0)` lookup or the JSON write), the temp dir leaks and accumulates across runs. Prefer a `tempfile::TempDir` RAII guard (it auto-cleans on drop even when the test panics) or wrap each test in a helper that ensures cleanup via a drop guard.

`append` has three data-integrity hazards stacked: (1) TOCTOU between `create_dir_all` and `OpenOptions::open` (file could disappear between the two calls); (2) no file locking, so two concurrent appenders (e.g. Tauri frontend command + backend worker) can race at byte granularity and produce interleaved/garbled JSONL lines; (3) `writeln!` returns success on the kernel write but `f` is never `sync_all()`'d, so a process crash (or power loss) can leave a half-written trailing line that `read_all` will then fail to parse, losing both the partial row and the next append. For a signal-of-truth log, hold an exclusive `fs2`/`fd-lock` across the open/write/sync, or write to a temp file + atomic rename, and call `f.sync_all()` before `Ok(())`.

Every public function returns `Result<T, String>` and immediately `format!`s the underlying `io::Error` / `serde_json::Error` into a Chinese-localized message. This violates the project rule "Errors converted to strings too early or discarded without context; prefer preserving the original error and adding actionable context at boundaries": callers lose the typed source (cannot match on `NotFound` vs `PermissionDenied` vs `InvalidData`), the `Error::source()` chain is dropped, and the i18n string is now baked into the API surface. Define a `thiserror` enum (e.g. `FeedbackError { Io(#[from] std::io::Error), Json(#[from] serde_json::Error) }`) and let the boundary layer add the localized message.

#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum FeedbackError {
    #[error("io error on {path:?}: {source}")]
    Io { path: std::path::PathBuf, #[source] source: std::io::Error },
    #[error("json error: {0}")]
    Json(#[from] serde_json::Error),
}

comments.content: `FeedbackEntry.value` is `f64` and the doc comments on `SignalType` specify tight domains (`{0.0, 1.0}` for thumbs, `1.0` for task_complete/task_failed, `1.0`/`0.0` for rollback, error code or `1.0` for tool_error), but `append` / `read_all` perform no validation. NaN and ±Inf round-trip cleanly through serde_json and will silently poison every downstream aggregate (mean thumbs score, success rate, error-rate histogram, sort key, etc.). Either reject non-finite values in `append` with a typed error, or wrap the field in a newtype like `FeedbackValue(f64)` with a `TryFrom<f64>` constructor that checks `is_finite()` and the per-variant domain.

`filter_session` and `filter_type` materialize every match by `cloned().collect::<Vec<_>>()`, forcing one heap allocation per matching entry and a second allocation for the result vector. Since `FeedbackEntry` derives `Clone` only to satisfy this API, returning a borrowed iterator (`entries.iter().filter(...).copied()` or `impl Iterator<Item = &FeedbackEntry>`) avoids the clones entirely for read-only callers and lets the caller decide whether to materialize. Combined with the `f64` validation gap above, every aggregate call also pays this cost twice (filter + iterate).

`read_all` opens the file directly (no `BufReader` is used for the file itself — `BufRead` is only a trait import for `.lines()`), and `append` writes to a raw `File` via `writeln!` (no `BufWriter`), so every append is a separate `write(2)` syscall. For a hot path that may be called per user action, wrap the handle in `std::io::BufWriter::new(f)` (with an explicit `.flush()` before `sync_all()`/`drop`). Also, `out.sort_by_key(|e| e.timestamp_ms)` on line 98 implies the file is *not* append-sorted in practice (multiple writers, clock skew, replay) — call out this assumption in the doc comment so callers don't assume chronological order without sorting.

TOCTOU race on the legacy DB migration path: `if !db_path.exists()` followed by a separate `legacy_db.exists() && legacy_db != db_path` check, then `paths::copy_legacy_db(...)`. Two concurrent `open_db` callers on a fresh install can both pass the existence checks and race on the copy plus the WAL/SHM sidecar handling inside `copy_legacy_db`. There is no per-process lock (e.g. a `std::sync::Once` or a `Mutex` guarded by the same `BOT_ASSIGNED_RESET_DONE` pattern used a few lines below) around this critical section, so a half-copied db/-wal/-shm triplet is possible on first-run contention. Consider serializing the "create dir + check legacy + copy" block with a static `Once`/`OnceLock<Result<(), String>>` so the migration runs exactly once per process.

Silent failure of the one-shot `bot_assigned` reset: `migrations::reset_bot_assigned_with(...)` returns a `bool` (the `reset_tests` module asserts `ok` / `!ok` on its return), but the result is dropped here — `open_db` still returns `Ok(conn)` whether or not the UPDATE succeeded. On first open against a DB where rows still carry the legacy `bot_assigned = 1` flag (the documented migration goal), a transient failure (SQLITE_BUSY, locked WAL, etc.) means the caller inherits a connection that silently violates the post-migration invariant, with no audit event and no error propagated to the Tauri command layer. Either propagate the reset failure (return `Err` from `open_db`) or at least emit an `audit::write_event(..., "bot_assigned_reset_failed", ...)` on `false`.

DDL built via `format!` with interpolated identifiers: `ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN {col} {ty}` (and the `bot_messages` mirror below). The literals are hardcoded today so this is not a current SQL-injection vector, but the pattern is exactly the shape of one and bypasses any audit / lint that flags dynamic DDL. Replace with static SQL strings (`"ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN schedule TEXT"`, `"... sched_last INTEGER"`, etc.) or a vetted whitelist helper, so the invariant is auditable and the `format!` surface disappears from the schema bootstrap path.

Same dynamic-DDL pattern as the tasks loop above — `ALTER TABLE bot_messages ADD COLUMN {col} TEXT` built via `format!`. Replace with the two static SQL statements (`"... ADD COLUMN thinking TEXT"` / `"... ADD COLUMN tools TEXT"`); the `col` iterator can stay as a list of `PRAGMA table_info` lookup keys.

Pervasive error stringification at the boundary: every rusqlite / io / serde error in `open_db` is funneled through `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())?`, destroying the structured `rusqlite::Error` (code / SQLSTATE / primary offset / database name) before it reaches the Tauri command layer. `CommandError` is imported in this module but never threaded through, so startup failures surface as flat strings only and triaging boot-time migration regressions becomes materially harder. Consider a thin `From<rusqlite::Error> for CommandError` (or preserving a `rusqlite::Error` and converting at the very top of the call chain) so the call site can keep context.

Dead `_unused` shim masking an unused import: `#[allow(dead_code)] fn _unused(_e: CommandError) {}` exists only to silence the unused-import warning on `use crate::error::CommandError;`. The real fix is to drop the unused import (and re-add it at the call site once `CommandError` is actually wired through per the comment above); the shim is a code smell that pretends the error type is connected when it is not, and leaves a misleading parameter slot.

Optimistic dedup flip causes permanent notification loss on transient send failure. `plan_round` sets `entry.h1`/`entry.t0 = true` and pushes the `Pending` in the same branch, before `run_round` ever calls `app.notification()...show()`. If the send fails (permission denied, plugin error, focus-assist suppressing on Windows, etc.), the flag is already committed and `save_state` persists it, so the user will never see this notification on any subsequent tick — directly contradicting the stated goal of '宁可重发不丢通知语义'. Either move the flag flip into `run_round` after `show()` returns `Ok`, or structure dedup as a separate 'attempted' set vs 'delivered' set so transient failures can be retried.

Notification-state `Mutex` is held across synchronous I/O (audit log write + atomic file write). `notify_state().lock()` is acquired here and not released until after `save_state(app, state)` returns; both `audit_log` (which takes `BOT_LOG_LOCK`, opens `bot.log`, may rotate it, and writes a line) and `atomic_write` (tmp+rename to disk) perform blocking filesystem I/O under that guard. Any other accessor of `notify_state` — or any future re-entrant call from `start_due_notifier` / a manual trigger — would block for the full duration of those syscalls. Release the lock between `plan_round` / notification send and `save_state` (e.g. drop `guard` after collecting the changes into a local `HashMap`, then take the lock briefly only to swap+persist), or split into a short critical section for state mutation and a separate persistence step.

comments.content: Background notifier loop has no shutdown coordination. `start_due_notifier` drops the `JoinHandle` returned by `tauri::async_runtime::spawn` immediately and the inner `loop { ticker.tick().await; run_round(&app).await; }` has no `select!` over a cancellation token / shutdown signal. On Tauri app exit, the task can be aborted mid-`run_round` — after `plan_round` has flipped flags but before `save_state` has flushed them, so the on-disk dedup state can diverge from in-memory state and re-fire (or never re-fire) notifications on next launch. Plumb a shutdown signal (e.g. `tauri::AppHandle` exit event, `tokio::sync::watch`, or a `CancellationToken`) and `select!` over it in the loop so the task drains cleanly on quit.

`has_time` is derived from `due.contains('T')` instead of from `parse_due_dt`'s result, coupling display logic to a string heuristic that can desynchronize from the parser. Today the heuristic matches the two formats `parse_due_dt` accepts ('T'-separator or date-only), but if the parser is ever extended — e.g. to accept "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M" (space separator), seconds, or a timezone suffix — `parse_due_dt` would still classify the input as datetime but `has_time` here would become `false`, producing `MM-DD` text for a task that was actually scheduled at a specific hour. Have `parse_due_dt` return the format alongside the `DateTime` (e.g. an enum `DueDt { DateOnly, DateTime }` or a struct), and use that discriminant for `has_time` and `render`.

With hundreds of historical tasks this is the slowest part of every 30 s tick. Build a `HashSet<&str>` of valid task ids once before `retain`, or just clear stale entries by intersecting via `state.retain(|id, _| valid_ids.contains(id.as_str()))`. Same pattern also applies if you ever switch `valid` to a different lookup structure.

The inline comment explicitly admits this is a TODO placeholder pending ChangeRecord integration, but downstream dashboards / trend tracking will ingest it as real data and skew every regression signal. Either populate an honest `case_passed` (e.g. 0) until R2 lands, or omit the metric / mark the period as draft.

comments.content: Two problems on the same filter: (1) it is executed inside a per-case loop, making the total work O(cases * feedback) — pre-group feedback into a `HashMap<&str, Vec<&FeedbackEntry>>` (or sort + binary_search) to get O(n+m); (2) the second clause `f.session_id == c.case_id` treats a session ID as if it could equal a case ID, conflating two unrelated identifiers and inflating `hit_fractions` with signals from completely unrelated sessions. Drop the OR branch (or rename the field) and only match by `case_id`.

The 0.0/1.0 hint carried by `f.value` is described in the inline comment ("value 0.0/1.0 = 失败/不一定（按 0 算）") but is then ignored for all three signal variants: `ToolError` always counts as failure, `TaskComplete` always counts as success, and `TaskFailed` always counts as failure. This silently corrupts `tool_call_efficiency` and the implicit task-success ratio. Use `f.value >= 0.5` (or whatever threshold the producer documents) when deciding whether a signal increments `succeeded` vs. plain `total`.

The inline doc-comment describes the contract as "evolution-applied.jsonl under data_dir, with a `--applied` CLI override", but the implementation (and `run()`'s signature) provide neither: `set_extension` rewrites `eval_set.jsonl` into `<name>.applied.jsonl` next to the eval set, and no override hook is passed into `run`. If applied records truly live at `evolution-applied.jsonl`, the runner will silently read a non-existent file via `read_applied`, return an empty list, and emit a metrics report with `applied_total = 0` / `rollback_rate = 0`. Either move the resolution responsibility up to the caller (and pass the resolved path into `run`), or actually take an explicit `applied_path` parameter and drop the misleading comment.

`r.get(0)` is called on a plain `String` column with no `COALESCE`, so any `NULL` `tags` value (likely after a future migration, partial write, or a legacy row inserted outside the producer) will abort the entire eval run, defeating the documented "graceful empty when dev DB lacks the table" contract. Also, the SELECT has no `LIMIT` and materializes every lesson row into a `Vec<String>`; on a large dev DB this is both a memory blow-up and an arbitrarily slow step on the hot path. TOCTOU race in the optimistic-concurrency guard: the baseline read runs as a separate `SELECT` before the `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`, so two writers that captured the same `expected_updated_at` snapshot can both pass the conflict check and both proceed to write, with the second silently clobbering the first. The SQL-level `WHERE tasks.updated_at IS NULL OR excluded.updated_at >= tasks.updated_at` is a different invariant (it only guards against older updates, not against the explicit baseline) and does not enforce the RMW contract that the Rust guard claims to provide. Either perform the comparison atomically with the write (e.g. hold the existing `DB_WRITE_LOCK` for the entire read-modify-write window, or move the conflict detection into a single SQL expression via `RETURNING` plus row-count comparison), and document the chosen guarantee precisely.

Silent mutex-poisoning recovery: `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` is used to acquire `DB_WRITE_LOCK` in `db_upsert_for`, `db_delete`, and `tasks_import`. If any task panics while the lock is held (e.g. inside `tx.commit()` or an `upsert_tasks` iteration), the lock becomes poisoned and its guard is silently discarded — meaning subsequent writers happily proceed against a connection/transaction whose invariants may already be violated. At minimum `eprintln!`/log the poisoning event and surface it (e.g. return `CommandError::DbError`), or document explicitly that this lock is best-effort and that connection state is reset elsewhere.

The `ON CONFLICT ... WHERE tasks.updated_at IS NULL OR excluded.updated_at >= tasks.updated_at` predicate silently no-ops the UPDATE when the SQL-level guard fails, and the caller has no way to tell "row updated" from "row rejected by SQL-level guard". This is inconsistent with the explicit error returned by the `expected_updated_at` path — one path errors, the other lies. Either (a) drop the WHERE and rely solely on `expected_updated_at`, or (b) detect the silent rejection via `stmt.execute(...).map_err(...)?` then `conn.changes()`/`RETURNING` and convert a zero-changes outcome into the same `CONFLICT_ERR_PREFIX` error so callers always know when their write was a no-op.

comments.content: `db_delete` is inconsistent with the other write paths: `db_upsert_for` and `tasks_import` wrap their work in `conn.transaction()`, but `db_delete` calls `delete_tasks(&conn, ...)` directly with no transaction and no rollback safety. The current single-statement DELETE is atomic, so this is not yet a correctness bug — but the inconsistency means a future multi-statement delete (cascade, soft-delete, audit row) added here will silently introduce partial writes. Bring this in line with the other writers (begin a transaction, hold `DB_WRITE_LOCK` across `conn.transaction()` so the connection isn't opened concurrently with another writer).

`db_load_for` (and the `db_load` Tauri command) takes no read-side synchronization with writers. `load_all` runs many row reads as separate statements, so a concurrent `db_upsert_for` can interleave between them; the frontend can be handed a snapshot that is neither the pre- nor post-write state (some rows updated, some not). Even with SQLite WAL (where individual statements still see a consistent snapshot), the multi-statement `load_all` does not. Wrap the read in a single transaction — `conn.transaction()` then `load_all(&tx)` — to guarantee a stable snapshot for the entire load.

`tasks_import` reads `std::fs::read_to_string(&path)` with no validation of the file extension, size, or canonical location, even though `tasks_export` validates its destination via `check_export_path`. A user-supplied path can therefore point at arbitrary files (e.g. `/etc/passwd`, a multi-gigabyte log) and the contents are then blindly parsed as JSON and merged into the database. At minimum: (a) verify the path ends in `.json` (reuse `check_export_path`), (b) cap the file size (e.g. `fs::metadata` then reject above a threshold, or read in bounded chunks) to prevent memory DoS, and (c) consider canonicalizing and rejecting paths outside an expected exports directory.

The comment block above `load_all` documents the contract "JSON 损坏 → warn + 按空读取" for `subtasks` and `files`, but `tags` silently uses `serde_json::from_str(&s).ok()`, dropping parse errors with no log and silently hiding on-disk corruption. Apply the same warn-and-fallback treatment as for `subtasks`/`files` (or document explicitly why tag corruption is intentionally silent) — otherwise the documented contract is misleading and corruption is observable only by users noticing missing tags.

comments.content: The append is not atomic per line and has no file-locking: two processes (or two threads) calling `append_jsonl` concurrently will have their `writeln!` calls interleaved at the OS write boundary, potentially producing a torn jsonl where two cases share one line — `read_jsonl` will then fail with a JSON error pointing at a line that actually contains fragments of two records. Add a process-level lock (`fs2`, `fdlock`, or `flock(2)` via `nix`) or write each case through a `tempfile` + rename to make each record crash-safe and serializable across processes. Also consider an explicit `sync_all()`/`fsync` so a crash between calls doesn't lose the latest batch.

`MetricSpec.weight` is documented as `0.0-1.0` but `f64` accepts anything, including negative values, values > 1, `NaN`, and `±infinity`. Serde happily persists them, so downstream aggregation can silently produce `NaN` scores or violate the documented contract. Validate at construction (e.g. `fn new(metric: String, weight: f64) -> Result<Self, ...>` checking `0.0 <= weight <= 1.0 && weight.is_finite()`), and/or deserialize via a custom `Deserialize` that rejects out-of-range weights with a precise error. Additionally, deriving `PartialEq` on a struct containing `f64` enables `==` comparisons that misbehave for `NaN` and precision-sensitive values; consider dropping `PartialEq` from this struct or replacing `f64` with a `Weight(u16)` / `Weight(u32)` newtype storing basis points (0-10000).

`read_jsonl` slurps the entire file into a `Vec<EvalCase>` with no size cap, no streaming, and no per-line byte limit. A malformed or accidentally huge jsonl (e.g. a multi-GB log mistakenly pointed at) will OOM the process. Add a size guard (e.g. `metadata().len()` check, or cap on `Vec::with_capacity`), a per-line max length before parsing (`line.len() > N => error`), or expose a streaming variant returning an iterator / `impl Iterator<Item = Result<EvalCase, _>>` so callers can bound memory themselves.

Inside the crate, callers that import via the submodule path will use the original short name; callers that `use eval::*` will see the suffixed alias. This split vocabulary makes grep-for-usage unreliable and forces readers to know which path a caller took. Either keep the original names and disambiguate at call sites, or rename at the declaration site so there is one name everywhere.

comments.content: The module doc-comment lists the submodules' responsibilities and external constraints ("不动 evolution 模块现有结构；不调 LLM；不写新数据库表；持久化一律 jsonl") but documents nothing about the public API contract — error model (typed `Result` vs. panic), thread-safety / `Send + Sync` guarantees of the re-exported types, or whether the jsonl helpers are atomic / append-only. Since this `mod.rs` is the only place that defines the eval layer's surface, those invariants belong here so downstream CLI/Tauri callers do not have to grep every submodule to discover them.

`evolution_key` is declared `pub` while every in-file caller and apparent external user is internal. This leaks the `evo:<id>` tag namespace as part of the public API surface, which makes the idempotency contract brittle (downstream code can mint colliding tags) and unnecessarily widens the crate's public ABI. Downgrade to `pub(crate)` (and inline its small body at the few call sites if desired) so the key format stays an implementation detail of the evolution module.

Embedding failures collapse silently into `None` here and are then forwarded as `embedding: None` to `store::insert_item`. Because `EvolutionProposal`'s `suggestion.text` is the entire cognitive payload of the lesson, any batch whose ONNX inference fails (model missing, OOM, etc.) will persist lessons with no vector and they will never be retrievable via semantic recall — silently degrading the whole "behavior changes next turn" guarantee this module exists for. Either (a) surface the error and abort the batch (treat failed inference as a hard failure of `apply_from_consolidation`), or (b) at minimum emit an `audit_event!` / `eprintln!` per `None` so the missing-embedding condition is observable in the audit trail.

`DB_WRITE_LOCK` is acquired once and held for the entire batch: it spans `open_db` (file open syscall), `ensure_table` (DDL), every `apply_one` (SQL writes), every `append_applied_record` (open/append/close JSONL, `create_dir_all`, `writeln!`), and every `audit_event!` (tauri emit). Every unrelated DB writer in the process serializes behind this whole pipeline, including the slow syscall portions that don't need to be inside the critical section. Restructure so the lock only covers the actual SQL mutations: open the connection and pre-compute `ledger` before taking the lock; for each proposal do `apply_one` under the lock, then release before `append_applied_record` and `audit_event!` (or do them inside a single short `sqlite3_step`/commit), or batch the JSONL appends and emit them after dropping `_g`.

`DB_WRITE_LOCK.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` silently recovers from a poisoned mutex, but this lock is the single global barrier protecting every DB write in the crate. If a previous holder panicked mid-transaction (e.g. between `insert_item` and the next statement), the on-disk state may be inconsistent relative to what this thread now assumes. At minimum add a safety comment (and ideally a `parking_lot`/`Mutex` with poisoning tolerance at lock-acquisition that records the poisoning in an audit event) explaining why proceeding is safe; otherwise this masks a real correctness hazard.

`append_applied_record` (a) opens and closes the file on every call inside `DB_WRITE_LOCK`, multiplying syscalls in the critical section; (b) drops the handle without `sync_all`, so the audit record can be lost on a crash between `writeln!` and the next flush, desynchronizing DB state from `evolution-applied.jsonl`; (c) has no size cap or rotation, so the ledger grows unbounded in `{data_dir}` for the lifetime of the install. Also note that `?`-propagating an `append_applied_record` error after `apply_one` has already mutated the DB leaves the memory item without an audit row and aborts the rest of the batch — partial-failure consistency hazard. Open the file once per batch (outside the lock), buffer the lines, `sync_all`/`flush` after the batch, and either rotate by line-count or document the bound; and either guarantee audit-before-DB or wrap both in a single critical section that retries/repairs on partial failure.

When `hard_constraint_compliance` is true, `approval_source` is unconditionally set to `ApprovalSource::Pending` regardless of the entry's proposal status. This produces internally inconsistent `ChangeRecord`s when `entry.status` is `Expired` or `Rejected`: a record with `status=Rejected` and `approval_source=Pending` implies the change is still awaiting approval, and `status=Expired` with `approval_source=Pending` implies a never-approved change that timed out. The `status` and `approval_source` should be derived together (e.g., `approval_source` derived from the resolved `status`, or both derived from the same `entry.status` branch), so a Rejected/Expired record carries a matching approval source instead of "Pending".

`hard_constraint_compliance: bool` is a classic boolean trap at a public mapping API boundary. It conflates two distinct concerns (compliance result + approval-source derivation) and makes it easy for callers to silently pass the wrong flag at call sites. Consider replacing with a typed newtype or enum (e.g., `enum ComplianceOutcome { Compliant, Failed { reason: String } }`) so call sites are self-documenting and invalid states (e.g., "compliant with reason") are unrepresentable.

The tests `to_change_record_expired_entry` and `to_change_record_rejected_entry` assert `approval_source: ApprovalSource::Pending` for `Expired` and `Rejected` statuses when `compliance=true`. This locks in the semantic inconsistency flagged above and will block any future fix unless these assertions are updated together with the production code. If `Pending` is genuinely intentional for these cases (e.g., the record is created before approval is finalized in a later stage), the doc comment on `to_change_record` should explicitly call that out; otherwise update these assertions to match a status-appropriate approval source.

save_state does read → mutate → write with std::fs::write, no atomic-rename and no file locking. A crash, power loss, or process kill between read_to_string and write (or mid-write) leaves bot-config.json truncated, empty, or partially flushed — losing `shadow`, `activation`, and unrelated top-level fields even though §12.7 requires preserving them. Two concurrent save_state callers will also race: both read the same baseline, last writer wins, the earlier transition is silently lost. Fix by writing to a sibling temp file and `std::fs::rename`-ing over the original (atomic on the same filesystem), and serialize concurrent saves behind a Mutex or an OS file lock.

Both `load_config_from_file` and `load_state_from_file` silently collapse any of {I/O error other than NotFound, JSON parse failure, missing `evolution` block, missing `activation`/`activation_state` key, schema mismatch, unknown state string} into `Default()` / `S0Observe` with no log and no Result. An operator shipping a malformed or partially overwritten bot-config.json gets zero signal that the evolution system is running in default mode — they will assume calibrating is configured when it may not be. `serde_json::from_value(activation.clone()).unwrap_or_default()` further hides schema drift on the activation block. comments.content: Semantic mismatch between `mark_expired` and `evict_expired`: `mark_expired` only transitions `Pooled → Expired`, but `evict_expired` deletes ANY expired entry regardless of status. A `Promoted` or `Rejected` entry older than TTL will be hard-deleted, silently losing the audit trail. This contradicts the file header's stated 'soft eviction, preserve history' intent and means the two helpers cannot be safely composed (calling both will drop history that `mark_expired` just preserved). Consider making `evict_expired` respect status (e.g., only drop entries where status is `Expired` or `Pooled`, never `Promoted`/`Rejected`/`Applied`), or document the destructive intent explicitly.

Unchecked i64 addition in `compute_expires_at` can overflow / wrap on corrupt or adversarial input. Since this function ingests `created_at_ms` straight from `evolution-proposals.jsonl` (untrusted file), a malicious or malformed producer value close to `i64::MAX` will cause `created_at_ms + TTL_MS` to wrap into a large negative `expires_at_ms`, which then makes `is_expired` return true for every reasonable `now_ms`, so the entry is immediately (and silently) expired/evicted on next sweep — effectively a TTL bypass. Use `checked_add` / `saturating_add` and treat the degenerate case (created_at_ms beyond reasonable range, or no valid expiry) explicitly.

Time-source contract for `now_ms` is not documented. Every public function takes `now_ms` from the caller but the module says nothing about whether this must be wall-clock Unix ms (`SystemTime::now()`) or monotonic. Wall-clock usage makes the TTL vulnerable to NTP corrections / clock rollback: a single backward jump can instantly mark or evict entries that were just pooled, defeating the 14-day guarantee. Document the expected source (and recommend monotonic / persisted `now_ms` snapshots at proposal creation time if the caller compares against persisted `expires_at_ms`).

`evict_expired` is destructive and irreversible: it permanently drops entries from the in-memory vec (and, if the caller persists, from the jsonl log) with no status filter, no log/tracing, and no dry-run option. `ProposalEntry` derives `PartialEq` but not `Eq`, even though every field (`String`, `i64`, `u32`, `Vec<String>`, and the enums which already derive `Eq`) supports `Eq`. comments.content: Side-effect ordering leaves partial-failure windows between three independent sinks (candidate pool, audit log, applied lessons). The current sequence is: derive → gate → `write_proposals` → `emit_proposals` → `apply_from_consolidation`, and the function still proceeds to `apply` even when `write_proposals` returns `Err`. The two dedup chains (24h in-process dedup in `emit` and `evo:<proposal_id>` persistent idempotency in `apply`) prevent double-application, but they do not prevent the inverse inconsistency: a proposal can be applied as a lesson while never landing in the candidate pool the shadow hooks read from. Worth either (a) short-circuiting apply on write failure with a warn-level audit, or (b) making `write_proposals` best-effort and adding a periodic reconciler that rebuilds the candidate pool from applied lessons + audit log. The current comment claims the two dedup chains "互不影响" (don't interfere), but the inconsistent-state window between write and apply is exactly the gap the dual dedup cannot cover.

Severity: high — this is a hot path called from the consolidation scheduler and any other emit site, and it blocks the entire pipeline behind per-proposal disk I/O.

The in-module comment explicitly warns that the kv fields are load-bearing for `grep evolution.proposal bot.log` parsing, yet any regression to those fields (renamed key, dropped field, wrong level, dropped audit call entirely) will pass tests. If any workflow ever needs to mark a live change as rejected without physically rolling it back (e.g. post-activation policy violation, audit/regulatory rejection), there is no transition. Confirm this is intentional; otherwise add the missing transition and a regression test covering it.

Global failure-rate counters are silently bypassed by `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app`. The trait-based variants (`shadow_apply_for_batch`, `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_reversibility`) increment `TOTAL_WRITES`/`FAILED_WRITES` on every write attempt, but the `with_app` variant — which is the documented "唯一对外入口" per the doc-comment — calls `change::append_change` and `audit_event!` directly without touching the atomics. Consequence: the documented `failure_rate() > 5%` invariant (老板 13:20 拍板) can never fire for production traffic routed through this path, and `total_writes()`/`total_failed()` under-report actual write volume. Either route the writes through `ShadowSink` (which already wraps these counters in its callers), or add explicit `TOTAL_WRITES.fetch_add(1, ...)` / `FAILED_WRITES.fetch_add(1, ...)` after each Ok/Err branch.

`shadow_apply_for_batch_with_reversibility` is missing the post-loop failure-rate warning that `shadow_apply_for_batch` emits. Both increment the same global `TOTAL_WRITES`/`FAILED_WRITES` atomics, but only the simpler variant re-reads them at the end and fires `sink.audit_warning` when the threshold is exceeded. The file header documents the `失败率 > 5% 告警` invariant as a hard requirement (老板 13:13/13:20 拍板), so this variant silently drops a documented safety signal. Add the same `let total = TOTAL_WRITES.load(...); let failed_count = FAILED_WRITES.load(...);` check + `sink.audit_warning(...)` call before constructing the `ShadowReport`.

All three `shadow_apply_*` batch entry points are `async fn` but call `change::append_change` (which performs blocking `std::fs::OpenOptions::create(true).append(true).open(...)` + `writeln!` — no `tokio::fs`, no `spawn_blocking`) synchronously inside the per-proposal loop. On a Tauri default multi-thread runtime each batch pins a tokio worker for every `OpenOptions::open` + write syscall (which on Linux can block on inode lock, fsync, ENOSPC, slow disks, antivirus scans, etc.), reducing throughput and risking worker starvation under contention. Either drive file I/O through `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` (and `tokio::fs` for the open), or drop `async` from these entry points and document them as blocking — but do not mix the two, because callers in `apply.rs` will treat them as awaitable.

The post-loop failure-rate check is not synchronized with concurrent batches. `TOTAL_WRITES`/`FAILED_WRITES` are mutated by every shadow batch in the process, but the `load(Ordering::Relaxed)` here happens with no sequencing against in-flight increments from other batches. Two near-simultaneous calls to `shadow_apply_for_batch` can both observe a shared counter snapshot that crosses 5%, causing duplicate `audit_warning` events for what is effectively one shared state transition — and conversely, a batch that produced all the failures may finish before the rate climbs and the warning never fires for that batch. At minimum, swap to `Ordering::Acquire` on the loads (matching a `Release` on the `fetch_add`) to give a coherent read of the post-increment state; better, snapshot per-batch rates locally and emit a warning only when this batch itself drove the ratio over the threshold.

`ShadowReport.total` has inconsistent semantics across the three batch variants and will mislead downstream tests/metrics. In `shadow_apply_for_batch` and `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_reversibility`, `gated` is the post-all-filters list and every entry is either written or failed, so `total == written + failed` is an invariant. In `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app`, `gated` only filters by `auto_apply_gate`, and irreversible items are skipped inside the loop via `continue` without incrementing `written`/`failed` — so `total > written + failed` whenever an irreversible proposal arrives. The `e2e_4_no_audit_in_normal_path`-style assertions (and any future ops dashboards that compute `written + failed == total`) will silently mis-report. Either move the `is_reversible` filter into the `gated` Vec construction here, or change the field semantics to mean "considered" and document it.

`shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app` defeats the `ShadowSink` abstraction the module was explicitly designed around. The file header says the trait exists so that "测试用 MockShadowSink 内存收集调用，验证副作用边界" — but `with_app` calls `audit_event!` and `change::append_change` directly, so the three e2e invariants (spy writes, real writes, no audit in normal path) cannot be verified through the `AppShadowSink`/`MockShadowSink` boundary for this entry point. The existing test `e2e_4_no_audit_in_normal_path` only covers the trait variant; production traffic routed through `with_app` is untestable for those properties. Either factor the per-proposal write/audit dispatch into a `ShadowSink` method (e.g. `sink.write_shadow_with_state(...)`) so the `with_app` path goes through the same abstraction, or rename `with_app` to make it explicit that it is an untestable alternative path.

Doc comment header claim is misleading: "完整 6 层" (complete 6 layers) suggests the function derives all 6 `EvolutionLayer` variants, but the match only maps 4 of them. The trailing paragraph clarifies the gap, but the opening line should be reworded (e.g., "派生 4/6 层") so readers don't expect exhaustive coverage and to keep the contract aligned with the implementation.

Unchecked arithmetic on caller-supplied epoch: `expires_at_ms: now_ms + TTL_MS` can silently overflow `i64` if `now_ms` is near `i64::MAX`, malformed (negative), or otherwise pathological — corrupting the TTL into a nonsensical value rather than saturating. Use `saturating_add` or document the invariant on `now_ms`.

comments.content: Three independent booleans with implicit precedence encode a kill_switch > shadow > default ladder, but the type itself does not forbid contradictory combinations. Concretely, the doc-comment for `should_shadow_only` says "all_auto_apply=true → 也只 shadow（隐含）", yet the struct accepts `all_auto_apply: true, shadow_only: false` as a valid deserialized state, and `should_auto_apply` will return `true` for that state — so the only thing keeping the precedence contract honest is the `||` inside `should_shadow_only`. Config writers can persist semantically invalid combos (e.g. all_auto_apply=true + shadow_only=false) that only behave correctly because the impl silently coerces them. Consider modeling the valid states as an enum (e.g. `KillSwitchState::Live | Shadow | AllBlocked | NotificationsMuted`) or `bitflags`-with-documented-rules so invalid combos are unrepresentable rather than silently re-interpreted at every call site.

comments.content: SyntheticConfig carries user-controlled ratios with no validation: promoted_ratio + rejected_ratio + expired_ratio are summed directly in generate() and any 'leftover' probability mass silently falls through to ProposalStatus::Pooled. Negative values, NaN, or a sum > 1.0 therefore skew the distribution without any signal — defeating the stated purpose of validating R6 metric logic. Add a validate() / TryFrom impl (or invariant in Default) that asserts each ratio is finite and in [0,1] and the three buckets sum to <= 1.0, and reject otherwise.

comments.content: distribution_reasonable asserts ±5 deviation for pooled (20), rejected (15), and expired (5) buckets. With a 5-digit SimpleRng (next_f64 modulo 100_000) over only 100 samples the LCG tail can legitimately exceed this window for some seeds, and seed 42 is hardcoded. Either widen the tolerance (±8 or ±10), use a better PRNG (xoshiro128p / rand_chacha), or run multiple seeds and assert on the mean. As written, the test is brittle to LCG artefacting.

Observation-window filter is missing. `completed` and `rolled_back` are computed over the entire input slice, but the docs and the boss's R6-A spec describe "观察到" (changes observed within the [start_ms, now_ms] window). The CLI caller (`bin/observe_run.rs`) loads `change::read_all(...)` with no time filter, so any pre-existing rows in `evolution-changes.jsonl` (e.g. changes from before the R6 A flag was turned on) will be counted and will trip `CompletedChangesReach30` / `FiveOrMoreRollbacks` immediately. This is also inconsistent with `observe::metrics::compute_metrics` (metrics.rs:63), which explicitly filters proposals by `created_at_ms >= window_start_ms && created_at_ms <= now_ms`. Fix: filter by `c.created_at_ms` (and consider `c.rolled_back_at.unwrap_or(c.created_at_ms)` for the rollback count) inside this function, so the caller's contract becomes "pass the full file; we window it ourselves".

Two independent `iter().filter().count()` passes compute overlapping subsets of the same slice. With a `created_at_ms` window filter added (see prior comment) this becomes more relevant: fuse into a single loop accumulating `(completed, rolled_back)`, or use one pass over a pre-filtered `Vec<&ChangeRecord>`. Avoids re-walking `changes` twice on a path described as a "daily check" and keeps the two counters consistent under future filter additions.

`((now_ms - start_ms) as f64 / 86_400_000.0).max(0.0)` silently swallows misconfigurations: a negative duration (clock skew, swapped `--start-ms`/`now_ms` args) or even i64 overflow on `now_ms - start_ms` collapses to `0.0`, making the FourteenDaysElapsed check report "no time elapsed" instead of failing loudly. For a stop-condition gate that decides when to disable `evolution.shadow.enabled`, a silent 0.0 is worse than a panic or a `Result`-returning API — the caller (`observe_run.rs:152`) will print `should_stop: false` and the dev will assume everything is fine. Consider returning `Result<StopConditionStatus, StopError>` (or at minimum logging a warning) when `now_ms < start_ms`.

comments.content: The `i64 → f64` cast happens after subtraction, so for the documented 14-day window (~1.21e9 ms) it fits well inside the 53-bit f64 mantissa and is fine. But `(now_ms - start_ms)` itself can overflow `i64` if a caller passes wildly different epoch values (e.g. `start_ms` accidentally in seconds), and the subsequent cast then produces `+/-inf`/`NaN` which the `.max(0.0)` will turn into `0.0` — the same silent-failure mode as the previous comment. Cheap fix: bound the subtraction with `saturating_sub` before the cast, or check `now_ms >= start_ms` first.
