comments.content: Test coverage does not exercise the missing time-window behavior. Every test in this module uses `start_ms = 0`, so the window filter (once added) will look like a no-op and won't catch a regression that double-counts historical rows. Add at least one test that mixes a pre-window change (`created_at_ms < start_ms`) with an in-window change, and asserts only the in-window one is counted toward `changes_completed` / `rolled_back_count`.

`should_auto_apply` returns `!self.all_auto_apply`, so it yields `true` even when `shadow_only == true`. That means any caller in `apply.rs` that consults only `should_auto_apply()` will happily write through to `mem_items` while the kill switch is in shadow-only mode. The local test `shadow_only_implies_no_real_apply` even spells out the footgun in a comment ("实际语义：apply.rs 应先看 should_shadow_only"). Relying on callers to remember a strict check order is fragile — collapse the two predicates into a single method that returns the resolved mode (e.g. `enum ApplyMode { Live, Shadow, Blocked }`) so the precedence rules live in one place and callers cannot accidentally skip the shadow check.

Three booleans with overlapping semantics, where `should_shadow_only` quietly ORs in `all_auto_apply`. Even if the precedence stays implicit, the doc-comment promises "all_auto_apply=true → 也只 shadow（隐含）" — that promise is only true for `should_shadow_only`; `should_auto_apply` does not honor it (see `should_auto_apply` review note). Until/unless the type is reshaped, this method should at least document that the result already accounts for `all_auto_apply`, and the whole API should be reorganized so the precedence is computed in exactly one place rather than being re-derivable (and re-derivable incorrectly) from raw fields.

Every failure path is collapsed to `String`, dropping the underlying `io::Error` / `serde_json::Error` / `serde_json::error::Category`. Callers therefore can't programmatically distinguish "file missing" from "malformed JSON" from "missing `evolution` block" — the tests demonstrate this by resorting to `assert!(e.contains(...))` substring matching, which is brittle if messages ever change. Use `thiserror` (or a hand-rolled enum) with variants like `Io { path, source }`, `Parse { path, source }`, `MissingEvolution`, `MissingKillSwitch`, and have `Display` carry the same human-readable text for log output.

The free function `default_off` is a one-line alias for `KillSwitch::default_off()` and adds no behavior. Keeping both the inherent method and the free function at the same crate boundary invites inconsistent call sites (one file uses `KillSwitch::default()`, another uses `default_off()`, another uses `KillSwitch::default_off()`). Pick one — `KillSwitch::default()` already exists via `#[derive(Default)]` and is the idiomatic choice — and delete the other.

`DefaultHasher` is explicitly documented by the Rust standard library as having an unspecified algorithm and hash output that may change between Rust versions (and is randomly seeded per-process). For audit deduplication this is a silent data-integrity bug: any rust-toolchain bump, or replaying audit logs across machines/containers, will produce different `proposal_id` values for the same proposal, silently breaking the dedup contract this file is built around. Replace with a stable hash (e.g. `siphasher` crate with a fixed seed, or `blake3`/`xxhash-rust`) and pin the algorithm in a regression test.

64-bit (8-byte) hash used as the sole dedup key has a birthday-bound collision around ~2^32 proposals. In an audit log that treats equal ids as 'same proposal', a collision causes two distinct proposals to be silently merged and one dropped, corrupting the audit trail. Consider widening to 128-bit (16 bytes) or keeping the 8 bytes but storing the normalized input alongside the id so collisions can be detected and flagged.

`is_alphanumeric()` matches Unicode letters/digits, but `to_ascii_lowercase()` only lowercases ASCII. Uppercase non-ASCII letters (Greek, Cyrillic, fullwidth Latin, etc.) pass through unchanged, so two semantically identical summaries differing only in non-ASCII case will hash to different `proposal_id`s — defeating the documented dedup goal. Also, NFC vs NFD forms of the same CJK/Latin text are not canonicalized. Use `char::to_lowercase()` (iterator) and apply Unicode normalization (e.g. `unicode-normalization` crate's `nfc()`) before hashing.

The doc comment itself flags `occurrence_count` as a Phase 1 placeholder with non-cumulative semantics, warning against future misreading as "N occurrences". A misleading field name on a serialized audit record is a real data-interpretation hazard: downstream analytics will treat it as a frequency count. Either rename to something unambiguous (e.g. `reflected_op_count`) until Phase 2 semantics land, or add a serde rename / wrapper type that makes the placeholder nature machine-readable.

Canary 与 A/B 复用同一个 `bucket`，两者并不独立。`is_canary` 取桶号 0–4，`is_ab_a` 取桶号偶/奇；canary 桶里 A 占 {0,2,4}=3 个、B 占 {1,3}=2 个，所以 canary 群体是 60% A / 40% B。如果 canary 和 A/B 是两个独立实验维度（典型 canary + A/B 部署），这里会同时让 5% canary 和 50/50 A/B 的边际分布正确，但联合分布被破坏，无法把效应归因到单一变量。规范里也把两条写成并列 spec，强烈暗示应正交。建议 A/B 用独立的 hash（如同一个 session_id 再走一次 fnv1a 或对高位取模），使两轴独立。
缺少对 canary 与 A/B 独立性的断言。当前测试只覆盖每个判定的边际分布（≈5% / ≈50%）和稳定性，但没有验证 canary 群体是否也近似 50/50 分布在 A/B 上。若回归成 canary 绑死 A 臂（例如改为 `< 2`），现有测试仍会全绿。建议补一个联合分布测试：统计 canary 集合中 A 的占比应在 ~50% 附近。

`bucket` 是实现细节，但以 `pub` 暴露。模块头注释明确强调"跨进程稳定"是契约，下游若直接依赖 `bucket(session_id) == N` 这种数值映射，未来任何调整（哪怕只是改 hash 算法或改 `% 100` 为 `% 128`）都会成为 breaking change。建议降为 `pub(crate)` 或完全私有，仅导出语义谓词 `is_canary` / `is_ab_a`。

空 `session_id` 会全部塌缩到 bucket 0（canary + A）。`fnv1a("")` 返回 offset basis 0xcbf29ce484222325，`% 100 = 37` 实际为 bucket 37（仍合法），但模块级注释提到的"`fnv1a("")` = offset basis"与真实行为已经不一致（`0xcbf29ce484222325 % 100 = 37`），且 test `fnv1a_known_value` 也写错了——offset basis 是 0xcbf29ce484222325，没错；但 `% 100` 之后是 37，不是 0。需要确认：(a) 上游是否会传入空 session_id；(b) 若会，是否需要规范化（拒绝/默认桶）。同时建议补一个空串测试明确其归属。

Sampling rule silently drops user-initiated aborts. `TraceOutcome::Aborted` only fires the recording path if the caller *also* flips the separate `was_aborted` flag — a test even pins `!should_record_trace(&TraceOutcome::Aborted, 0, 100, false)`. `Failure` always records, but `Aborted` (the user /stop case) does not. Either fold `was_aborted` into the enum and treat `Aborted` like `Failure` (always record), or drop the `Aborted` enum variant entirely. The current shape lets a caller emit `outcome: Aborted` and lose the trace entirely.

Two parallel ways to say "aborted" — `TraceOutcome::Aborted` *and* a separate `was_aborted: bool` — with independent `with_outcome`/`with_aborted` setters. The two can disagree (e.g. `Success + was_aborted=true`, or `Aborted + was_aborted=false`), and the comment block on `TraceContext` doesn't document the invariant. Collapse to one source of truth: either drop the variant and let `was_aborted` carry the signal, or derive `was_aborted` from `matches!(outcome, TraceOutcome::Aborted)` and remove the bool field. As written, this is an unsound state-machine API for an enum that claims to model the outcome.

comments.content: `compute_trace_id` relies on `std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher` while the docstring markets the result as a "deterministic" cross-process dedup key. DefaultHasher's algorithm (SipHash variant) is *not* part of Rust's stability contract and has changed historically across toolchain versions. If it ever shifts again, every existing trace_id becomes a one-way door and dedup silently breaks. Either pin a vetted stable crate (e.g. `seahash`, `blake3` with a fixed key) or add an explicit test that pins the exact 16-hex output for known inputs and document the toolchain-version lock-in.

The audit event emits `outcome` via `format!("{:?}", outcome)` which produces Rust `Debug` text (`Failure { reason: "llm_5xx" }`), while the very next test (`trace_outcome_serializes_with_snake_case_tag`) locks the snake_case serde shape (`{"kind":"failure","reason":"llm_5xx"}`). Two different serialization forms for the same field will trip any audit-side parser that trusts the locked JSON. Either serialize via `serde_json::to_string(&trace.outcome)` / extract `(kind, reason)` into separate audit keys, or drop the locked-serde-shape test claim — pick one canonical form and pin both code and tests to it.

comments.content: Test name and inline comment promise verification ("duration > 60s 应被记录") but the body contains zero assertions — it only invokes `maybe_record_trace` and relies on "no panic". If the function silently regresses to never recording, this test still passes. Either rename to `maybe_record_long_duration_does_not_panic` to match the assertion set, or actually capture the audit emission (e.g. inject a fake AppHandle via a test seam, or assert on stderr/eprintln side effects) so the test guards what its name claims.

Concurrent append race + non-atomic write. `OpenOptions::create(true).append(true).open(path)` followed by a single `writeln!` is not safe under concurrent writers: two threads / async tasks / processes opening the same JSONL in append mode can interleave bytes at the OS level, producing one or more corked lines that every later reader will fail to decode. There is no advisory or exclusive file lock (e.g. `fs2::FileExt::lock_exclusive` / `fd_lock`), no `fsync` before close, and no write-to-temp-then-rename, so a crash / `ENOSPC` / panic mid-`writeln!` can leave a truncated record. Either gate the open/write/close with a process-wide `Mutex` keyed by `path`, take an exclusive OS lock around it, or serialize via `tempfile::NamedTempFile` + atomic `fs::rename` so partial lines cannot survive. The identical problem affects `append_ab`.

`Result<_, String>` + `format!("…: {e}")` erases the underlying error. Every `append_*` / `read_*` returns `Result<T, String>` and converts `io::Error` / `serde_json::Error` into a Chinese error string via `format!`. Callers cannot match on `NotFound`, `UnexpectedEof`, `InvalidData`, etc., the original `Error::source()` chain is dropped at the boundary, and the Chinese literal lives in the error type. Define a typed error and `?`-convert through it so the cause is preserved and Tauri / boundary code can format with `{:#}` for the full chain.

comments.content: Test tempdir naming + cleanup are unreliable. `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_nanos_opt().unwrap_or(0)` silently collapses to the literal `"0"` on platforms / clock configurations where nanosecond precision is unavailable, so concurrent test runs (or repeated `--test-threads=1` runs on the second-resolution boundaries) will collide on `sb-sh-0` / `sb-ab-0` / `sb-pd-0` under `std::env::temp_dir()` and corrupt each other's files. Cleanup is also swallowed (`let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(...)`) and, more importantly, is not run if an `assert!` panics — leaving orphan temp dirs on every failed test. Use `tempfile::tempdir()` for auto-`Drop` cleanup and a guaranteed-unique path, and stop hiding the `RemoveDirAll` error.

comments.content: main() is a fire-and-forget delegation: `wmessage_lib::run()` returns `()` and panics internally on startup failure (the library calls `.expect("error while building tauri application")` on the Tauri builder). Combined with `windows_subsystem = "windows"` here, any startup panic on Windows release builds disappears with no console, log file, or dialog — the user just sees the process exit silently with exit code 0 (panic message goes nowhere). Consider either having the library surface failures via a user-visible dialog / non-zero `app.exit(code)` and still run in release, or have `run()` return `Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>` so this `main()` can propagate `ExitCode::from(1)` and write the error to a log file before detaching the console.

Concurrent read-modify-write race on JSONL files: toggle_inner, delete_inner, evolution_keep_shadow, and evolution_rollback_change all do load → mutate → rewrite_jsonl on the shared evolution-proposals.jsonl / evolution-changes.jsonl with no file-level mutex, advisory lock, or transactional mechanism. Two concurrent calls (e.g. UI toggle while a rollback is in flight, or parallel bot-driven Promote/Reject) can each read the same snapshot, both mutate, and the second rewrite silently overwrites the first — losing ChangeRecords, regressing proposal.status, or creating duplicate Pending entries. Serialize access via an in-process Mutex keyed on the path, or migrate the store to SQLite (already used for mem_items).

Non-atomic JSONL rewrite (data-integrity hazard): rewrite_jsonl opens with truncate(true) and writes line-by-line without fsync, temp-file-then-rename, or any crash-safety. A SIGKILL, OOM, power loss, or panic between the truncate and the final writeln leaves evolution-proposals.jsonl / evolution-changes.jsonl empty or partially written, and the very next load_* call returns an error or a corrupted subset — for a JSONL file that is the only persistence for proposal lifecycle, this is a real data-loss bug. Write to a sibling temp file, fsync, then rename into place (and fsync the parent directory).

Blocking filesystem / SQLite I/O on the async runtime: every pub async fn command (evolution_list_proposals, evolution_toggle_proposal, evolution_delete_proposal, evolution_promote_proposal, evolution_reject_proposal, evolution_keep_shadow, evolution_list_changes, evolution_rollback_change) performs synchronous std::fs::OpenOptions / read_to_string / write, plus db::open_db + memory::store::delete_by_* (synchronous SQLite). Tauri runs these on Tokio; a contended DB or a large JSONL rewrite stalls the worker thread and degrades concurrent commands (including the ask_user_confirm round-trip). Wrap each command body in tokio::task::spawn_blocking, or switch to tokio::fs + a SQLite connection pool.

TOCTOU between confirm, toggle, and the final re-read in evolution_promote_proposal: the entry.status check, ask_user_confirm (which may sleep), toggle_inner, and the final load_changes + .find are four separate read sites on shared mutable JSONL files. A concurrent delete / rollback / second promote between any of them can (a) make toggle_inner dedup against an already-Promoted record, or (b) cause the final .find to return None with the misleading 'toggle_inner 写完未找到 ChangeRecord' message — which actually means another command deleted it, not that toggle_inner failed. The user just approved an action and the API tells them it didn't happen. Either return the ChangeRecord from toggle_inner directly, or run the whole flow inside the file-level lock from finding 1.

evolution_reject_proposal can fail mid-flow after the user already approved the action in ConfirmMap: the only record toggle_inner OFF removes is one with status == Pending. If the proposal has advanced to Shadowing / ShadowPassed / Active (a perfectly normal progression from a long-running evolution pipeline), toggle_inner returns 'proposal ... 没有 pending ChangeRecord，无法 toggle OFF' — the user clicked Approve and nothing in either JSONL changes (only an audit log entry is appended). Detect this state before ask_user_confirm and surface a typed 'already advanced past Pending; use evolution_rollback_change instead' error so the user is not given an Approve button that does nothing.

JSONL files grow unbounded and are fully rewritten on every command: toggle_inner, delete_inner, evolution_keep_shadow, and evolution_rollback_change all call rewrite_jsonl on the entire evolution-proposals.jsonl / evolution-changes.jsonl — including for tiny changes like resetting a single TTL. With long-running installations the changes file accumulates every historical record (RolledBack, Expired, etc.) and each UI toggle re-serializes / re-writes the full file. Append-only writes (with a periodic compaction step) for the toggle_inner ON branch (it already uses change::append_change — don't rewrite proposals for it), and at minimum skip the rewrite when nothing changed in the loop.

Dead-code pattern: `candidate_importance` is computed but consumed only by a no-op `with_dummy_for` helper that exists solely to silence the unused-variable warning. The value is dropped on the floor, which strongly suggests an incomplete feature (it likely was supposed to feed the decision logic, e.g. influence `Pass`/`Fail`). Either wire the value into the decision (e.g. emit a different `note` when below some threshold) or delete the variable and the helper trait entirely.

comments.content: Security-relevant migration failures are invisible to users: `migrate_legacy_key` and `migrate_search_keys` move plaintext API keys from `bot-config.json` into the OS keyring. On failure they only `eprintln!`, so a failed migration leaves plaintext keys on disk with no audit trail — the user has no way to discover this from `bot.log` or the in-app audit panel. Use `audit::write_event(AuditLevel::Warn/Error, "legacy_key_migration_failed", ...)` (or the `audit_event!` macro used elsewhere in this file) and consider alerting on next launch if the plaintext key still exists after a failed migration attempt.

Cleanup chain does not stop `bot_scheduler` or pause its timer before the drain window. Between `stop_all_executions` (step 1) and `mark_exiting` (step 5), a scheduler tick (30s cadence) can spawn a brand-new execution that is not in the registry yet — it will not see the stop flag set in step 1, and `wait_executions_drained` will see its `active_execution_count` rise and keep polling until grace expires. After grace, `kill_py` runs but the in-flight model loop may still be writing output. Either stop the scheduler first, or have scheduler's spawn path consult the `bot_py::EXITING` flag before registering an execution.

`bring_main_to_front` spawns an uncancellable thread that holds a cloned `WebviewWindow` for ~80ms. During shutdown (`cleanup_on_exit` → `RunEvent::ExitRequested` → `main.destroy()`), the main window is destroyed while these threads are still alive; the trailing `set_always_on_top(false)` then runs against a dead handle. The current `let _ =` swallow makes this safe today (Tauri returns Err), but rapid repeated invokes (e.g., user mashing the shortcut) accumulate threads racing to flip always_on_top off, and on slower systems the cleanup thread can still be mid-sleep when `main.destroy()` runs. Either check `app.run_iteration`-style cancellation, or simply skip the timer thread if a "shutting down" flag (or the same `bot_py::EXITING`-style signal) is set.

Mutex-poison recovery pattern in tests silently extracts the poisoned inner guard and continues. If a panic occurred mid-mutation of `ApiState.0`, the test proceeds to write `Some(running)` into potentially corrupted state and then asserts invariants on it — the test can pass while exercising wrong behavior, masking real regressions in production code that also relies on this state. Prefer to fail-fast (`unwrap()`/`expect("ApiState mutex should not be poisoned")`) in tests so a real concurrency bug surfaces immediately rather than being papered over by `eprintln!` + `e.into_inner()`.

comments.content: Global-shortcut handler swallows `is_visible()` errors and defaults to `false`, which means a hidden/erroring window is treated as if it were never visible — the handler will then call `bring_main_to_front` and likely `show()` a window that the user cannot see or that doesn't exist. On the Wry backend `is_visible()` failure is rare, but for visibility-decision logic it should be surfaced (audit/log) rather than silently inverted. Same caveat applies to `let _ = main.hide();` — silent hide failure means the next keypress toggles the wrong direction.

The `WithDummy` trait and its `with_dummy_for` impl are pure no-ops (return `self`) used only to suppress one unused-variable warning. Adding a public trait to a production module just to silence a warning is an anti-pattern: it pollutes the module surface, hides intent, and trips lint tools that flag no-op methods. Remove the trait, the impl, and the chained call.

comments.content: Delete the no-op `WithDummy` trait and its impl. It exists only to make the `.with_dummy_for(...)` call above compile; once that call is removed, the trait is dead. Leaving it in the production binary bloats the public surface of the module.

Importance bucketing uses a catch-all `_ => 3`, which silently collapses every non-`High` `ImpactLevel` variant to the same importance. If `ImpactLevel` grows new variants (e.g. `Low`, `Critical`, or future levels from R3-L4), this match will silently mis-rank candidates without any compile-time signal. Replace the catch-all with an exhaustive match so additions are surfaced as a compile error and each variant gets an explicit, intentional score.

Two full deep clones of the lesson list are performed back-to-back on every shadow run: `input.existing_lessons.to_vec()` and then `existing.clone()`. Both lists are tiny (top-3) so this is not catastrophic, but it is wasted work in the inner loop. A single sorted vec, with `hash_before` computed before `push`/`sort` for the hypothetical case, removes the second clone.

`hash_lessons_content` takes `&[&ShadowLesson]`, forcing every caller to allocate a `Vec<&T>` via `.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>()` (visible in the test code and would be required everywhere). Accepting `impl IntoIterator<Item = &ShadowLesson>` (or simply `&[ShadowLesson]` plus iterating by reference) eliminates that allocation and makes the call sites trivially `hash_lessons_content(&top3)`.

The `ShadowOutcome::hash_before`/`hash_after` fields are described in the doc comment as "FNV-1a", but the algorithm body (`h ^= b; h = h.wrapping_mul(0x100000001b3)`) is exactly FNV-1a-64. FNV-1a is a non-cryptographic, collision-prone hash. While that is acceptable for a "did anything change" guard inside one process, the public field type (`String`) and the doc comment do not call out that the hash is for fast inequality checks only — not for integrity, fingerprinting, or cross-process comparison. Worth a one-line note so future readers do not lean on it for stronger guarantees.

Scheduler has no in-progress guard, so the scheduler loop and `memory_consolidate_now` can run `run_consolidation` concurrently. While `DB_WRITE_LOCK` serializes the writes, the LLM call (`bot_chat::summarize_messages`) and the embedding batch run outside the lock, so two concurrent runs issue duplicate LLM requests, compute embeddings twice, and may both try to merge/contradict the same ids. Additionally, if a single run takes longer than `SCHED_TICK_SECS` (LLM latency + 100-item embedding), `MissedTickBehavior::Burst` (tokio's default) will fire missed ticks back-to-back once the run completes, producing a tight loop of runs until the schedule "catches up". Track an `AtomicBool` "consolidation in progress" (or use `tokio::sync::Mutex<()>` around the run) and short-circuit / skip ticks when the flag is set.

Both occurrences of `DB_WRITE_LOCK.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` silently recover from a poisoned mutex. If a previous worker panicked mid-transaction the SQLite connection (and thus the DB state visible to subsequent operations) may be inconsistent, but we happily proceed to issue more writes/reads against it as if nothing happened, masking a potentially serious correctness problem. At minimum log/audit the poison with the originating thread panic info; ideally return an error so the caller can decide whether to reopen the DB or restart the app.
`apply_ops` also silently recovers from a poisoned mutex in its `spawn_blocking`, with the same concerns as the candidate-gathering block above.

`apply_ops` calls `store::load_all(&tx)` once per op branch (merge, contradiction, distill), and each call scans the whole memory table. With `CONSOLIDATE_BATCH_LIMIT=100` and N ops this is O(N × table_size) per consolidation round — wasteful even for small tables and quadratic in growth. Build a `HashMap<&str, &MemItem>` once at the top of the function and reuse it across all branches (also avoids re-iterating inside `ids.contains(&m.id)` and `all.iter().any(...)` which are O(table_size) per id).

`persist_last_run` writes `bot-config.json` outside `DB_WRITE_LOCK` and independently of any other `crate::bot::update_config_file` callers. The scheduler's post-`Run` `persist_last_run` and a concurrent manual `memory_consolidate_now` (or any other component writing the config) race on read-modify-write of the JSON file: last-writer-wins can drop the scheduler's `last_run_at` or any other field. At minimum guard with an exclusive file lock inside `update_config_file`, or move the last_run_at update into the same lock-protected path as the candidate-gathering / apply_ops spawn_blockings so all bot-config.json writes are serialized.

Short English keywords `go`, `run`, `do` are matched as raw substrings against the user's instruction segment. Common conversational phrases like "let's go check…", "do you want…", or "running tests" all match — and because this trigger gates `RouteAction::ExecuteTasks` (batch execution of the selected task cards), an unintended match silently dispatches a destructive batch run whenever the message also carries a `[已选任务]` block (e.g. one the user selected previously but is no longer relevant). The Chinese keywords are far less prone to false positives than these three English ones. Require ASCII word boundaries for English keywords (split on non-alphanumeric, compare case-insensitively) or drop the English keywords from the whitelist entirely and rely on the Chinese set.

`compile_rules` swallows `Regex::new` failures with `.ok()` and silently drops rules whose every pattern failed to compile. A skill author who typoes a pattern (or whose frontmatter drifts after a refactor) becomes completely unroutable with zero diagnostic — the user just sees `PassThrough` and there is no log line, counter, or surfaced error. The comment "技能作者写错不拖垮整张表" justifies *not panicking the whole table*, but does not justify *silently dropping*. Return the invalid patterns out-of-band (e.g. `Vec<(String, String)>` of `(skill_name, pattern)`) so `rebuild_intent_routes` can log/emit a metric, or change `rebuild_routes` to return a `Result` / count.

`parse_selected_tasks_block` splits the line body on the first comma and requires the LEFT half to start with `id=`. A hand-edited, copy-pasted, or reordered line like `- title=Hello, id=abc` (or any order where `id=` is not the first field after the dash) is silently dropped: `id_part.trim().strip_prefix("id=")` returns `None`, the `continue` swallows the whole line, and the user's selected tasks vanish from the `ExecuteTasks` payload without any indication. Make the parser order-independent — split on `，`/`,` into all segments and accept `id=`/`title=`/`标题=` regardless of position.

`global_table_rebuild_and_route` mutates the process-wide `LazyLock<RwLock<Vec<CompiledRule>>>` and only resets it on the success path (`rebuild_routes(vec![])` at the end). An `assert!` panic between the setup probe-write and the cleanup leaves the probe pattern resident for any subsequent test in the binary (and depending on panic timing can poison the lock). Today only this test reads the global via `route_user_input`, so the blast radius is small — but the design is fragile and one future test that uses `route_user_input` becomes order-dependent. Use a panic-safe RAII guard (Drop impl or `scopeguard::defer!`) so cleanup runs on every exit path.

`rebuild_routes`'s `Err(e) => *e.into_inner() = compiled` branch silently recovers from a poisoned write lock. In the current code there is no panic-prone operation between acquiring the write guard and the assignment, so poisoning cannot actually occur — but the silent recovery means any future modification that adds a panic-prone step inside the critical section (e.g. validation that calls `unwrap`, logging that can fail) will mask the bug rather than surface it. Since `rebuild_routes` is the only mutator of `ROUTES`, poisoning here is a strong signal of a programming error worth investigating; consider `clear_poison()` after logging the underlying panic, or propagate the `PoisonError` to the caller so the failure is visible at the rebuild site.

Every failure path in mark_subtask_done is silently swallowed: `let Ok(all) = ... else { return; }` (db_load Err), the `None` arm of the `find` (task not found), and `if ... .is_ok()` on the db_upsert result. The RMW optimistic-concurrency check (`expected_updated_at = t.updated_at`) is the most concerning: when the user edits the task between our `db_load` and our `db_upsert`, the upsert is rejected and the 'done' status is silently dropped with zero observability. The 3 Silent-return points also mean the user-visible UI never reflects the persistent failure. At minimum, log these cases (especially the upsert conflict) so concurrent edits are detectable, and either retry once after a fresh load or surface the failure to clear_for/set_bot_assigned so the task card doesn't appear stuck.

`lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` silently recovers from poisoned mutexes everywhere this file touches `pending_map`. A thread panic while holding this lock can leave pending_map and any sibling ExecGuard bookkeeping (see `exec_guard: ExecGuard` field) in an inconsistent state; subsequent calls will then proceed as if nothing happened and may silently corrupt or double-allocate state (e.g., the next park after a poison can race with whatever half-state the panicking thread left behind). At minimum, audit-log poison recovery so it's visible, or replace with `lock().expect("pending_map poisoned")` to fail loud.

`db_load(...).await.unwrap_or_default()` turns a DB transport/decode error into an empty Vec, so the user-facing error becomes "任务卡不存在或已删除" — that's misleading and hides DB failures from telemetry. Distinguish `Err(_)` from `Ok(empty)` and surface a proper error (or at least audit-log) when DB access itself fails, e.g. "DB unreachable: <e>" instead of "task does not exist".

`PendingExec` has no TTL/timeout. If the user closes the app, abandons the session, or just never sends a confirmation between a step's completion and their next interaction, the parked entry (and its RAII `ExecGuard`) is never cleared, `set_bot_assigned` stays true on the task card, and no termination audit is written. Add a `parked_at: Instant` (or millis timestamp) to `PendingExec` plus a lazy expiry check at the top of `has_pending_for`/`take_pending_for`/`resume`, or a background sweep, that calls `clear_for(..., "超时未确认")` on stale entries and resets `bot_assigned`. The audit "session_key/clear for"的路径对漏的状态完全没有可见性。

`cleanup_on_err` is named like a cleanup routine but only logs and returns a bool — the actual `set_bot_assigned(false)` is at the two call sites (`if cleanup_on_err(app, &task_id, &r) { set_bot_assigned(...) }`) and easy to forget on the next refactor. `start()` has a separately hand-rolled version (lines 313-318 region) which is asymmetric with `resume()`. Either move the side effect into the closure (capture `task_id` and `app`, do the `set_bot_assigned(false)` inline), or rename to `log_if_err`/`needs_cleanup` so the call sites don't read like the closure already did the cleanup. As-is, a future maintainer adding a new branch may easily drop the `set_bot_assigned(false)` call and leak the bot-assigned flag.

The `apply_ops` implementation in `consolidate.rs` wraps the loop in `conn.transaction()` and uses `?` on every store call, so any failing op does roll back on drop — but no test injects a mid-batch failure to lock that contract in. comments.content: Merge target selection tie-break is not exercised. Production uses `max_by(|a,b| a.importance.cmp(&b.importance).then(a.updated_at_ms.cmp(&b.updated_at_ms)))`, so when two sources share the same max importance the *more recently updated* one wins. Here importances are 3/4/2 so the strict max path is the only path covered. Add a case where two sources share the highest importance but differ in `updated_at_ms` (or `now+1` vs `now+2`), and assert the newer one survives with the merged content — otherwise a regression that drops the secondary sort key would not be caught.

This test pins down a dangerous default: any unrecognised `interval` string silently disables consolidation forever, even when `enabled = true`. The current behavior is "测试与生产完全一致"，但配置错字（粘贴空格、全角符号、用户手写错）会变成静默特性失效，且不会留下任何告警/日志。建议要么降级为默认 `daily` 并在配置加载处 `log::warn!` 一次，要么至少在视图层校验并在保存时拒绝；测试侧至少应加一条覆盖「合法值改坏后回退到默认」的契约。

`since_ms` semantics are only verified for the future-time edge case (`now + 1000` → only active items qualify). The realistic case — `since_ms` is a real previous-run timestamp in the past — is never asserted. Production (`gather_candidates`) does `since_ms.unwrap_or(now_ms - CONSOLIDATE_DEFAULT_WINDOW_MS)` and the predicate is `updated_at_ms >= threshold || access_count >= CONSOLIDATE_ACTIVE_ACCESS`, so a past `since_ms` should include (a) items updated since last run and (b) items updated earlier but still active. Add a test where one item was updated between last run and now, and another was updated long ago but is active, and assert both are present — otherwise the window-vs-since interaction is unverified.

Only the all-phantom path of distill is covered. Production's guard is `if !ids.iter().any(|id| all.iter().any(|m| &m.id == id))` — i.e. even *one* real id lets distill proceed and silently drops the phantoms. The contract is non-obvious (a future maintainer could reasonably flip it to `all(...)` and break LLM robustness), so it must be pinned by a test: insert one real item, mix it with a phantom id, assert the reflection is created from the surviving source. Without this, both the current "drop phantoms silently" behavior and a future "strict all-or-nothing" change are undetected regressions.

Distill reflection embedding is not asserted, even though `apply_distill_creates_reflection` checks `kind`/`importance`/`source`. The merge and contradiction tests both assert `embedding.is_some()` on the updated target, but this distill test does not. Production passes the precomputed `emb` to `store::insert_item(&tx, &item, emb, now_ms)`, so a regression that drops the embedding arg (or a `None` slipping through from the embed pipeline) would yield a `reflection` row that is invisible to similarity search — a correctness regression the test wouldn't catch. Add `assert!(r.embedding.is_some(), "reflection 应带向量以参与后续检索");` next to the existing assertions.

comments.content: db_write_lock silently recovers from a poisoned DB_WRITE_LOCK. If a previous holder panicked mid-SQL write, the SQLite connection may be left in an inconsistent state (partial UPDATE/INSERT, half-applied transaction) and this module will keep writing journal rows as if nothing happened, silently corrupting the very source of truth used for startup replay. Either propagate the poison (let the caller see a typed error) or, at minimum, log loudly and reset the journal's invariant before proceeding.

journal_find_pending is intentionally unlocked, but the documented caller pattern is "find pending → caller decides → journal_committed/cleared". There is no atomicity between the SELECT and the follow-up UPDATE; a concurrent writer can flip the row's state between find and act. The UPDATE itself is idempotent, but the caller's decision (e.g. "another worker is already operating on this src, skip") is made on stale data and can lead to lost work or to two operations acting on the same (task_id, src) simultaneously. Either take DB_WRITE_LOCK around the find+act pair, or expose an atomic "claim pending" helper that returns the id only if it can be transitioned.

journal_pending unconditionally INSERTs a new pending row without checking whether one already exists for the same (task_id, src). Concurrent or retried callers (or any path that re-enters after a transient error) can create multiple pending rows for the same key, which then confuses replay/reconciliation: journal_find_pending picks the latest by id DESC, so older pending rows become invisible orphans and may cause the replay path to act on a row that no longer reflects the operation the caller is about to perform. Enforce "at most one pending per (task_id, src)" via a UNIQUE partial index on (task_id, src) WHERE state='pending', or by an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT that reuses the existing id.

// Enforce at most one pending row per (task_id, src) so replay/claim see a single canonical id.
    conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO migration_journal (op, src, dst, task_id, state, created_at)
         VALUES (?1, ?2, ?3, ?4, 'pending', ?5)
         ON CONFLICT(task_id, src) WHERE state = 'pending'
         DO UPDATE SET created_at = excluded.created_at
         RETURNING id",
        rusqlite::params![
            op,
            src.to_string_lossy(),
            dst.map(|p| p.to_string_lossy().to_string()),

comments.content: All rusqlite errors are erased to String via `e.to_string()` at the public API boundary. When replay fails or a journal write aborts, callers (and the replay path that depends on this module) get only a flat string with no SQL context, statement, or underlying cause. Define a typed error (e.g. a `JournalError` enum carrying `rusqlite::Error`) and convert at the FFI/tauri boundary instead.

state is a free-form TEXT column populated with string literals ('pending', 'committed', 'cleared') and there is no CHECK constraint enforcing the set. A typo, a future refactor that introduces 'commited'/'cancelled', or a manual DB edit would be silently accepted and would mislead journal_find_pending (which filters on state='pending') and replay/reconciliation logic. Add a CHECK(state IN ('pending','committed','cleared')) to the migration_journal schema, or model state as an INTEGER backed by a typed enum at the Rust layer.

comments.content: `migration_run` `await`s a `spawn_blocking` `JoinHandle` with no abort/cancel wiring. If the frontend cancels the invocation (window close, navigation, app shutdown) the future is dropped, the handle is dropped, but the migration keeps running on the blocking pool — mutating the log file and shared migration state with no observer and no way to gate a subsequent invocation. Wrap the blocking work in a `tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken` (or `JoinSet`/`AbortHandle` so cancellation is observable), and ensure `run_migration` itself checks the cancel signal between phases so partial work can be rolled back / marked failed.
comments.existing_code: tauri::async_runtime::spawn_blocking(move || super::run::run_migration(&app))

comments.content: `migration_rules_load` is declared as a synchronous `#[tauri::command]` but calls `load_rules(&app)`, which performs filesystem reads — this runs on Tauri's main/UI thread and can freeze the window for slow disks. The module's own B3 comment in `migration_run` explicitly mandates `spawn_blocking` for long IO, yet this command doesn't follow it. Make it `async` and route through `spawn_blocking` like `migration_run`, or have `load_rules` itself be non-blocking (cached/in-memory snapshot) so the command stays cheap.

`serde_json::from_str(...).map_err(|e| format!("JSON 解析失败：{e}"))?` discards the typed `serde_json::Error` (which carries line/column and expected-token info) and reduces it to a bare `String` before it is coerced into `CommandError` via `From<String>`. The audit log and any caller-level handling therefore lose actionable context. Add a dedicated `CommandError::ParseError { kind: "json", source: Box<dyn Error> }` (or similar) variant and `.map_err(|e| CommandError::ParseError { kind: "json".into(), source: e.into() })`, keeping the original error in `source`. The same stringification pattern appears for `into_path()` and `fs::read(&path)` — they should likewise preserve the underlying `io::Error` / `tauri_plugin_dialog::Error` rather than collapsing it into a formatted string at this boundary.
comments.existing_code: serde_json::from_str(&text).map_err(|e| format!("JSON 解析失败：{e}"))?

comments.content: `migration_status` is a sync `#[tauri::command]` and re-runs `load_rules(&app)` (filesystem read) on every poll — the polling cadence plus the UI-thread blocking violates the same B3 rule called out elsewhere in this file. The status payload is just `rules.len()`, which can be served from a cached `Arc<RulesFile>` updated on `save_rules`/`migration_rules_import`, or — at minimum — load the file through `spawn_blocking`. Right now both `migration_status` and `migration_rules_load` re-read the rules file from disk on every call.

UTF-16 detection is BOM-only: a UTF-16 LE/BE file without a BOM (e.g. output by `iconv`, some Windows tools, or PowerShell `Out-File -Encoding Unicode` without explicit BOM) fails both `starts_with` checks and falls through to the GBK branch, where it is silently mis-decoded as a different CJK encoding. Additionally, `bytes[2..].chunks_exact(2)` silently drops any trailing odd byte after a UTF-16 BOM, returning a string with no indication data was lost. Detect UTF-16 by attempting `String::from_utf16le(&bytes)` / `String::from_utf16be(&bytes)` directly (treating the un-BOM'd case as a probe) and surface the trailing-odd-byte case as an explicit `CommandError` rather than silently truncating.

Same `spawn_blocking` + dropped-`JoinHandle` shape as `migration_run`: a frontend cancel during the log read silently drops the future mid-`fs::read_to_string`, and the work either runs to completion wastefully or is torn down without informing the caller. The 5MB cap means the read is fast in practice, but the underlying pattern is not cancellation-safe — chunk the read (e.g. `BufReader::take` with a periodic cancel check), or at minimum move the read behind an abort-aware primitive so cancellation is observable.

`tail_log_lines` materializes the entire log into a `Vec<&str>` on every call (the file's own comment caps the log at 5MB), then re-allocates a copy via `to_vec()` when `lines.len() > limit`, then `reverse()` + `join`. The hot long-log case is O(n) allocs instead of O(limit). A bounded ring buffer during the read, or — given we already have the full `&str` — `let start = lines.len().saturating_sub(limit); lines.drain(..start); lines.reverse();` keeps the function O(limit) and removes the second allocation. For the small-file case `drain(..0)` is a no-op so the behavior is identical.

Module docstring claims "共 5 个 #[tauri::command]" but the file actually declares 6 (`migration_rules_load`, `migration_rules_import`, `migration_rules_template_save`, `migration_run`, `migration_log_read`, `migration_status`). Update the count to 6 so future readers don't grep for a missing command.

comments.content: Every rusqlite::Error is collapsed to String via `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())` throughout this file (ensure_table, load_all, evict_if_needed, insert_item, insert_new, update_by_id, delete_by_key_tag, count_by_kind, oldest_by_kind, delete_by_ids, touch_accessed). This loses error kind (Busy/Locked/Constraint/Io), the underlying error chain, and the ability for callers/tests to discriminate. Consider a thin `MemoryError` enum (or `thiserror`) that wraps `rusqlite::Error` plus a `RejectedFull { protected_count: usize }` variant, and let `InsertOutcome::RejectedFull` carry that typed error instead of a free-form String.
comments.existing_code:
.map_err(|e| e.to_string())
}

comments.content: Tag codec is not round-trip safe. Write side does `item.tags.join(",")` with no escaping; read side splits on `,` then `trim()`s and filters empties. A tag like "a,b" round-trips as two tags ["a","b"]; tags with leading/trailing whitespace are silently mutated (" foo " -> "foo"); and `find_by_key_tag`'s exact-match contract is violated by any caller-provided tag containing whitespace/commas. Either (a) use a join table `mem_item_tags(item_id, tag)`, (b) JSON-encode the tags vector (`serde_json`), or (c) use a proper delimiter escape. Also reject empty/whitespace tags at the write boundary.

Hot path does two full-table scans per insert. `insert_item` calls `load_all` for the dedup loop, then on the no-merge branch delegates to `insert_new` which calls `evict_if_needed`, which calls `load_all` again. For a 500-row cap that's up to 1000 row reads plus per-row BLOB decode per insert. Pass the already-loaded `all: Vec<MemItem>` down to `insert_new`/`evict_if_needed` (or have `evict_if_needed` accept a preloaded slice) and skip the second `load_all`. Also remove the `ensure_table(conn)?` from inside `insert_item` — the module doc says it's done once at open_db; doing it on every write is redundant.
comments.existing_code:
ensure_table(conn)?;
    let all = load_all(conn)?;

comments.content: `delete_by_ids` and `touch_accessed` issue one statement per id in a plain loop with no surrounding transaction and no error short-circuiting with rollback. Mid-loop failure leaves the table partially mutated and the return value `n` is the count from the failed statement onward (rusqlite returns `Ok(0)` for the rest? actually it returns the error and stops, but earlier successful deletes stay committed). Wrap in `conn.transaction()` (or use a single `UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (?1,?2,...)` / `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (...)` with a chunked batch).

`oldest_by_kind` silently swallows row-level errors via `filter_map(|r| r.ok())`. If a row's columns can't deserialize (type mismatch, future schema drift, NULL in NOT NULL column), the affected rows are dropped from the result with no error and no log. Reflection's "oldest 10 summaries" would silently return fewer than 10 entries without the caller knowing. Either propagate the error (`collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()`) or at minimum log the dropped rows.
comments.existing_code: .map(|iter| iter.filter_map(|r| r.ok()).collect::<Vec<_>>())

comments.content: Timestamp helpers silently produce degenerate values that propagate. `ts_to_text` returns `""` on out-of-range ms; `ts_to_ms("")` returns 0; so a row written with a bad timestamp persists as `""`, reads back as `0`, and `evict_score` computes `age_days = now_ms/86_400_000` -> very low score -> row gets evicted first. The "parse failure -> 0 = oldest" comment acknowledges this, but the failure is unobservable from the API and depends on the caller-supplied `now_ms` being valid. Either return `Result<String, _>` from `ts_to_text` (and surface the error in `ensure_table`/`insert_*`), or clamp/validate `now_ms` at the entry points and reject bad input.

`is_protected` uses `importance >= 5`, but the importance range is only enforced by `clamp(1, 5)` at this crate's insert/update sites — there is no `CHECK (importance BETWEEN 1 AND 5)` on the table, no enum/typed value, and no migration step that backfills. A direct write (admin tool, future code path, manual SQL) that stores `importance = 7, source = 'user_stated'` would be over-protected relative to the docstring's contract ("importance=5 且用户口述"). Add a CHECK constraint in `ensure_table` (note: SQLite needs `PRAGMA writable_schema` or a version-gated migration if the table already exists) and consider `== 5` instead of `>= 5` to match the clamp invariant.

`find_by_key_tag` (and therefore `delete_by_key_tag`) does a full table load + linear scan for what is conceptually a primary-key-style lookup on the first tag. For 500 rows this is fine, but it's also unbounded: anyone tightening the cap will keep paying O(n). Push the predicate into SQL: `SELECT ... FROM mem_items WHERE tags = ?1 OR tags LIKE ?1||',%' OR tags LIKE '%,'||?1 LIMIT 1` (or move tags into a join table with an index on the tag column). Same applies to `count_by_kind` if it ever sees hot usage — today it's bounded but a `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE kind = ?1` is already SQL-side, so that one is fine.

`delete_by_key_tag` is not atomic: it does `find_by_key_tag` (SELECT) then a separate `DELETE`. Under any concurrent writer (the comment says locking is in the facade layer, so this matters even on a single connection if a future caller wraps the facade in a transaction-aware way) the row could be deleted between the two statements, causing the second `execute` to return `Ok(0)` and `delete_by_key_tag` to return `false` even though the key WAS present at the SELECT. Either rely on `RETURNING` / `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id ...)` so the existence check and delete happen in one statement, or wrap both in a `conn.transaction()`.

`insert_new` returns `Ok(InsertOutcome::RejectedFull(...))` when eviction can't free a slot. The `Result` is `Ok`, so callers using `?` will propagate it as success — if any caller maps `Result<T, String>` to a hard error without inspecting the variant, a full-but-protected memory state would be silently treated as success. The doc comment says this is intentional ("拒写，信息给模型"), but it's an easy footgun; consider making `insert_item` return `Err(String)` for the rejected case (the merged/inserted/hint triple is then only the success path) or naming the variant more loudly (e.g. `RefusedCapacityFull`).

Every failure path in embed_text (tokenizer encode, ONNX run, output extraction, shape mismatch) is collapsed to `None` via `.ok()?` with no logging. Once the engine has loaded successfully, any subsequent runtime failure (e.g., ONNX runtime internal error, unexpected model output shape) becomes completely invisible — operators only see "no vector". The `load_engine` path logs a one-line failure, but the hot path stays silent. At minimum, log `eprintln!` (with a rate-limit or first-occurrence guard) before returning None for the `try_extract_tensor` failure and the shape-mismatch guard so model drift / corruption is detectable in production.

`eng.session.lock().ok()?` discards `PoisonError`. If any thread holding the `session` Mutex panics (e.g., during ONNX inference or inside a user-supplied callback in the future), the Mutex becomes poisoned and `lock()` returns `Err` forever — meaning every subsequent `embed_text` call across the whole process lifetime silently degrades to `None`. This is a permanent, invisible failure mode triggered by an unrelated panic. Either call `lock().unwrap_or_else(|p| p.into_inner())` to recover from poisoning (the session is still valid if the panic didn't corrupt it) or surface a clear error so the caller can distinguish "model degraded" from "engine poisoned".
comments.existing_code: let mut session = eng.session.lock().ok()?;

comments.content: The warmup thread is spawned and its `JoinHandle` is immediately dropped. If the dummy inference panics (e.g., a tokenizer edge case on the literal `"预热"`, or an ONNX runtime init that failed at session.run time but succeeded at commit time), the panic silently aborts the thread and no one notices. The whole point of warmup is to fail fast on the dummy path so the real path is hot — silently swallowing warmup failures defeats that. Either `let handle = std::thread::spawn(...);` and `std::mem::forget(handle)` (with a comment) or use `std::thread::Builder::spawn(...).expect(...)` and at least log via a panic hook, or move the warmup logic into a function returning `Result` and have the caller decide.

`outputs.iter().next()` blindly picks the first tensor with no validation against the bge contract. If the `ort` runtime ever returns a map-like container (or if a future model variant emits multiple outputs such as `pooler_output` alongside `last_hidden_state`), iteration order is undefined and we could silently select the wrong tensor. The shape-mismatch guard (`data.len() != seq * EMBED_DIM`) masks this as `None` rather than an explicit "wrong output selected" error. Either assert the output name (e.g., match on `"last_hidden_state"` / index 0) and log+return None if it's not what we expect, or document the model contract and add a startup-time sanity check that the first output has the expected shape.

The error message claims all three locations were checked, but `pick_model_dir` short-circuits and never tries `exe_dir` / `dev_dir` whenever the explicit env var is set but the directory is missing/malformed (the `return usable(&p).then_some(p)` falls through to `None` without trying the fallbacks). When triaging "model missing" in production this will mislead operators into checking exe/root locations that were never actually probed. Either change the message to reflect what was actually checked, or — arguably better — make the env-var path also fall back to exe/dev (matching the existing test that documents "显式目录不可用时不回退" as the *intentional* behaviour but the user-facing message shouldn't lie about what happened).

Mutex-poison recovery is inconsistent across the file: only `tool_remember_fact` logs poisoning via `eprintln!`, while every other acquisition (e.g. `injection_block`, `tool_recall_facts`, `tool_record_lesson`, `save_summary`, `apply_reflection`, `auto_lesson_on_task_failure`) silently calls `e.into_inner()` with no audit trail. Silent recovery from a poisoned `DB_WRITE_LOCK` is itself dangerous — the panicking writer may have left the rusqlite `Connection` in an inconsistent state (uncommitted transaction, half-applied schema change), and a follow-up writer will not know to re-validate. Pick one policy and apply it everywhere (preferably an `audit_event!` at `Warn` level, matching the pattern used by the read/write failure paths in `injection_block` / `auto_lesson_on_task_failure`), or stop recovering from poisoning entirely and propagate it so callers can fail closed.
comments.existing_code: let _g = crate::db::DB_WRITE_LOCK.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!("[mutex_poisoned] db::DB_WRITE_LOCK: {e:?}"); e.into_inner() });

comments.content: `category_to_kind` silently drops the `project` category. The tool-level match in `tool_remember_fact` accepts `"project"` as a distinct, valid category, but `category_to_kind` only maps `"profile"` and `"preference"`; everything else (`"project"`, `"general"`, and any unknown string) collapses to `"fact"`. So `project` and `general` memories are indistinguishable in storage and in `recall_facts` output. Either fold the two-level mapping into one (so the schema contract "4 categories" matches the kind actually persisted), or extend `category_to_kind` to handle `project`/`general` explicitly and reject unknown values.

`task_failure_lesson` returns `(content, Vec<String>)` with hard-coded `vec!["lesson", "task_exec"]` tags, but the only caller (`auto_lesson_on_task_failure`) destructures as `let (content, _tags) = …` and discards them. `record_lesson_core` then re-derives the same tags from its `scenario` parameter, so the returned tag vector is dead code that misleads readers about how lesson categorization works and creates two parallel sources of truth for the same data. Either drop the second tuple element so callers don't think they can override the tags, or thread `_tags` through to `record_lesson_core` so a caller can override the default `"lesson" + scenario` schema.

`block_chars` walks every section and every line on each iteration of the trim `while` (guarded only by `guard < 10_000`), so trimming is O(sections · items · trims). With the 500-item cap and the four sections this is bounded, but it's still wasted work and the `10_000` magic guard is only there to bound this recomputation. Cache per-section char counts once and maintain a running total, subtracting the popped line's length on each pop, so trimming becomes O(1) per pop and the guard can be dropped.

The 50 ms warmup is unreliable on slow CI (especially Windows): if the OS scheduler delays the holder thread and it has not actually acquired `db_write_lock` when the main thread resumes, the writer's `journal_pending` / `journal_committed` / `journal_cleared` calls may not contend with the lock at all — and the test will silently pass without verifying the serialisation invariant. The current design also only verifies that *some* lock acquisition happens during the three calls; if `journal_pending` locks but the other two are refactored to bypass `db_write_lock`, the assertion still passes. Use a deterministic signal (e.g. `AtomicBool` flipped immediately after `db_write_lock()` is taken, or a `std::sync::mpsc` oneshot) so the main thread only starts measuring after the holder is confirmed to hold the lock, and consider measuring each call separately so every operation is independently proven to serialise.

Several `parse_rules_csv_*` tests assert on specific Chinese substrings inside `err.to_string()` (`"飞行"`, `"第 2 行"`, `"四列"`, `"没有解析出任何规则"`). This couples test maintenance to the exact wording/format of user-facing error messages: any i18n refactor, message rephrasing, or row-numbering format change in `rules::parse_rules_csv` will fail these tests even though the parser's behaviour is unchanged. Prefer asserting on typed error variants / structured fields (e.g. `ParseCsvError::UnknownAction { row: 2, token: "飞行" }` or `ParseCsvError::HeaderColumns { expected: 4 }`) rather than substring matches against the rendered string.

`record_lesson_validation` couples 4 separate assertions to specific substrings of user-visible error messages ("不能为空", "太长", "scenario", "逗号"). Any wording tweak in `validate_lesson` / `validate_fact_kv` / `record_lesson_core` will silently break these tests even though the behavior is still correct. Consider either returning typed errors and asserting on error variants, or accepting a wider set of stable tokens (e.g., key substring like "≤" or a stable error code).

`record_lesson_semantic_dedup_merges` asserts `msg.contains("合并")` to detect that the second lesson was merged with the first. This couples the test to the exact user-visible wording of the merge success message in `record_lesson_core`. Prefer asserting on the structural invariant (e.g., `store::load_all(&conn).unwrap().len() == 1` already done below) or on a typed `InsertOutcome::Merged` instead of the formatted string.

`capacity_full_of_protected_rejects_write` asserts `msg.contains("上限")` on the `RejectedFull` string. Since `InsertOutcome::RejectedFull(String)` already carries the typed payload, prefer asserting on the discriminant only or on a stable token (e.g., the constant `MAX_MEM_ITEMS`). The current assertion would break if the message is reworded to a synonym like "已满" or "容量".

`task_failure_lesson_content_shape` asserts `content.contains("401")` to verify that an HTTP-style status code survives shaping. This is a tight coupling to the literal digits "401" appearing in the output. If `task_failure_lesson` ever decides to redact numeric codes (e.g., replace with `[HTTP_<code>]`) or reorders content, this assertion will fail even when behavior is improved. Consider passing a more semantic sentinel (a uniquely recognizable phrase) or asserting on presence of both `task` description and the error category only.

Coverage gap: there is no test exercising the `cosine` dimension-mismatch branch (`a.len() != b.len() -> None`) with the full `hybrid_score`/`hybrid_search` path. All test vectors are 512-dim via `onehot`/`tilted`. If a caller (e.g., a future ONNX model producing 384/768-dim vectors) injects a query vector of a different length than stored items, `cosine` returns `None`, `semantic = 0.0`, the guard at `kw == 0.0 && (query_emb.is_none() || item.embedding.is_none())` does NOT fire (because `query_emb.is_some()` and `item.embedding.is_some()`), and the score becomes the importance/recency baseline (≥ 0.15) — meaning dimension mismatch silently degrades to "constant positive baseline" rather than zero. Add a test that calls `rank::hybrid_search` with a 128-dim query against the 512-dim corpus and asserts the hit list is empty (or that the score reflects the intent, depending on the design decision).

Coverage gap on dedup threshold boundaries: `DEDUP_MERGE_COSINE = 0.92` and `DEDUP_HINT_COSINE = 0.75` are never exercised at exactly the boundary. The tests only sample cos = 1.0 (merge), 0.8 (hint), 0.0 (no hint). If `insert_item` ever flipped `>=` to `>` at either threshold, the test suite would not catch it. Recommend adding two boundary tests using `tilted(0.92)` and `tilted(0.75)` (acknowledging the small floating-point drift from `sqrt`) and verifying the expected branch.

`assert_eq!(rank::hybrid_score(...), 0.0, ...)` uses strict float equality on the vectorless/zero-overlap guard path. The current `hybrid_score` happens to `return 0.0;` literally, so the test passes, but a future refactor (e.g., `return kw * 0.0;` or `return Some(0.0).unwrap()`) would either compute a subnormal and break the test for the wrong reason, or silently introduce drift. Use the same epsilon pattern already used in `hybrid_score_degraded_renormalizes_weights` (`(s - 0.0).abs() < 1e-9`) for consistency and resilience.

`capacity_eviction_order_and_protection` promotes `store::load_all(&conn).unwrap()[0]` as the protected row. `load_all` is `SELECT ... FROM mem_items` with **no `ORDER BY`**, so the row returned at index 0 is implementation-defined (effectively rowid order). The assertion that follows ("受保护条目存活") is independent of WHICH row is protected (eviction filters out any `is_protected` row), so the test still verifies the right invariant — but the comment "提为受保护" misleads a future reader into thinking `[0]` is "the oldest" or "the first inserted". Either explicitly document that the choice is arbitrary, or pick a specific row by content/timestamp so the test's intent is unambiguous.

Silent fallback to `RulesFile::default()` on parse error is a data-integrity hazard: if a caller (see `commands.rs::migration_rules_load`, `run.rs::run_migration`) then triggers `save_rules` (e.g. re-save after an edit, or first-save after an upgrade), the corrupt file is overwritten with an empty ruleset — the user's rules are gone with only a log line as trace. Consider either quarantining the bad file (`rules.json.bak-<ts>`) before returning the default, or returning a structured error (`Result<RulesFile, LoadError>`) so the UI can surface "rules file corrupt — recovery options" rather than silently presenting an empty editor.

log_line: rotation target and write target resolve to different filesystem locations when `db::data_dir(app)` is not already canonical. Rotation is done on `super::rules::log_path(app)` (= `db::data_dir(app).join(LOG_FILE)`), but the open below uses `canonicalize(db::data_dir(app)).join(LOG_FILE)`. On platforms where the data dir traverses symlinks (very common on macOS, also possible on Windows under `%LOCALAPPDATA%`), `log_path` and the canonicalized path point to different inodes — rotation can rename a file while writes keep going to the original one, producing a stale log that grows without bound and never gets rotated. Use a single, canonicalized path for both rotation and writing.

copy_dir_recursive: on mid-copy failure the destination is left in a partially populated state. The function pre-creates `dst`, then iterates entries; if any `fs::copy` or nested `copy_dir_recursive` returns Err, the caller gets an error but already-copied siblings are not removed. Combined with `move_entry`'s cross-volume path — which delegates to this function and does not roll back `dst` either — a failed cross-volume move will on retry have `claim_dst_name` pick a *new* directory suffix (because the original `dst` now exists), silently duplicating the user's tree in the archive. Either roll back `dst` on error or document and require the caller to clean up.

MOVE_REMOVE_FAILS bookkeeping has two compounding issues: (1) the HashMap grows without bound — every unique src path is inserted on first failure and never removed, even after a successful move, so over a long-running daemon this leaks memory and, more importantly, retains the full set of files the user ever touched; (2) the count is monotonic and never decremented on success, so a path that hits MAX transient failures, later succeeds once, then fails again is already past threshold — but more subtly, *any* path that ever crosses the threshold is blacklisted for the life of the process. Either evict entries on success or document the invariant and bound the map (e.g., an LRU), and ensure the failure counter resets on a successful move (i.e., delete the entry when `move_entry` reports Ok).

move_entry discards the original `fs::rename` error with `if let Err(_e)`, then synthesizes a generic "复制失败" / "复制成功但删除源文件失败" message at the failure boundary. When rename fails with EXDEV (cross-volume), the kernel-vs-filesystem error semantics matter for diagnosing layered quirks; when it fails with permission/IO/NotFound, callers currently see a misleading cross-volume-flavored message even on a single volume. Chain the underlying error into the returned message (or return a structured error type) so logs/audit retain the real cause.

copy_dir_recursive relies on `entry.file_type().is_symlink()` to refuse symlinked subtrees. On Windows, `DirEntry::file_type` is implemented in terms of `FindNextFileW` semantics and on some configurations can report the target's type rather than the symlink itself, so a symlink under `src` may slip through into the destination as a real file/directory. If the source directory is user-controlled (a Downloads folder, or anything reachable via rule matching), the migration could materialize content the user did not intend to archive, and `move_entry`'s cross-volume branch would then `fs::copy` the symlink target into `dst`. Either do an explicit `fs::symlink_metadata(&entry.path())` check before deciding to descend, or refuse the entire move when the root is not provably symlink-free.

Header matching uses `h.contains(needle)`, which is too permissive and can silently bind to the wrong column. For example, a CSV with both "归档目录" and "目标目录" picks whichever appears first, and a custom header like "子关键字" would satisfy the "关键字" needle. Also, two different needles can match the same column. Use exact, full-token matching against a normalized header (trim + lowercase) and reject ambiguous matches with a row-level error.

comments.content: `validate_rules` only checks that `archive_dir` is non-empty; it does not constrain the path. A tampered `cleanup-rules.json` or a crafted CSV import can set values like `../../etc`, `/etc`, or `C:\Windows` and the migration runner will move files there. DEVLOG already documents an earlier production incident where a missing `rename_all = "camelCase"` caused `archive_dir` to deserialize empty, sending files to the desktop root — the same class of bug, different root cause. Add a path-containment check (reject `..` components, reject absolute paths, and ideally require the resolved path to live under an allow-listed base directory such as the user's Documents/Desktop).

Two silent defaults mask user typos in the CSV: an empty `动作` cell coerces to `"move"` (and then the row needs an `archive_dir` it never had), and any `启用` value outside an explicit allow-list (`是/true/TRUE/1`) coerces to `false`. Both can turn a rule the user thought they wrote into something else — and the resulting rule can still pass `validate_rules` and run, silently deleting/keeping files. Treat empty action as a row error (or require explicit `移动归档`/`删除文件`), and reject unknown enabled tokens instead of defaulting to `false`. Also note the asymmetry with action parsing, which lists `"移动"` alone — that's a substring-like footgun for any column containing that text.

Error handling in this module is fragmented across three shapes — `Result<(), String>` (`save_rules_to`, `validate_rules`), `Result<RulesFile, CommandError>` (`parse_rules_csv`), and inline `format!("...{e}")` strings (`save_rules_to`, header-error path) — and `format!("{e}")` discards the underlying error chain. Callers in `commands.rs` end up pattern-matching on free-form strings, and the original `io::Error` / `serde_json::Error` is lost. Pick one error type per layer (CommandError for the public boundary, internal `thiserror` enum for internals) and preserve the source error via `#[source]` / `Display` chaining instead of `to_string()`.

The age computation `(now_ms - base) as f64` is an unguarded `i64` subtraction that can panic in debug builds (integer overflow) and silently wrap in release builds if `now_ms < base` by a large amount (e.g. misconfigured clocks, far-future timestamps, mixed time sources). The `.max(0.0)` afterwards only clamps the resulting `f64`, not the `i64` arithmetic that produced it. Use `i64::saturating_sub` to make the clamp happen at the right stage:

```rust
let age_days = (now_ms.saturating_sub(base) as f64 / 86_400_000.0).max(0.0);
```

comments.content: Two independent implementations of the same log line format (paths::write_fallback_warn vs audit::write_at) with a documented 'byte-level identical' contract that is asserted only by `write_fallback_warn_format_matches_audit` checking the structural shape of *its own* output — it never calls `audit::write_at` and compares bytes. If audit changes its format (kv separator, timestamp precision, escape rules, line terminator), paths silently produces lines the log viewer / grep pipeline can no longer parse — breaking exactly the diagnostic the WARN is meant to provide. Either (a) add a test that calls `audit::write_at` with the same inputs and diffs output bytes, or (b) factor a single `build_event_line` helper into a third module that both audit and paths consume, eliminating the duplication and the drift risk. The header comment also inconsistently names the audit function ('audit::write_at' in the doc, 'audit::build_event_line' in the body comment) — that's an early signal the duplication is already drifting.

`escape_for_log_inline` strips only `\n` and `| ` — yet the doc mandates byte-level parity with `audit::escape_for_log`, and that parity is asserted only by `escape_for_log_inline_strips_newline_and_pipe` testing this function in isolation (no cross-implementation test exists). Two divergent copies of an escape function are a hazard waiting to happen. Concretely: a single unescaped `\r` in `exe_dir` / `resolved` / `reason` can split the rendered line in many log viewers, and any other control char audit happens to escape will desync the kv parser here. (a) add a parity test that feeds identical inputs to both functions and asserts `==`, and (b) at minimum extend this escape to also strip `\r` and `\0` so a downstream viewer's row boundary can never be corrupted by user-controllable path components.

Detached `std::thread::spawn` whose `JoinHandle` is dropped. The thread can be killed mid-write if the process exits — and the fallback WARN is most likely on first launch / install / after an upgrade, exactly when the user is shutting the app down. Any panic inside `write_fallback_warn` (e.g. permission denied, malformed utf-8 in `reason`) is silently swallowed by `std::thread`'s default handler. The diagnostic you want the most is the one you can never observe. Consider attaching the `JoinHandle` to a `OnceLock` so a shutdown hook can flush it, or wrap the closure in `catch_unwind` so panics are surfaced to stderr instead of vanishing.

`ends_with(".app")` matches any path component ending in those four characters — including `wmessage.appdata`, `my.appmodified`, `foo.append`, `my.appbackup`, `notapp.app`. A genuine portable install whose parent dir happens to end in `.app*` will be mis-classified, skip the portable branch, and have its DB / `AI_Gen_Files` / logs redirected to `~/Library/Application Support` — silently splitting user data from the portable payload. The existing test only covers the false-negative direction (`MacOSub`); add positive cases like `…/wmessage.appdata/Contents/MacOS` and change the check to a strict component-name match (e.g. require the suffix to be exactly `.app` and the component to look like a bundle, or anchor the bundle name in a constant). Also note `to_string_lossy()` substitutes U+FFFD on non-UTF8 components — using `as_os_str().to_str()` or direct byte compare avoids that lossy step.

All three branches of `probe_dir` return a `PathBuf` without ensuring the directory exists. Every caller (`db.rs` / `profile.rs` / `audit.rs` / `bot.rs`) must independently remember to `mkdir` before first write, and the `temp_dir()` fallback is a real shared location where a missing dir (cleaned `%TEMP%`, fresh container, transient I/O error) turns into a hard-to-reproduce `No such file or directory` on first run instead of a recoverable error. Either have the function create the chosen directory before returning (single source of truth), or rename to `probe_dir_path` and document the `create_dir_all` contract loudly in the doc-comment so a future caller doesn't skip it.

The `?` operator here short-circuits out of `copy_file_windows` without calling `CloseClipboard()`. Since `OpenClipboard(None)` succeeded a few lines earlier, every exit path from this function MUST drain through `CloseClipboard` — otherwise the clipboard remains owned by this process and every subsequent `OpenClipboard` in the app stalls (intermittent "another program is using the clipboard" errors). As a bonus, this also stops discarding the original `windows::core::Error` via `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())`.

comments.content: The `ENGINE` `OnceLock` caches a failed `load_engine` result for the lifetime of the process (`失败原因进程内只算一次` per the comment). Combined with the doc's expectation that users run `scripts/fetch_ocr_models.sh` to populate `pp-ocr-v6/` after install, a user who downloads the models mid-session will not be able to use OCR until they restart the entire Tauri app — there is no way to retry loading, even after the precondition becomes true. Either re-evaluate the cache (e.g. swap to `OnceLock<Mutex<Result<Engine, String>>>` so a successful load replaces a cached error) or document this limitation prominently. Also note the inconsistent logging: this function uses `eprintln!` for both success and failure, while every other runtime signal in the file goes through `crate::bot::audit_log`. URI schemes are case-insensitive per RFC 3986 §3.1, but this guard compares the raw `path` against lowercase `http://`/`https://`/`data:` prefixes only. An input like `HTTP://attacker.tld/x.png`, `Data:image/png;base64,...`, or `HTTPS://...` slips past the red-line check and falls through to `resolve_with_perm`, where the user sees a generic "file not found" / permission error rather than the explicit "网络地址不予抓取（隐私红线）" message — undermining the documented UX contract for the privacy boundary. Downstream `resolve_with_perm` is the actual safety net (URLs cannot be canonicalized to a local file), so this is not an exfiltration risk, but the explicit guard is part of the privacy contract and should be case-insensitive (e.g. `let lower = path.to_ascii_lowercase(); lower.starts_with(...)`).

comments.content: `std::fs::read(&canonical)` has no size cap, and the downstream `image::load_from_memory` (in `win::recognize`) will fully decompress a PNG/JPEG before the caller can refuse. A multi-GB file or a pathologically crafted image (e.g. a small header advertising huge dimensions) at a path the user already has permission for can OOM the entire Tauri process. Reject oversized inputs early — read metadata first (or use `metadata().len()` and bail out above e.g. ~64 MB) — so the rest of the pipeline can rely on bounded memory. Same concern applies on macOS where `image::load_from_memory` is invoked with the unbounded byte slice.

`run_first` holds the `Mutex<ort::session::Session>` across `session.run(ort::inputs![tensor])` with no timeout, no cancellation, and no recovery from a panic inside inference. Two real hazards follow from this single design choice:

1. **Hang on pathological input / model regression**: a malformed tensor or a degenerate ONNX op can wedge the blocking task forever; the async caller is stuck on the JoinHandle and the OCR tool never returns. There is no surrounding `tokio::time::timeout` and no `ort` cancellation hook. Consider bounding the call (e.g. spawn the inference inside its own `spawn_blocking` with a timeout, or run inference on a thread you can detach/kill) — at minimum, document that the caller must enforce a wall-clock budget.

2. **Mutex poisoning cascades**: if `session.run` ever panics, the `Mutex` becomes poisoned. The next call returns "session 锁失败" and every subsequent OCR request fails for the rest of the process lifetime (combined with the `OnceLock` above, this requires a full app restart). Either drain the error via `.lock().unwrap_or_else(|p| p.into_inner())`, or wrap the call so a panic inside the engine doesn't poison the lock.

The flood-fill uses 4-connectivity (no diagonals). For text regions this is known to fragment a single character/glyph into multiple boxes whenever a thin diagonal stroke connects two parts of the same glyph or whenever text is rendered with subtle antialiasing gaps on the thresholded probability map — a 1-pixel diagonal hole at, say, `((cx, cy), (cx+1, cy+1))` will split the component. PaddleOCR's reference DB post-processing uses 8-connectivity precisely to avoid this fragmentation, which directly translates into fewer text boxes and cleaner rec crops here. Add the four diagonal neighbors (with `cx > 0 && cy > 0`, `cx + 1 < w && cy > 0`, etc.) so `prob_to_boxes` matches the upstream convention.

comments.content: `unclip_box` clamps `x0`/`y0` with `.max(0.0)` and `x1`/`y1` with `.min(max_w)`/`min(max_h)` independently. For a box that touches the image edge (e.g. `x0 = 0.0`, margin = 5.0), the left edge can't expand and stays at 0 while the right edge expands by the full 5 — yielding an asymmetric box (effectively `(0, ?, x1+5, ?)` instead of `(x0-2.5, ?, x1+2.5, ?)`). Downstream this asymmetric crop is fed to `rec`, which sees text whose padding on one side differs from the other and may mis-recognize it. Reduce the margin by the amount it was clamped on the opposing side so the unclip stays balanced (or equivalently, subtract the clipped portion from the margin before applying it).

Forward-compatibility hazard: the module doc explicitly states 'Widget/未标记 = 挂件上报' (widget-reported), meaning the JSON `source` field can be absent or carry an unknown value.
