The `SYSTEM_PROMPT` anchor loop pins the prompt to a specific tool-naming contract (`create_task`, `list_tasks`, `complete_task`, `link_file_to_task`, `web_search`, `AI_Gen_Files`) with no link to the actual tool registry that the runtime dispatcher uses. If a tool handler in `bot_chat.rs` / dispatch code is renamed, or the registry is extended, neither the prompt nor this test knows — so the model can be instructed to call tools that no longer exist or silently bypass new tools. There is also a subtler risk the test itself does not catch: the anchor can appear inside a quoted JSON example or even inside a `// note` style instruction comment, so a renamed-to-still-substring-match rename (`tasks_create` still contains `create_task`) would pass this test while breaking dispatch. Consider an integration assertion that reads the prompt, extracts each referenced tool name, and verifies it exists in the tool registry the dispatcher loads.

`journal_find_pending(...).unwrap_or(None)` silently swallows real DB errors as 'no pending'. If the journal table is unreadable (lock contention, corruption, schema drift), `decide_src_missing` will not see the pending row and route through `Unbind`, zeroing `file_path` on a task whose real dst may still exist on disk — permanently orphaning the binding until a manual DB edit. The pending journal will also 'successfully' unbind on the next poll, masking the failure. Use `.unwrap_or_else(|e| { log_line(...); None })` or change `journal_find_pending` to return `Result<Option<Entry>>` and treat `Err` as a hard abort of the migration.
Same `unwrap_or(None)` anti-pattern in the delete branch — identical orphan-binding consequence for any task whose prior move+db_upsert was interrupted when journal lookup itself fails.

`panic::catch_unwind(...)` only catches the panic arm. `Ok(Err(String))` returned by `run_migration` (DB locked, archive-dir config invalid, journal write contention, etc.) is silently dropped — no log line, no counter, no emitter, no metrics. The polling thread effectively swallows every non-panic failure of the migration step and just sleeps another 10 minutes. Also: payload extraction matches only `&str`/`String`; any other panic payload collapses to '未知 panic', and `AssertUnwindSafe` blanket-trusts the captured `AppHandle` without verifying any invariants. Pattern-match on `r` and handle both `Ok(Err(e))` and panic payloads uniformly (e.g., to_string_lossy().into_owned() fallback), and add a guard/wrapper that converts non-panic `Err` into a logged event.

`run_migration_inner` is synchronous but bridges every DB call into async via `tauri::async_runtime::block_on(...)` (db_load, every per-file db_upsert, final batch db_upsert). For any non-trivial task set this dominates runtime: each call constructs an async context and serializes blocking work on the polling thread. With ~10 such calls, this is essentially one-tokio-bridge-per-DB-call from a std::thread. Move the whole inner fn onto tauri::async_runtime or spawn_blocking, then `await` directly (no block_on). File I/O is the only sync part and belongs in `spawn_blocking`. The `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())` conversions also discard typed `db::Error` context repeatedly; keep the typed error to the top boundary instead of eagerly stringifying at every step.

comments.content: Both `Unbind` arms (move + delete src-missing branches) push the modified task to `changed` and increment `report.skipped` WITHOUT a local `db_upsert`. All unbinds are persisted only via the single final `db_upsert(changed)` at the bottom; if that final write returns Err the function returns Err after having already emitted '解除绑定' log lines and bumped skipped counters, leaving UI / log analyzers with misleading telemetry. The migration is idempotent on retry (next tick sees src still missing, same Unbind path), but the log lines stay wrong and there is no signal that the previous tick's unbinds were ever meant to be retried. Either call `db_upsert` locally here (and only push to `changed` for emit), or defer `log_line`/`report.skipped` until after the bulk write succeeds.

`move_remove_permanently_failed(src_str)` is a process-global permanent skipper with no companion inspect/clear API. Once `record_move_remove_failure` crosses `MAX_MOVE_REMOVE_FAILURES`, the src is excluded from every future poll — restarting the app, clearing the stale archive copy, or fixing a transient Windows file lock does NOT un-stick it. The accompanying 'ERROR ... 已永久跳过该源' log is the only signal and there is no surface to list/reset permanently-skipped entries, so operators and users alike have zero visibility into the global sticky-skip set. Also consider extending the same protection to the `delete` branch for symmetry.

`db_load` pulls the entire tasks table into memory on every poll, and `tasks.iter()` is walked twice (once for archive due, once for rule migration). comments.content: Silent failure of audit writes: both `open_log_append(path)` returning `Err` and the `writeln!` returning `Err` are discarded (`if let Ok ...` + `let _ = ...`). For an audit log, silently dropped entries create misleading forensic gaps — exactly the evidence loss an incident review would flag. Surface failures (at minimum `eprintln!`/tracing error, ideally return `Result<(), io::Error>`) so callers and operators know when the audit trail is incomplete.

Process-wide mutex held across I/O: `BOT_LOG_LOCK` is acquired before `rotate_log_if_large`, `open_log_append`, and the `writeln!`, so all audit writes (and any other code sharing this global lock via `crate::audit`) are serialized behind synchronous disk I/O. If `py_audit` is reached from a Tauri command handler or async task this blocks the runtime, and a single slow rotation stalls every other audit caller. Narrow the critical section to just the open+write (do rotation outside, or under a separate, finer-grained lock), and consider an async-aware writer.

Silent poison recovery masks prior panic state: `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` quietly takes the inner value out of a poisoned mutex. A previous holder that panicked — very plausibly inside one of the `crate::audit` helpers that share `BOT_LOG_LOCK` — leaves the log file in an unknown shape, and this function proceeds as if nothing happened with no record that recovery occurred. At minimum log the recovery; preferably propagate as `Err` and let the caller decide whether the entry is still trustworthy.
comments.existing_code: .unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());

comments.content: The header doc-comment claims the original 3694-line `bot_py.rs` was split into **8** submodules ("按 SRP 拆为 8 个子模块"), but the bullet list that follows enumerates only **7** items (`env`, `runtime`, `io`, `harvest`, `audit`, `document`, `commands`) and the file declares exactly **7** `pub mod` lines. Either the count is wrong or one submodule is missing; reconcile them so the module-level docs match reality and don't mislead readers navigating the SRP split.
comments.suggestion_code: //! 原 `bot_py.rs`（3694 行）按 SRP 拆为 7 个子模块：

comments.content: `pub mod io;` here will shadow `std::io` for any caller that imports via glob (e.g. `use crate::bot_py::*;` or `use crate::py::*;` — both patterns this facade explicitly encourages). Glob-re-exporting a module named `io` is a well-known footgun in Rust and will silently break any call site that relies on unqualified `io::Read`/`io::Write`/etc. Consider renaming to a non-colliding name (e.g. `bounded_io`, `process_io`) before consumers start depending on the re-export.
comments.suggestion_code: pub mod bounded_io;
comments.existing_code: pub mod io;

comments.content: read_to_end errors are swallowed with `let _ =`, so a mid-stream read failure returns `truncated=false` together with whatever bytes happened to be buffered, indistinguishable from a complete short read. Callers that rely on the `(buf, truncated)` tuple to decide whether the Python output is trustworthy cannot detect the partial / corrupt read. Propagate or attach the error (e.g., return `io::Result<(Vec<u8>, bool)>` or a third `bool`/`enum` indicating an I/O failure occurred).

Stream kind is communicated as a `&'static str` ("out"/"err") and matched with raw `==`. This is exactly the kind of stringly-typed API the type-design checklist calls out: typos and extra variants become runtime-only errors, and the match is non-exhaustive. Introduce a small enum (e.g., `enum Stream { Stdout, Stderr }`) and convert the receiver type to `Receiver<(Stream, Vec<u8>, bool)>` so the dispatch is exhaustive at compile time.

stdout/stderr are overwritten, not appended. The loop assigns the latest message for each kind and exits as soon as `got == 2`. The contract "each reader sends exactly one final message per stream" is implicit and undocumented; if a reader ever sends two stdout chunks (or the protocol evolves to stream incrementally), all but the last chunk are silently lost. Either append the bytes into a shared `Vec<u8>`/`String`, or assert/document the single-message invariant and return an error if a second chunk of the same kind arrives.

On join timeout the `JoinHandle` is dropped (which detaches the thread), but the leaked reader still owns its `mpsc::Sender`. Because the Sender outlives this scope, the receiver will never observe `Disconnected`, so any later `recv_timeout` / `drain_output` call (or shutdown logic that relies on channel-close) will hang. Either: (a) ensure the reader thread also holds the `StopToken` so it observes stop and exits, then drop the receiver after `drain_output` and check `disconnected()`, or (b) actually `thread::detach()` while explicitly logging that the channel may remain open, and add a follow-up wait-for-disconnect bounded by another deadline so the caller's shutdown can't wedge.

truncate_output walks the entire UTF-8 string twice on every call (`chars().count()` then `chars().take(OUTPUT_CAP).collect()`). On the output hot path this is O(2n) plus an extra `collect()` allocation in the common no-truncation case (well, none when not truncated — but the count scan alone is wasted). Use `s.char_indices().nth(OUTPUT_CAP)` to do the work in one pass and avoid a second traversal; or, since `OUTPUT_CAP` is a constant, switch the byte-vs-char handling here too if the surrounding code already relies on bytes.

`py_env_check_blocking` bypasses the 3s timeout probe that the rest of the file is designed around. It calls `silent_cmd(&py).arg("--version").output()` and `silent_cmd(&py).args(["-c", probe]).output()` directly — both are unbounded. A broken/hung Python shim (the exact failure mode the top-of-file rationale warns about) will block this function indefinitely, which is the very problem `probe_version_ok_with` exists to solve. Reuse `probe_version_ok_with` (or extract a shared timeout-bounded `output` helper) for these calls instead of raw `.output()`.

Read version from stderr as well as stdout: on Windows, `python --version` writes to stderr by default, so `String::from_utf8_lossy(&o.stdout).trim()` will silently produce an empty `version` string. Capture stderr too (or merge both pipes) when reading the version.

Resource leak: `dir` (a freshly UUID-named subdirectory under `py_runs_root()`) is created and never removed on either success or failure. Every invocation of `run_dotnet_revisions` permanently leaves a `params.json` and any side effects on disk. Wrap the directory in a RAII guard that removes it on drop, or schedule cleanup after `run_python_at` returns, so temp dirs don't accumulate indefinitely.

Holding `PY_CACHE` / `DOTNET_CACHE` guards across the entire `detect_*()` call serializes every concurrent caller behind a probe that can take up to ~3s per candidate (potentially 15s+ across all candidates). The slow work is also done while holding the lock, which is exactly the "Mutex held longer than necessary" pattern. Compute `detect_*()` outside the lock and only acquire the lock to read/write the slot — accepting a benign race on the first concurrent call is preferable to holding a global lock across blocking process spawns.

`_unused_imports` is an explicit dead function whose only purpose is to silence `dead_code` for `CommandError` / `CommandResult` imports that have no real call site. This is a design smell: either the module genuinely has error paths that should be returning `CommandResult` (e.g., from `run_dotnet_revisions` / `py_env_check_blocking`), or the imports should be removed. Don't keep unused error types in scope "for the future" — let `cargo` enforce unused-import hygiene.

`PY_PROBE_COUNT` is a debug/statistics counter with no synchronization requirements beyond monotonic visibility — `SeqCst` is unnecessarily strong here and adds a full fence on every increment. `Relaxed` is sufficient and makes the intended synchronization contract honest.
comments.suggestion_code: PY_PROBE_COUNT.fetch_add(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed);
comments.existing_code: PY_PROBE_COUNT.fetch_add(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::SeqCst);

comments.content: strip_known_ext uses O(n) chars().count() + chars().take() to trim an ASCII suffix; allocates a String even when nothing is stripped. Use str::strip_suffix with eq_ignore_ascii_case (or a single to_lowercase comparison) — cheaper, clearer, and correct for Unicode. Returning Cow<str> at the API boundary would avoid the unconditional allocation on the no-op path.

gen_out_path_in has both a TOCTOU race and weak filename sanitization: (1) while candidate.exists() is a check-then-act race — concurrent doc_make_* calls (the py_run_gate is acquired later in run_doc_*, not around path generation) can both pick the same n and overwrite each other; (2) Path::file_name() returns ".." for an input like "..", so the literal file "..docx" can be created in the output dir. Validate the basename (reject "." / ".." / names containing separators on Windows) and use an atomic create (e.g. OpenOptions::create_new) to avoid the race.

run_doc_revisions recovers from a poisoned py_run_gate via e.into_inner(). If a previous holder panicked mid-operation, the gated state (e.g. the run id counter and children bookkeeping inside py_run_gate) may be in an inconsistent state, and silently continuing can corrupt subsequent runs. Either return an error to the caller, or explicitly clear / re-initialize the protected state after the panic — and at minimum also py_audit the poison event instead of just eprintln!.
comments.existing_code: let _gate = py_run_gate().lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!("[mutex_poisoned] py::runtime::py_run_gate: {e:?}"); e.into_inner() });

comments.content: file_path_to_string returns u.to_string() for FilePath::Url, handing back a URL string that downstream code uses as a filesystem path. On mobile / sandboxed targets the URL cannot be opened with std::fs; for desktop it's typically Path but the Url arm should still resolve to the local path (url.to_file_path()) or surface a clear error.

run_doc_script and run_doc_revisions flatten errors to String at the async/sync boundary (.map_err(|e| e.to_string()) followed by Err(e.to_string()) from spawn_blocking_map). The original RunFail / CommandError discriminants and any structured fields are lost, so callers (and audit logs) only get a stringified message. Propagate the typed error through, or attach .with_context() / source chain before stringifying.

py_audit calls log raw user-controlled strings — full file paths, user-supplied filenames, and the entire Python source passed to py_exec_sync — verbatim (truncated only by escape_for_log's length cap). If the user includes secrets, PII, or credentials in a chosen file path or in py_exec code, they will land in the audit log. Hash or hash-prefix such fields, and document the retention/redaction policy for these log entries.

The _unused_refs fn exists solely to silence unused-import warnings on Path / mpsc / Duration / Instant / PyEnv / RunFail; rather than touching those imports in one place, prefer marking only the actually-used items with #[allow(unused_imports)] at the use site, or just delete the unused imports (the underlying modules are presumably used elsewhere in the crate).

Sweeper can delete the working directory of a still-running Python run. The decision is based purely on directory mtime vs `max_age` (default 1 hour) with no PID/lock sentinel or running-process check. A long-running script (training, batch job, anything >1h) will have its run dir removed mid-execution, causing IO errors on subsequent writes and lost output. Add a per-run lockfile / PID check, or skip directories whose child process is still alive, before removing.

TOCTOU race in dedup name resolution. The `.exists()`-then-join loop is a classic check-then-act pattern: two concurrent harvest/sweep invocations (or two threads walking the same run dir) can both observe "no candidate" and both pick the same `candidate`, after which one `rename` silently overwrites the other's file. Use `O_EXCL`-style creation (e.g., `OpenOptions::new().write(true).create_new(true)`) or an atomic primitive; at minimum, hold a per-process lock around harvest+rename.

Failure paths in the harvest fallback are silently swallowed. If `rename` fails (e.g., EXDEV across devices) but `copy_rec` succeeds and `remove_rec` fails, the source file is left behind in the run dir with no audit entry — the `audit` callback only fires on success and only emits the success count. This masks data-integrity drift (growing run dirs across many runs). Either audit failures explicitly, or have `remove_rec` propagate the error and emit a `harvested={moved} failed={failed}` line.

`remove_rec` collapses every I/O failure to a `bool`. Callers cannot distinguish a permission error from a missing file or surface the underlying `io::Error`. Combined with the harvest fallback (which gates `remove_rec` on `copy_rec.is_ok()` and then drops the bool), this means partial state is invisible. Return `std::io::Result<()>` like `copy_rec` does, and have the caller propagate or log the error.

Both entry points bail on `read_dir` failure without recording anything. Permission denied, broken mount, or transient IO errors will be invisible to operators and to `py_audit`. At minimum, log/audit the read_dir error before returning so failures are diagnosable.

Silent swallow of `std::sync::Mutex` lock results. After the first panic-while-holding-lock, `register_exec_session` will fail to register (silently), `unregister_exec_session` will leak entries, and `is_task_execution_flow` will return `false` — which means tools downstream will conclude they are *not* running inside a task-card execution flow and may take an alternate (possibly unauthorised) code path with no log trace. Either propagate the error, or at minimum log the poisoned state (`tracing::error!`/`eprintln!`) so an operator can reset the registry.

`is_task_execution_flow` silently maps a poisoned-mutex lock to `false`. Because this function is the legality gate for `link_file_to_task`-style flows, returning `false` in a degraded state means tools will *miss* the legitimate execution-flow context and take the non-task branch — exactly the silent regression you cannot afford here. At least log/return `Result`, or document that callers must restart on poison.

`is_atomic_tool` is now a perpetually-false no-op because `ATOMIC_TOOLS` is empty. Every blacklist test (`create_word_revisions_is_not_atomic_anymore`, `atomic_blacklist_is_empty`, `single_point_tools_are_not_atomic`) asserts `!is_atomic_tool(...)` and passes trivially even if the entire atomic-tool enforcement path is removed or wired wrong — so reintroducing an atomic tool tomorrow will not be caught. Either delete the function outright, or change the tests to assert the *invariant* the design depends on (e.g. a snapshot of `ATOMIC_TOOLS`, or a property that no tool name in `tools::SCHEMA_LIST` appears in the blacklist) so the regression lock remains meaningful.

`SESSION_ORIGINS` is guarded by `std::sync::Mutex` and the comment claims "async context 里短临界区 OK". That justification is only valid if *every* call site is purely synchronous between `lock()` and the subsequent drop of the guard. Nothing here audits that — a future caller that adds `.await` between `register_exec_session` returning and the guard dropping (or that uses this from an async future across an await) will block the tokio runtime and surface as the silent-poison bug above. Either move to `tokio::sync::Mutex` if any caller is async, or add a `static_assertion`-style comment plus a debug check that the calling task is not inside a tokio worker.

`dead_command_bind_file_not_in_dispatcher` reads `src/bot.rs` and `src/bot_model_loop.rs` from disk on test execution with `unwrap()`, and matches a string that is hand-concatenated via `concat!` to dodge self-matching. Problems: (a) any non-functional reformatting (quote style, extra spaces, line breaks, comments) silently breaks the regression lock; (b) a missing/unreadable file panics the whole test binary instead of returning an actionable diagnostic for the offending path; (c) the test runs in `cargo test` and forces a `Cargo.toml`-relative path lookup that depends on the test runner's CWD. Either drive this from a single source-of-truth list (e.g. parse `tools.rs` / a generated registry) or guard each `read_to_string` separately so failures identify which file is missing.

`atomic_block_message` returns user-facing text that leaks internal refactor history ("黑名单已废弃，但保留该消息以兼容调用方"). Since `is_atomic_tool` is always false this function should be unreachable in production, but if it ever does fire the user sees a message about internal deprecation that contradicts the post-D4d semantics. Either delete the function (preferred — only one external caller in the test) or return a neutral message ("⚠️ {name} 不能直接调用，请通过对应的 Skill 使用") so accidental invocations do not advertise the blacklist status.

Vacuous camelCase assertion — `obj.contains_key("botAssigned") || !obj.contains_key("bot_assigned")` is always true in this test because `sample_task()` sets `bot_assigned: None`, which serde omits from the output entirely. The disjunction thus reduces to `true || true` regardless of whether `rename_all = "camelCase"` is actually applied. This defeats the file's stated purpose of "线缆形状契约锁" (per `docs/AUDIT-TESTS-2026-08-28.md:58`, this file was created specifically because earlier serde attribute breakages were undetectable). To actually pin camelCase, set `bot_assigned: Some(true)` (or any non-None value) in `sample_task()` so `bot_assigned` is present in the serialized object, then assert `obj.contains_key("botAssigned") && !obj.contains_key("bot_assigned")` (and ideally pin a few more field names like `filePath`/`fileIsDir`/`createdAt`/`updatedAt`/`deletedAt`/`expectedUpdatedAt`/`schedLast`/`completedAt`/`botAssigned` to catch any future rename regression).

Wasted heap allocation for `status` — `db::TaskStatus::as_str` (in `src-tauri/src/db/tasks.rs:42`) is `pub const fn as_str(&self) -> &'static str`, so `t.column.as_str().to_string()` performs a heap allocation on every event/task construction. In SSE/bulk-list paths that emit many `TaskOut`s this becomes measurable garbage. Since the wire form is the static str itself, store `Cow<'static, str>` (zero-cost for the common case, alloc only if a future variant ever needs runtime composition) or `&'static str` (with a lifetime on `TaskOut` if that fits the call sites). At minimum, change `status: String` to `status: Cow<'static, str>` and assign `Cow::Borrowed(t.column.as_str())` here.

Unnecessary full-task clone in `from_task` — the function takes `&db::Task` and immediately `t.clone()`s the entire task just to hand it to `TaskOut`. For SSE/event emission the caller already owns the task it is about to emit (and is throwing the clone away after serialization). Prefer one of: (a) `impl From<db::Task> for TaskOut` that moves the task in; (b) `pub fn from_task(t: &db::Task) -> Self` with `inner: db::Task` taken by value behind a helper, i.e. make `TaskOut::from(task)` consume the task; (c) `pub fn from_ref<'a>(t: &'a db::Task) -> TaskOut<'a>` with `inner: Cow<'a, db::Task>` so bulk emission borrows and individual emission can move. The current `&db::Task` + clone signature hides a per-event O(task-size) copy that becomes a hotspot when the API streams large task lists.

Implicit flatten + `status` collision contract on `db::Task` — `#[serde(flatten)] inner: db::Task` together with the explicit `pub status: String` field relies on `db::Task` never gaining a `status` member. Today that holds (verified by searching `db*.rs`), but there is no compile-time or test-time guard. If a future contributor adds `status: Option<String>` to `db::Task` (e.g. as a derived lifecycle field like the `evolution::change::record::ChangeRecord.status` pattern), serde will silently let `db::Task.status` shadow this field on serialize, and the API will start emitting whatever the new field contains — possibly None-skipped, possibly a different string — without any test firing. Consider either (a) adding an assert in this test that `db::Task` does NOT contain a `status` field via reflection over `serde_json::to_value(&sample_task())`, or (b) moving `status` into the flatten by giving `db::Task` an actual `status` accessor (Cow<'static, str>) so the wire shape is owned by the data layer and cannot diverge.
comments.existing_code:
#[derive(Serialize, Clone)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct TaskOut {
    #[serde(flatten)]
    pub inner: db::Task,
    pub status: String,
}

comments.content: ChildRegGuard/PY_CHILDREN use raw OS PIDs as the HashSet key. PIDs are reused by the kernel: after `kill_tree` kills and reaps a child, a freshly-spawned unrelated process can immediately acquire the same PID. When the original guard then drops, `remove(&self.0)` yanks the new process's PID from the registry (or leaves the orphan in there if it has not yet registered). Conversely, `kill_all_py_children`/`kill_py_children` may target a recycled PID and signal an unrelated process. Either key the registry on something stable (e.g., an opaque `Child` wrapper / generation counter / `Child::id()` paired with a unique guard id) or invalidate by the original handle rather than PID value alone.

`py_run_gate` poison is silently swallowed — logging is fine but the code then proceeds as if the lock were healthy. If the original holder panicked mid critical section (e.g., while another thread was already queued on the gate), subsequent "serialized" runs will run as if serialization is intact, masking a real concurrency bug and risking overlapping transient state. Consider returning a `CommandError` when poisoning is observed (at least on the gate, which is the only serialization point in the file), or use `parking_lot`/`try_lock` semantics so a poisoned mutex becomes visible to the caller.
comments.existing_code: let _gate = py_run_gate().lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!("[mutex_poisoned] py::runtime::py_run_gate: {e:?}"); e.into_inner() });

comments.content: Brittle control-flow assertion: the `for attempt in 0..2` loop is structured so that every iteration returns, but the trailing `unreachable!()` will panic the worker if the loop is later changed (e.g., switched to `while`, removed the `continue`, or extended to N attempts). Replace with an explicit error path (`Err(CommandError::DomainRule { ... })` with a "retry budget exhausted" message) or wrap in a helper that returns `Result` without the `unreachable` invariant.
comments.existing_code: unreachable!("最多 2 次尝试，循环内必然返回")

comments.content: The polling loop uses `std::thread::sleep(50ms)` synchronously, and `drain_output(&rx, Duration::from_secs(2))` blocks the calling thread for up to 2s after the child exits. `run_python` is invoked from Tauri command handlers (typically an async context), so this stalls the runtime thread for the entire timeout window plus drain window — concurrent UI/IPC work scheduled on the same executor is starved. Move the wait onto an async-friendly primitive (e.g., `child.wait()` in a `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, or expose async output drain) and remove the busy-polling `try_wait` loop.
comments.existing_code: std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));

comments.content: Same blocking-during-async concern as the sleep loop: `drain_output(&rx, Duration::from_secs(2))` performs a synchronous 2-second wait on the calling thread before falling through to `kill_tree`. Combined with the 50ms poll loop above, the entire `run_python_at` is effectively a 5+ minute blocking call when invoked from a Tauri async command, which is the documented hot path.
comments.existing_code:
let (stdout, mut stderr, drained, truncated) =
        crate::py::io::drain_output(&rx, Duration::from_secs(2));

comments.content: `setrlimit(RLIMIT_AS, ...)` and `setrlimit(RLIMIT_CPU, ...)` return values are discarded in the `pre_exec` closure — if the kernel refuses (capability, overcommit/RLIMIT_AS settings, ulimit inheritance), the child will execute with no enforced memory or CPU ceiling while `mem_limit_bytes`/`cpu_limit_secs`/the audit log imply otherwise. Check the return value (and at minimum emit an audit line via the `audit` closure if it fails) so callers can react when the resource-limit contract documented at the top of the file is not actually in force. Note that `RLIMIT_CPU` here also means the child is killed with SIGXCPU when it trips — neither condition is surfaced today.

`silent_cmd("kill").args(["-9", &format!("-{pid}")]).status()` synchronously forks+waits an external `kill` binary on the cleanup path. The caller is already inside a 50ms polling loop and a Tauri async command; this is a third blocking step on top of `child.kill()` + `child.wait()` in the same function, all on the runtime thread. Prefer `libc::kill(-pid, SIGKILL)` directly (this whole `kill_tree` already runs in a sync context) to drop the extra subprocess spawn cost and risk of `kill` itself hanging.

`kill_tree` and the post-drain `kill_tree(&mut child, &limits)` both invoke `limits.terminate()` (it's the first thing `kill_tree` does). On Windows that means a second `TerminateJobObject` call on the same handle; on Unix the second `kill -9` will ESRCH but still forks a process. Factor the killpg/TaskKill step into its own helper so callers don't double-terminate, and have `kill_tree` call that helper once.

Two tightly-coupled cleanup helpers have divergent bodies: `cleanup_after_fail` routes through `kill_tree` (which calls `limits.terminate()` then process-group/taskkill), while `cleanup_after_spawn_fail` calls `limits.terminate()` directly with no `child` to kill. After the refactor suggested in the previous comment, both should funnel through the same `kill_tree`-equivalent (no-op on the empty job) so the safety story in the module-level docstring ("kill_tree / ChildRegGuard / RunLimits 逻辑一字不动") stays accurate.

Each `scheduler_e2e_*` test binds `let _serial = SKILL_SCHED_TEST_LOCK.lock()` whose MutexGuard lives until end-of-function; every one of them then `.await run_skill_scheduler_core(...)` (and inside it `.await` mock executor + DB writes + bot.log writes) while still holding a `std::sync::Mutex`. Under tokio this blocks the worker thread for the entire awaited scheduler — and combined with `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`, a panic mid-scheduler silently discards the poisoned guard, allowing the next test into the critical section while the process-level SKILL_RUNS hook table still carries half-written state. Prefer a tokio `tokio::sync::Mutex` acquired only around the synchronous setup (test_hook_insert + log_offset + executor closure build), or scope `_serial` to a block that ends before the `.await`; and remove the `into_inner()` panic-recovery so a real failure surfaces instead of silently re-entering.

`pre_step_routes_installed_skill_intent_to_skill` mutates a process-global routes table via `intent_router::rebuild_routes(...)` and only resets it to `vec![]` after the `assert_eq!(s, "minimax-ppt", ...)` succeeds. A panic in the assertion (or in `run_pre_step` for fixture regressions) leaves the routes table populated with `minimax-ppt` intents for every later test in the same `cargo test` process — silently polluting other modules. Wrap the rebuild→assert→reset sequence in a `std::panic::catch_unwind` (or a small RAII guard struct whose Drop calls `rebuild_routes(vec![])`) so the global state is restored regardless of how the test exits.

`mock_handle()` does `Box::leak(Box::new(tauri::test::mock_app())).handle().clone()` on every invocation. The file calls it five times (one per test), and the four scheduler tests additionally drive `test_hook_insert_skill_run` / `test_hook_skill_run_state` against process-global SKILL_RUNS registers shared across the same binary. There is no per-app registry isolation — the serial Mutex is the only barrier — so a stale guard from an earlier interrupted test can surface in a later test via `test_hook_skill_run_state`. Cache a single `tauri::AppHandle<MockRuntime>` in a `OnceLock` (each test still clones the cheap handle) so the suite stops leaking a full Tauri app per test and the hook-table coupling becomes one-app-per-process instead of one-app-per-test.

`bot_log_tail_since(offset)` slices from a recorded byte offset and the assertions match prefixes like `skill_dsl_start | name: minimax-ppt | steps: 2`. If the log is truncated/rotated to a smaller size mid-test, `data[(offset as usize).min(data.len())..]` will begin mid-line and a previous run's tail can still contain a substring that matches the needle. There is no monotonic-id / sequence check to distinguish this test's writes from concurrent or historical ones; only the `SKILL_SCHED_TEST_LOCK` orders them. Either embed a unique tag in each test's invocation (e.g. append `format!("| run_id: {}", uuid)` to the DSL and assert on the full line) or read until EOF + assert line-by-line containing the tag, so rotation/truncation or interleaved writers fail loudly instead of silently passing on stale tails.

`fixtures_parent_path()` returns `tests/fixtures/` and three tests assert `skills.len() == 1` plus only `minimax-ppt` exists; `intent_rules_from_dirs` and `scan_skill_dirs` will also enumerate any future fixture dropped into the same directory. Adding a second fixture will silently break the `== 1` assertions and make `intent_rules_from_dirs` emit rules for skills no test asserts on, with no per-fixture filtering. Restrict the scans to `&[ppt_fixture_path()]` (single-skill paths), or assert `>= 1` and filter to `minimax-ppt` before checking length, so the suite stays green when more fixtures land in the directory.

In `scheduler_e2e_failed_step_runs_rollback_window`, the executor closure synchronously re-inserts a `Failed` run via `test_hook_insert_skill_run(&app, make_run(...))` while the test's outer `_serial` guard is held (and is itself called from inside `.await run_skill_scheduler_core`). This is intentionally inside the serial section, but it documents a sharp invariant: anyone adding a scheduler test must not call `test_hook_insert_skill_run` from inside the executor closure unless they hold `SKILL_SCHED_TEST_LOCK`. Add a comment near `test_hook_insert_skill_run` (or a `// SAFETY:`-style contract in this file's T1-2 banner) explicitly stating "must be called under SKILL_SCHED_TEST_LOCK; the executor closure in `scheduler_e2e_failed_step_runs_rollback_window` qualifies because it runs on the same task that acquired the lock before `.await`", so future test authors don't break the assumption.

`ConfigListenAddr::Unix` binds directly to the path without unlinking any pre-existing socket file. After a crash or unclean shutdown the stale socket remains on disk and `UnixListener::bind` returns `EADDRINUSE`/`EADDRNOTAVAIL`, preventing restart. This is a well-known Unix-socket footgun. Either `unlink` the path before `bind` (with appropriate safety checks) or document that the caller must remove stale sockets.

```rust
#[cfg(unix)]
Self::Unix(a) => {
    let _ = std::fs::remove_file(a); // tolerate ENOENT
    unix_net::UnixListener::bind(a).map(Listener::from)
}
```

`ConfigListenAddr::from_socket_addrs` unconditionally collects into a `Vec<SocketAddr>` even though the vast majority of callers supply a single address. For a config-time API this is acceptable, but the allocation is avoidable when only one address resolves. Consider a `try_from_socket_addr` fast path or, at minimum, use `Vec::with_capacity(1)` for the common single-address case to avoid a heap allocation on the hot config-init path.

Source-grep assertions in `scheduler_uses_run_task_in_chat_not_exec_steps` are brittle: the negative checks `!src.contains("exec_steps::start") && !src.contains("exec_steps::resume")` only catch the exact path-qualified token, so a renamed module (e.g. `exec_steps::spawn`), an aliased import (`use exec_steps::start as kickoff`), or a method-call form (`exec_steps.start()`) silently evades the test. Likewise `!bot_chat.contains("fn execute_task_core")` only rejects the bare `fn` definition; references via `super::execute_task_core`, `pub fn execute_task_core`, doc-comments, or re-exports pass through. The `notification()` substring check has the same problem (would also match in unrelated contexts). These tests verify source cosmetics rather than scheduler behavior — replace with a behavioral test (e.g. mock the scheduler entry and assert the call goes through `run_task_in_chat`) or, at minimum, anchor the assertions with surrounding tokens (e.g. `contains("exec_steps::start(")` or a `Regex`-based check that ignores comments).

`failure_persists_error_reply_in_session` identifies its session through `WHERE title LIKE '⏰ 定时：%'` + `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` instead of the session id returned by `run_task_in_chat_with`. The failure run returns `Err`, so capturing `session_id` requires plumbing it out of the error variant — but doing so is the only way to deterministically point at "this test's session". With LIKE matching, any leftover Scheduled-origin session from a prior run, a concurrent test, or a retry makes the assertions validate the wrong row, and the inline `DELETE` based on `WHERE title = ?1` then silently destroys unrelated data. Either return the created session id from the failure path (preferred) or use a unique title token per run (e.g. include the uuid task id in the title) so the lookup is unambiguous.

`Box::leak(Box::new(tauri::test::mock_app()))` is intentional but accumulates a full `tauri::App` allocation per test run (and is invoked once per `setup_task` call — i.e. at least three times for the current suite). Across `cargo test` runs and `--no-fail-fast` retries this leaks enough that long CI loops can OOM. Prefer an owned `tauri::test::mock_app()` returned by value (the type is `MockRuntime` and `'static`), or wrap it in a `Box<...>` dropped by a panic-safe guard. As a minimum, document the leak in the file header so the cost is visible.

Read-then-act race inside the source-grep test: the preamble claims "cargo 各测试二进制之间本就串行", but that is only true when `--test-threads=1` is *not* overridden; a developer running `cargo test -- --test-threads=4` will run this `#[test]` concurrently with the two `#[tokio::test]` cases above, both of which are still mutating the shared `wmessage.db`/`bot-enabled.flag` while this test reads `bot_scheduler.rs`. The source files themselves are static so the read is safe, but if any of the parallel `tokio::test`s panic mid-setup (e.g. assertion failure before reaching `cleanup`), the leaked rows will surface here as a confusing failure rather than as the original panic. Consider marking the test `#[ignore]` or folding it into the SERIAL-protected flow.

From<i32>/From<u32> for StatusCode silently truncate out-of-range values with `as u16`. `StatusCode::from(1_000_000_i32)` becomes a meaningless code (with no Result the caller can't detect the overflow) and gets propagated to every downstream consumer. Prefer `TryFrom<i32>` / `TryFrom<u32>` returning a `Result`, or use `u16::try_from` to validate the range at the conversion boundary.

From<i8>/From<i16>/From<i32> for StatusCode cast negative values directly to u16 via two's-complement wrap, so `StatusCode::from(-1_i8)` becomes `StatusCode(65535)` and `StatusCode::from(-1_i32)` becomes `StatusCode(0xFFFF)`. Negative HTTP codes are not defined; this conversion should reject them rather than wrap into an apparently valid but nonsensical status.

HeaderField::from_bytes only validates ASCII bytes via AsciiString::from_ascii and never rejects whitespace in the field name, while FromStr<HeaderField> does reject it. The `test_strict_headers` RUSTSEC-2020-0031 mitigation therefore only protects the FromStr path: callers that build a Header programmatically through Header::from_bytes can still inject field names like b"Transfer Encoding" (or with tabs), bypassing the smuggling defense at the construction boundary. Add a whitespace check before wrapping the AsciiString.

Header::from_bytes, Header::from_str and HeaderField::from_str all flatten their underlying error (`FromAsciiError` carrying the offending bytes, or `HeaderField::from_str`'s own whitespace check) into the unit type `()`. Callers cannot tell apart 'non-ASCII bytes', 'whitespace in field name' or 'missing/duplicated colon', which is a real loss of actionable context at the public library boundary. Expose a proper error enum (or re-export the inner error) so the different failure modes are distinguishable.

Pre-save deletion of old avatar files is a real data-loss path. The read_dir/remove_file loop runs BEFORE fs::copy and save_data; if save_data later fails, the previously-live avatar file is already gone from disk while the JSON on disk (never re-mutated) still references it. cleanup_set_avatar_failure only handles the just-copied dest, not the files already deleted in the loop — so a failure here silently drops the user's existing avatar and leaves a dangling JSON reference. The existing test set_avatar_save_failure_new_ext_removes_orphan only asserts the new file is gone and never checks the old one survives. Fix: defer the old-file cleanup until AFTER save_data succeeds, and either (a) track which files were targeted so they can be restored on failure, or (b) build dest as a new temp file and only rename it onto the live path after save_data, keeping the old file untouched until that point.

PROFILE_WRITE_LOCK is held across substantial blocking I/O — create_dir_all, read_dir + per-entry remove_file, fs::copy (up to 5MB), load_data (read_to_string + maybe rename), and atomic_write. A slow disk, antivirus, or panic in any of these stalls every concurrent profile command and is the only realistic way for this mutex to become poisoned (which the recovery below silently absorbs). Scope the lock tightly around just the JSON read-modify-write pair; perform the file-side operations (create_dir, copy, cleanup) either before acquiring the lock or in a separate critical section.

Same-extension save failure leaves a silent content swap. When the new avatar has the same extension as the live one, dest's path equals the live avatar name; fs::copy has already overwritten the on-disk bytes with the new image, and cleanup_set_avatar_failure correctly preserves dest — but the JSON still names the old avatar. The next profile_get will serve the new image bytes as if they were the old avatar. The caller gets an Err so the operation appears to have failed, yet the on-disk file is now new-content-under-old-name, which is at least as surprising as the current conservative cleanup. Either save the live avatar's bytes before copy and restore them on failure, or move the copy into a staging path (e.g. avatar-<kind>.new.<ext>) and only rename onto the live path after save_data succeeds.

Broadcast re-reads profile.json from disk and rebuilds the view, while the returned Ok(build_view(&app, &data)) reuses the just-saved local copy. The lock has already been released by the time broadcast runs, so another writer can intervene and the 'profile-changed' payload can diverge from the value the caller receives — inconsistent event semantics for any concurrent widget/listener. Also wastes one disk read per command. Build the view once from local data and emit that same value: let view = build_view(&app, &data); let _ = app.emit("profile-changed", &view); Ok(view).

`std::env::set_var` has been marked `unsafe fn` since Rust 1.86 (early 2025) due to data-race hazards with concurrent readers of the process environment. On any current toolchain this call will fail to compile (or trigger an error) unless wrapped in `unsafe { ... }`. Use a scoped alternative — e.g. spawn a subprocess via `Command::new(env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_<bin>"))` with `Command::env(...)`, or drive the test through a `#[ctor]`-free harness — instead of mutating the process-global environment.

Panics during normal teardown and risk of double-panic during stack unwinding: `Sender::send(()).unwrap()` will panic if the receiver has already been dropped (e.g., during server shutdown). Because `Drop for Request` may run while another panic is unwinding, this can abort the process — exactly in the failure-recovery path the doc comment promises will still send a 500 response. Use `self.sender.send(()).ok();` or check for disconnection, and consider a thread-local / catch_unwind guard for the auto-500 path.

Double-panic risk in `Drop for Request`: it calls `respond_impl`, which calls `extract_writer_impl` whose `assert!(self.response_writer.is_some())` will panic if the writer was already taken (e.g. via `upgrade` or `into_writer`). Combined with the `sender.send(()).unwrap()` in the same `drop`, a single failure can abort the whole process. The auto-500 cleanup path must not panic; use `if let Some(writer) = self.response_writer.take() { ... }` instead of going through `respond_impl`.

`Sender::send(()).unwrap()` in `respond` can panic after a successful response if the notify receiver has been dropped (e.g., server shutdown), masking the actual `Result<(), IoError>` with a panic. Use `let _ = sender.send(());` so the operation never panics.

Multiple `unwrap()`s on internal state in `as_reader` (`self.response_writer.as_mut().unwrap()` twice, `self.data_reader.as_mut().unwrap()`) can panic if the request has been partially consumed (e.g., after `into_writer`/`upgrade` or in error/panic paths). Since `as_reader` is `&mut self` and callable from arbitrary user code, these invariant panics turn ordinary state misuse into aborts. Use `if let`/`?` patterns or document the precondition more loudly.

`upgrade()` silently swallows I/O errors via `.ok()` on both the 101 response write and the flush. A failed protocol upgrade (e.g., broken pipe mid-101) becomes invisible to the caller, making protocol-handshake bugs hard to diagnose. Return the I/O error to the caller (or at minimum `eprintln!`/`log` it with context).

Unbounded blocking read of the declared body: the small-`Content-Length` branch loops on `source_data.read()` with no per-read deadline, no socket-level read timeout, and no per-iteration backoff. A peer that advertises a small `Content-Length` (≤ 1024 bytes) and then stalls will block the accepting thread forever — a classic slow-loris DoS. Enforce an overall timeout or a per-read deadline (e.g., rely on `set_read_timeout` on the underlying socket). The TODO on the `EqualReader` line shows the same concern for the larger branch.

The second tuple element returned by `EqualReader::new` is discarded (`let (data_reader, _) = ...`). Without seeing `EqualReader`'s definition, the existing TODO and the fact that the second value exists strongly suggest it holds a complementary side (writer/notifier/handle) that must be kept alive for the reader to function correctly. Dropping it can cause subtle bugs (data loss, deadlocks, or use-after-free) when reading the body. Hold onto it on the `Request` (e.g., `equal_writer: Option<...>`) or document why it is safe to drop.

`Transfer-Encoding` header value is cloned (`.map(|h| h.value.clone())`) only to test for `is_some()` later. Replace the clone with `is_some()` / `any()` to avoid an unnecessary `String` allocation per request.

The result is multi-line JSON inside `data: {...}` SSE events; line-based SSE parsers will split the `data:` line mid-JSON and produce malformed fragments, defeating the very regression baseline this fixture is supposed to validate. Use `serde_json::Value::to_string` (or at minimum a real JSON escaper that also handles `\n`/`\r`/`\t`/control chars) instead of two chained `String::replace` calls.

comments.content: `request_bodies()` stores captured request bodies via `String::from_utf8_lossy`, which silently substitutes `U+FFFD` for invalid UTF-8 bytes. The doc comment above explicitly calls this the *"memory regression baseline"* used to assert what gets sent to the LLM, so any invalid UTF-8 in the body (partial multi-byte chars, BOM fragments, exotic tool payloads, NULs in arguments) will produce a lossy string and tests can pass on corrupted data or fail spuriously on phantom replacement chars. Use `std::str::from_utf8` with explicit handling, or store raw `Vec<u8>` and let assertions decode — also note the *same* lossy conversion is used for the request line, which is even more lossy-sensitive because header lines are required to be ASCII.

Multiple `.unwrap()` on `Mutex::lock()` results inside the server thread (`behaviors`, `bodies`, `paths`). Because this file is `include!`'d into other test modules (see the E0753 note at the top of the file), a panic while holding one of these mutexes poisons it and every subsequent `lock().unwrap()` cascades into another panic — the server thread dies silently (`_handle` is dropped without being joined), and tests that send more requests hang on `read_to_string` waiting for a response that will never come. Either replace with `lock().expect("mock_llm mutex poisoned")` for actionable diagnostics, or recover from poisoning via `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`, so one bad request does not kill the whole fixture.

Split variant handling combined with `unreachable!()` is a maintenance hazard. `FragmentedTextReply` is serialized outside `build_http_response` (in the connection-handler dispatch), `AnthropicJsonReply` is in a separate outer match arm, and the inner match falls through to `_ => unreachable!()`. Any new `MockBehavior` variant requires touching both the connection-handler dispatch and the response builder, or it will panic at runtime the first time a test pushes one. The same fragility applies to the outer `match behavior` — `HttpError` and `AnthropicJsonReply` are special-cased and the `_ => { let body = match behavior { ... } }` path silently relies on the inner `unreachable!()` to catch omissions. Replace the `unreachable!()` with an exhaustive match over a helper method like `fn body_bytes(&self) -> Cow<[u8]>` (or at minimum list every variant explicitly in the catch-all arm) so adding a variant is a compile error rather than a runtime panic.

comments.content: `num_connections` is a `pub fn` whose body is `unimplemented!()`, so any caller aborts the process. This is a soundness bug at the crate boundary, not just missing implementation: either the method must return a real value (e.g. by tracking clients via the messages queue / TaskPool) or be removed/feature-gated until the count is wired up.

The HTTPS branch uses `receiver.recv().unwrap()` after pushing each Request. The Request holds one end of `sender` via `with_notify_sender`; if the consumer drops the Request without responding (e.g. after `Server::unblock`, after `recv()` is told the queue is unblocked, or any error path that discards the Request), every clone of `sender` is dropped, `recv()` returns `Err(RecvTimeoutError::Disconnected)`, and `unwrap()` panics inside the `tasks_pool.spawn` closure. A single dropped/short-circuited HTTPS request kills the worker handling that connection, and because there is no task supervision the failure is silent.

Any error from `server.accept()` is logged, pushed exactly once into the messages queue, and then `break`s out of the accept loop, terminating the accept thread permanently. After the single error is consumed by a caller, the messages queue stays empty while the accept thread is dead, so subsequent `recv()`/`recv_timeout()` calls block forever — the server is effectively dead even though `unblock()` was never called and no shutdown was requested. This is a real availability bug for transient accept errors (e.g. `EMFILE`, `ENFILE`, `EINTR` after a noisy signal), not just fatal ones.

Panic-during-drop bug: in `Drop`, the Unix branch does `addr.as_pathname().unwrap()`. `as_pathname()` returns `None` for any Unix socket that is not bound to a filesystem path (Linux abstract namespace sockets, unnamed/bindless sockets). When the listener was bound that way, dropping the `Server` will `unwrap()` a `None` and abort the process from inside a destructor — exactly the situation where panicking is most harmful (it can prevent other fields from being dropped and chain into a double-panic abort).

`IncomingRequests::next` maps every `Err` from `recv()` — including the `Message::Error` produced when the accept thread dies — to `None`. Consumers iterating `server.incoming_requests()` therefore cannot distinguish a clean `unblock()` / `Drop` from a silently-broken server that has already enqueued its one and only accept error. Either surface the error (e.g. make `IncomingRequests::Item` a `Result<Request, IoError>` or store the last error) or call this out in the docs.

All best-effort cleanup in `Drop` discards errors: the self-connect probe, the resulting `Connection::shutdown(Shutdown::Both)`, and the Unix socket file removal. If the probe fails (e.g. the listener has not started accepting yet, the local network is unreachable, or the listen addr is loopback-only and the OS briefly rejects `connect`), the accept thread keeps blocking on `accept()` and the `Drop` itself blocks until that thread finally exits — i.e. `Server::drop` is not actually best-effort. Worse, on Unix a stale socket file from a previous crash will be silently left on disk when `remove_file` fails (e.g. permission denied, ENOENT), causing the next `bind()` of the same path to fail. Log at least the cleanup failures and consider polling close_trigger before the probe so Drop does not block forever.

SSL handshake errors are silently discarded with `Err(_) => continue`. In production this means a misconfigured certificate, a client speaking an unsupported TLS version, or a peer that disconnects mid-handshake looks identical to "no clients" in the logs — there is no way to tell why HTTPS requests stopped arriving. Log at least at debug/warn level so failures are observable.

The `additional_headers` channel is drained at construction time (before the response is ever sent), which contradicts the documented contract that the receiver "may provide headers even after the response has been sent". The marked `// dummy implementation` suggests this was never finished. Consequences: (1) any sender that intentionally waits for the response to be flushed before pushing trailing headers will block `Response::new` forever, and (2) headers that arrive on the channel after `new()` returns are silently dropped. The receiver should be stored on `Response` and drained after the headers/body have been written (or at minimum, the documentation should be corrected to reflect that this parameter is currently a no-op prefetch).

`raw_print` hard-codes `has_additional_headers: false /* TODO */`, which makes the "if we have additional headers, using chunked" branch in `choose_transfer_encoding` unreachable. Per RFC 7230 §4.1, trailing headers can only be sent when the body is framed with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. If the trailing-headers feature is ever wired up without also fixing this flag, responses with trailing headers would be framed with `Content-Length` and the trailer section would be parsed by the client as part of the body, producing a malformed/cut-off response.

Invalid `Content-Length` header values are silently swallowed (`if let Ok(val) = usize::from_str(...)`), so a malformed or negative/overflowing value from the caller produces no diagnostic and the header is dropped without ever being added to the response. A caller passing `Content-Length: -1` or `Content-Length: 99999999999999999999` will see no error and the response will be framed without a content-length, falling back to chunked or an unbounded read. Consider returning a `Result` from `add_header`, or at minimum logging/tracing the dropped header.

The `assert!(data_length.is_some())` followed by `unwrap()` encodes a fragile invariant: it only holds because the earlier `(self.data_length, transfer_encoding)` match arm guarantees `data_length = Some(l)` whenever `transfer_encoding == Some(TransferEncoding::Identity)`. The two code paths are non-adjacent and any future refactor of the buffering match (e.g. adding another `Identity`-producing branch, or re-introducing Identity for the upgrade path) would silently panic in `raw_print` at request time rather than failing at compile time. Consider propagating this as an `unreachable!` with a justification, or restructuring so the value is destructured once and reused.
Spelling error in the public module-level rustdoc: `Reponse` should be `Response`. Downstream Tauri users browsing this vendored crate's docs will see the misspelling.

Grammar/tense error in the public rustdoc for `with_chunked_threshold`: `where we chose chunked transfer` should be `where we choose chunked transfer` (present tense, since this describes the API behavior, not a past event).

Fused state is only entered on a 0-byte (EOF) read; the `?` operator propagates `Err` without dropping the inner reader. As a result, once the inner reader starts returning errors, every subsequent `read`/`read_vectored` will keep retrying the same broken source and surface the same error repeatedly, instead of being "fused" in the sense of becoming an inert, empty stream. If a transient `WouldBlock`/interrupted error is the concern, consider a configurable policy (or at least documenting that errors are not terminal), so callers know not to treat the wrapper as fully fused across errors.

The derives `Clone, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash` are very restrictive for what is essentially a thin, stateful wrapper around any `R: Read`. Each derive forces `R` to implement the corresponding trait, so `FusedReader<File>`, `FusedReader<TcpStream>`, etc. become unusable even though they are perfectly fine as readers. Ordering/equality on a reader wrapper is also semantically meaningless (two readers at different stream positions aren't really comparable). Consider dropping `PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash` entirely, and possibly `Clone` unless cloning the inner reader is a real use case.

`into_inner` is annotated `#[allow(dead_code)]`, which means nothing in this crate actually exercises it but the lint is being suppressed. For a vendored upstream module it may simply be part of the upstream's public API surface, but it is worth confirming the suppression is still warranted: if no caller in this crate (and no documented external consumer) relies on it, the method and the suppression are dead weight that can be removed.

The `Read::read` impl forwards directly to `self.reader` without ever touching `self.writer`. For full-duplex streams where the writer side is buffered (e.g. `BufWriter` over a TCP socket, a pipe, or a child's stdio), there is no way for a caller to flush the bundled writer before issuing a read through the `Read` interface. Because the `writer` field is private, the only way to flush is the awkward workaround `s.write(&[]).ok(); s.flush()?;`, which is easy to forget and makes buffered writes invisible to the peer at the moment the next read happens. Consider exposing a `flush_writer(&mut self)` (or making the writer accessible) so callers can express flush-before-read semantics through the wrapper.

The public `CustomStream` struct has no `Debug` (or any other standard) derive. Any error/panic message, log line, or test assertion failure that mentions a `CustomStream<R, W>` will print only the type name with no field information, which makes diagnosing connection-handling bugs in the surrounding HTTP server code much harder. Adding `#[derive(Debug)]` (gated on `R: Debug, W: Debug` via a manual impl if needed) would materially improve observability at the crate boundary.

The `From` conversion destructively mutates its input: it walks `mock.headers` with `iter_mut()` and pushes a synthetic `Content-Length` when the field is absent. While this is safe (the value is moved into the function), a `From` impl is conventionally a pure transformation and this surprising side effect is hard to discover from a call site. Consider handling the default header inside `new_request` (or a small helper) so `From` stays a pure conversion, or document the mutation explicitly.

`with_header` unconditionally appends to the header vector, so multiple calls (or a single user-supplied `Content-Length` followed by another header) can produce duplicate fields. That is semantically wrong for singletons like `Content-Length` and can silently mask test bugs. Either replace an existing header with the same `HeaderField`, or document that duplicates are intentional and make sure `new_request` tolerates them.

The conversion ends in `new_request(...).unwrap()`. If `new_request` ever rejects an input this test helper supplied (malformed path, weird `HTTPVersion`, etc.) the caller gets a bare panic with no actionable context. Test code is allowed to panic, but `expect("test request must be valid")` (or making `From` fallible via `TryFrom`) would make a test failure much easier to diagnose.

comments.content: `Default::default()` hard-codes `127.0.0.1:23456` via `parse().unwrap()`. This embeds a magic port into every test request, which is brittle (and a future maintainer editing the literal could end up with a confusing panic if it ever becomes invalid). Consider using `SocketAddr::from(([127,0,0,1], 0))` so the port is left unspecified and never collides with real services.

The Drop implementation only signals on error or premature EOF, but never on the success paths. If `self.size` is already 0 when Drop runs (the common case where the caller fully consumed the limit), the while loop never executes and no signal is sent. Likewise, if the drain completes normally (the source returned enough bytes to satisfy `self.size`), the loop exits without signaling. In both cases the receiver will block forever waiting for a notification that the drain finished, which contradicts the documented contract of handing a receiver to the caller. The receiver should be guaranteed a single terminal signal (success or failure) once `EqualReader` is dropped.

The destructor allocates `vec![0; remaining_to_read]`, a buffer the size of the remaining byte budget on every loop iteration. `remaining_to_read` originates from caller-supplied input (e.g. HTTP `Content-Length`), which can easily be hundreds of MB or more, so dropping `EqualReader` can attempt to allocate gigabytes at once and panic the process before any progress is made. A bounded scratch buffer (e.g. 4–8 KiB) iterated until the drain completes is sufficient and avoids any large allocation in the destructor.

            let to_read = remaining_to_read.min(buf.len());

Renaming to something like `drop_signal` (and documenting that it carries the terminal result of the destructor drain) makes the lifecycle explicit.

comments.content: `remaining_to_read -= other` performs unchecked subtraction in the destructor. The `std::io::Read` contract says a well-behaved implementation will not return more bytes than the buffer size, but `EqualReader` is generic over `R: Read` and any third-party or custom reader that violates that contract will cause a panic in `Drop`. Use saturating arithmetic (or cap `other` against `remaining_to_read`) so a misbehaving reader cannot abort the process during teardown.

`Stream::clone` calls `tcp_stream.try_clone().unwrap()`. `try_clone` returns an `IoResult` because the underlying `dup`/`DuplicateHandle` syscall can fail (EMFILE/ENFILE on Unix, resource exhaustion on Windows, or an invalid socket). Panicking on this path crashes every worker thread that splits a stream into read/write halves via `RefinedTcpStream::new`, turning a recoverable I/O failure into a process abort. Propagate the error or fall back to a non-cloning design (e.g., share an `Inner` via `Arc` and forward shutdown to one owner on Drop).

Both shutdown calls in `Drop` discard their `IoResult` via `.ok()`. Drop cannot return errors, but unconditionally swallowing them hides broken-pipe / not-connected conditions that may indicate a real bug (e.g. a half that was supposed to stay open being closed early, or a peer that already terminated). At minimum, log the error through the crate's logger so the failure is observable; ideally gate the `ok()` behind a feature flag if the maintainers genuinely want silence in release builds.

`RefinedTcpStream::secure` is declared `pub(crate)` but is not referenced anywhere inside this module. Without a call site, it either is dead code (invite drift) or is consumed elsewhere in the crate; either way, leaving an unused access path on a public(-ish) surface complicates future refactors. Verify callers and either remove it or note its purpose with a doc comment.

from_pem is declared to return `Result`, but `pkcs8_private_keys(...).expect(...)` panics on a recoverable parse failure (e.g. malformed PEM, encrypted PKCS#8 key). The function should propagate the underlying error via `?` (mapping `rustls_pemfile::Error` into the boxed error) so misconfigured TLS material doesn't crash the process during startup. The docstring in the panic message ("encrypted keys are not supported") also does not match what is actually being checked.

If the input is not a PKCS#8 key and the RSA parser returns an empty `Vec` (non-PKCS#8, non-RSA, encrypted, or simply malformed input), `rsa_keys[0].clone()` panics with index-out-of-bounds even though the preceding `expect` already succeeded. There is also no check that the file contained *any* parseable private key before indexing. Both branches must validate `is_empty()` and surface a real `Err`, rather than indexing blindly.

`private_key.clone()` deep-copies a `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` (private key material) just to immediately re-borrow it as `&mut [u8]`. `rustls_pemfile` only needs a mutable slice of the bytes, so `private_key.as_slice()` (or `&mut *private_key`) is sufficient. Cloning here doubles the lifetime of sensitive bytes in heap memory and partially defeats the `Zeroizing` wrapper.

Every `Mutex::lock()` site uses `.expect("Failed to lock SSL stream mutex")`, so a poisoned mutex panics in library code during `Read::read`, `Write::write`/`flush`, `peer_addr`, and `shutdown` instead of returning `io::Error`. Poisoning on the *write* path is particularly bad: if a reader thread panicked mid-read, every subsequent `write`/`flush` from request handlers aborts the process. Prefer mapping `PoisonError` into `io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::Other, "ssl stream mutex poisoned")` (or similar) so callers can handle it.

comments.content: `ServerConfig::builder().with_safe_defaults().with_no_client_auth().with_single_cert(...)` is the rustls 0.20 API. `with_safe_defaults` was deprecated in 0.21 and the entire builder was replaced by `with_safe_default_protocol_versions()` + a typed `ConfigBuilder` in 0.22/0.23. With current rustls this file will no longer compile, and the "safe defaults" implicitly include cipher suites/versions that newer rustls no longer enables. Migrate to the explicit `ServerConfig::builder_with_protocol_versions(...).with_no_client_auth().with_single_cert(...)` form.

The struct doc-comment claims the `Mutex` exists "to permit disparate reader & writer threads to access the stream independently." In practice the lock forces `read`/`write`/`flush` to serialize strictly, which is required by `rustls::StreamOwned` but contradicts "independently." Either tighten the comment (e.g. "to give cloned `RustlsStream` handles exclusive access to the inner stream") or — if true concurrency is desired — split into separate `rustls::ServerConnection` halves (read-only `Reader` + write `Writer`) so an in-flight read no longer blocks writes.

pop_timeout passes the original `timeout` on every iteration of the wait loop, not the recomputed remaining `duration`. Any spurious wakeup (or empty-queue retry) resets the wait to the full requested timeout, so the function can block for multiples of `timeout` instead of at most `timeout`. Replace `wait_timeout(queue, timeout)` with `wait_timeout(queue, duration)` and recompute `duration` before each wait so the loop honors the cumulative deadline.

Every `Mutex::lock()` / `Condvar::wait()` / `Condvar::wait_timeout()` call uses `.unwrap()`, so once the mutex is poisoned (e.g. by a panic in a guarded code path) every subsequent `push`, `unblock`, `pop`, `try_pop`, and `pop_timeout` panics with a poisoned-mutex message instead of returning a recoverable error. In a library, prefer propagating `PoisonError` (or document the invariant and keep this in mind for callers).

comments.content: `unblock()` unconditionally appends a new `Control::Unblock` to the deque rather than coalescing or checking whether one is already queued. Repeated `unblock()` calls (or an `unblock()` interleaved with pushes) leave `Control::Unblock` markers in the deque that each cause `pop`/`try_pop`/`pop_timeout` to return `None` once before any later `Elem` is delivered, which is non-obvious and can lead to lost work or confusing shutdown behavior. Either coalesce consecutive `Unblock` markers or document the semantics clearly.

`with_capacity` returns `Arc<MessagesQueue<T>>`, which silently imposes `T: Send` (the `Mutex<VecDeque<Control<T>>>` must be both `Send` and `Sync` for the `Arc` to be `Send`). The bound is correct, but neither it nor the `Send + Sync` requirement on `MessagesQueue<T>` is documented, surprising callers who try to enqueue non-`Send` payloads. Document the threading contract on the type and/or on `with_capacity`.

`Ssl::new(&self.0).expect(...)` panics inside `OpenSslContext::accept`, which is a public library entry point whose signature already returns `Result<_, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync + 'static>>`. If `SslContextBuilder::build()` ever fails to produce a context from which `Ssl::new` can allocate (e.g. an OpenSSL version/runtime mismatch or resource exhaustion), the entire caller crashes instead of receiving a recoverable error. Use `?` / `map_err` so the failure propagates through the existing `Result` return type.

comments.content: `SplitOpenSslStream` does not document why a shared mutable `OpenSslStream` is necessary (it's because `SslStream` is `!Sync` and we want split read/write halves), and the field is a bare `Arc<Mutex<...>>` newtype tuple struct. Expose either a doc comment explaining the invariant or wrap the inner stream so the mutex isn't part of the public-looking surface; right now the tuple-struct field makes it trivial to clone the handle and break the abstraction later.

Every `SplitOpenSslStream` method (`peer_addr`, `shutdown`, `read`, `write`, `flush`) calls `self.0.lock().unwrap()`. If any caller panics while the mutex is held, the mutex becomes poisoned and every subsequent I/O on this stream panics instead of returning a recoverable error. Use `lock().expect("non-poisoned")` at minimum, or convert the lock error into `std::io::Error::other(...)` so callers see the real failure.

The `Read`/`Write` impls on `SplitOpenSslStream` repeat the same `self.0.lock().unwrap()` pattern. In addition to the poisoning issue, this holds a synchronous `std::sync::Mutex` guard across the entire OpenSSL I/O call, so these methods must not be invoked from an async runtime context without an off-thread bridge. Apply the same lock-error handling here and consider documenting the synchronous-I/O contract on `SplitOpenSslStream`.

SequentialReader::read panics on `recv().unwrap()` in the `Waiting` branch. A `std::sync::mpsc::Receiver` returns `Err(RecvError)` whenever the corresponding sender has been dropped, but here the error is unwrapped, so any out-of-order drop or interrupted handoff turns an ordinary I/O sequencing error into a panic in the middle of `read`. Return `Err(io::ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof.into())` (or similar) instead of unwrapping, and consider a try_recv loop to surface the disconnection deterministically.

comments.content: SequentialReader's `Drop` calls `recv().unwrap()` while holding the `Waiting` receiver. If the predecessor's sender is dropped without delivering (e.g. that predecessor panicked in its own drop, or the chain is torn down out of order) this panics during unwind — aborting the process or masking the original failure. Worse, if the predecessor is still alive but not yet dropping, this blocks the current thread inside `drop`, deadlocking cleanup. Forward the predecessor's reader through a `try_recv`/timeout, or thread the receiver into the next `SequentialReader` so the handoff never has to block during destruction.

SequentialWriter::write and SequentialWriter::flush both `recv().unwrap()` on the trigger channel. If the previous writer's `on_finish` sender has been dropped (chain torn down, or its `Drop` already fired), `recv()` returns `Err` and the unwrap converts a recoverable sequencing violation into a panic in the middle of a normal write/flush. Handle the error and translate it to an `io::Error`, or use `try_recv` with backoff before giving up.
Same `recv().unwrap()` panic hazard as `write`: a disconnected trigger panics the caller of `flush`, which is meant to be a recoverable operation. Convert the disconnect into an `io::Error` instead.

`Write::write` and `Write::flush` hold the `Mutex` guard across the underlying `write`/`flush` call. If `W` is a blocking sink (pipe, socket, file with backpressure, etc.), every other `SequentialWriter` sharing this `Arc<Mutex<W>>` stalls for the entire duration of the syscall. For typical sequential usage you don't actually need a `Mutex` at all — each stage owns the writer exclusively for its lifetime — consider moving ownership of `W` between stages (the same way the `SequentialReader` chain moves `R`) and dropping the lock entirely.

In a multi-stage writer pipeline one stage's panic will poison the mutex and turn every subsequent stage's write/flush into a panic too, instead of an `Err(PoisonError)`. Either clear the poison with `lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` or surface a proper `io::Error`.

comments.content: Both `MyTurn` and `Waiting` branches of `SequentialReader`'s `Drop` use `self.next.send(...).ok()`. If the successor receiver has already been dropped (e.g. the builder was discarded before the next stage was consumed) the underlying `Read` is silently discarded. At minimum, log the failure or surface it; ideally detect the disconnection and propagate the reader rather than relying on `ok()` to mask data loss.

`SequentialWriter::drop` swallows `self.on_finish.send(()).ok()`. If the next stage's receiver is gone, the "I am finished" signal is lost and the next writer's first `write` will block forever waiting for a signal that will never arrive. Detect the disconnected receiver and either skip the send (which will surface as the panic in `write`) or replace the trigger field so the next stage does not block on a dead channel.

`Drop for TaskPool` does not actually wait for the worker threads to finish. The `JoinHandle` returned by `thread::spawn` in `add_thread` is discarded immediately, so `TaskPool::drop` returns while workers can still run for up to ~5s (the `wait_timeout` duration), and the `Arc<Sharing>` clone held by each worker keeps `Sharing` (and any captured closures) alive long after the `TaskPool` itself is gone. There is also no way for a caller to await in-flight tasks. A correct shutdown should store `JoinHandle`s (e.g., `Mutex<Vec<JoinHandle<()>>>` on `Sharing`) and join them in `Drop`, or signal shutdown and join with a bounded timeout.

Using `999_999_999` stored into `active_tasks` as a kill signal is a code smell: it conflates "number of live workers" with "shutdown requested", and the worker loop's branch on `active_tasks <= MIN_THREADS` becomes load-bearing for shutdown semantics. It also makes the design fragile (any future code that legitimately grows the counter past that sentinel would silently break shutdown). Replace with a dedicated `AtomicBool` (or `Receiver<()>`) shutdown flag that the worker loop checks explicitly.

TOCTOU race in `spawn`: the `waiting_tasks == 0` check is performed outside (or in parallel with) any synchronization with respect to other `spawn` callers, so two concurrent callers with no idle workers can both observe `0` and both call `add_thread`, producing a redundant worker that will sit idle until its 5s `wait_timeout` fires. The "push vs. spawn" decision should be made under the `todo` mutex (combined with an `is_empty()` check on the queue) so the two outcomes are mutually exclusive.

`fetch_add`/`fetch_sub` on `active_tasks` and `waiting_tasks` use `Ordering::Release`, but these are standalone observability counters that do not publish or synchronize with any other data — there is no acquire-load that needs to pair with them. `Ordering::Relaxed` is sufficient and more accurately expresses the intent. The `Acquire` load of `active_tasks` in the worker loop is fine (and pairs correctly with the `Release` store in `Drop`, though even that pair isn't strictly needed for a pure counter).

`MIN_THREADS` is declared as `static` but is a compile-time literal with no interior mutability, no fixed-address requirement, and no need for linkage. `const` is the idiomatic form for plain numeric constants in Rust and avoids the implicit promotion to a global memory location.

comments.content: `args?: string` is a leaky abstraction. Tool call arguments are structured payloads (the file's own JSDoc on `SkillFailure` describes JSON-shaped step summaries flowing over the same channel), but typing them as `string` silently forces every consumer to `JSON.parse`, loses type information on the argument shape, and pushes parsing-error handling into renderer code. Prefer `args?: Record<string, unknown>` (or `unknown` with a narrowing helper) so consumers can rely on structured access and parsing failures surface as type errors at the boundary.
